en: Preface to the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules for the Zen Garden), compiled by the Dharma-transmitting Master Cijue, Zongze,
while serving as Abbot of the Shifang Hongji Chan Monastery in Zhending Prefecture.
Although the examples within the Chan school do not differ from the Vinaya in their fundamental principles, the internal customs of the patch-robed monks follow a distinct set of regulations.

If these are put into practice on one's journey, they naturally result in an extraordinary purity and loftiness; conversely, if one encounters them with a wall-like obstruction, it truly diminishes the respect of others.
Therefore, all the eminent practitioners have collectively deliberated and gathered examples from every quarter, so that whatever may be of benefit to present-day practitioners [is hereby compiled].
I have heard that all these matters have been fully set forth in the *Gangmu*. Alas! The news from Shaolin is already like carving a wound out of flesh;

the regulations of Baizhang may be called a set of new rules established ex nihilo. How much more so when the monastic groves have proliferated and become increasingly untenable, and furthermore, when laws and decrees have multiplied, resulting in even more complications?
Nevertheless, one must adorn the monastic community and erect the banner of the Dharma; this is the work of Buddha.

It is not permissible for even one section to be missing from among these gates. This is just as with the Bodhisattva’s Three Collections (Tri-saṃgraha) or the Śrāvaka’s Seven Sections (Saptādhikaraṇa).

How could it be that the establishment of the Dharma values complexity? Rather, the teachings are formulated according to the capacities of beings. May beginners and those of later study examine this well; may those of superior virtue and lofty character deign to provide verification.
Preface written on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the second year of Chongning.
The previous edition of this collection circulated widely in the world; however, it was regrettable that its characters had become worn and blurred.

I have now transcribed them again in large characters and carved them into woodblocks for transmission. May those who receive this work examine it with care. Respectfully submitted by the Imperial Preceptor Yu Ba on the Renxu year of Jiatai.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time all declared that one must leave the household life to achieve the Way. Among the twenty-eight patriarchs of India and the six patriarchs of the Tang land who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal, all were śramaṇas.
This is because it is only by strictly purifying the *vinaya* that one can establish the great model for the three realms.

Thus, while practicing Chan and seeking the Way, the precepts must come first. Since they are not for the purpose of merely avoiding faults or preventing transgressions, how could one thereby become a Buddha or a Patriarch?

Regarding the method of receiving the precepts: one should prepare the three robes, the alms bowl, and other requisites, as well as new and clean clothing. If new clothes are unavailable, they should be washed and dyed until clean.
When entering the altar to receive the precepts, one must not borrow robes or bowls; one must focus the mind with single-minded concentration and exercise great care.

Do not let your attention wander. One who possesses the physical form and deportment of a Buddha and observes the Buddha’s precepts attains the Buddha’s enjoyments. This is no small matter; how could it be treated with a casual mind?

If one merely borrows robes and bowls, even if they ascend the altar to receive the precepts, they will not obtain them. If one does not increase their vows through formal reception, they remain a person without precepts for their entire life.
They would then improperly occupy the gates of the Dharma and vainly consume the offerings of the faithful. Thus begins the entry into the Path for those of initial resolve.

You are not yet familiar with the Dharma; it was not my intention as your teacher to lead you into this state. My current bitter words are offered in the hope that you will engrave them in your heart.
Having already received the śrāvaka precepts, you ought now to receive the bodhisattva precepts; this is the gradual entry into the Dharma.
After receiving the precepts, one should constantly guard them. It is better to die with the Dharma than to live without it.
For example, in the Small Vehicle’s *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, two *aniyata* offenses, and thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
The ninety *pāyattika* rules, the four *pratideśanīya* rules, the one hundred *śaikṣa* rules, and the seven methods for settling disputes;

as well as the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the Mahāyāna *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: all must be recited until they are thoroughly mastered. One must have a clear understanding of what constitutes an offense (*āpatti*) and its non-offense (*anāpatti*), as well as the conditions for permission (*kṣepa*) and prohibition (*niṣedha*).
Rely solely upon the holy words spoken from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha]; do not arbitrarily follow the common crowd. For example, regarding the prohibition on eating [onions and leeks...]

One should not consume garlic, onions, scallions, wine, meat, fish, rabbit, or dairy products such as cheese, ghee, and curd; nor should one eat locusts, eggs, or the fat of pigs and sheep. Even when encountering circumstances of illness, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever violate the prohibitions by consuming wine, meat, or worldly flavors.

Regarding eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana*): small meals, medicinal stones, fruits, rice drinks, bean soups, vegetable juices, and the like—any food other than those consumed during the two designated times of the fast (*upavāsa*) and the morning meal—are considered food at improper times and should be strictly avoided.

The calamities of wealth and sensual desire are more dangerous than venomous snakes; one must distance oneself from them even further. One should regard all sentient beings with compassion, as if they were one's own children.
My son, let your speech be truthful and let your mind and mouth be in accord. Recite the Mahāyāna sūtras to support the practice of your vows.
When the *śīla* (precepts) are pure, the Buddha-dharma will manifest before you. If the hide does not exist, where can the fur be attached? Therefore, a sūtra says:
"To diligently uphold the pure precepts is like guarding a bright pearl."
Discriminating the Requisites for Entering the Forest: First, one discriminates the requisites, namely:

the mountain hat (*sanka*), the staff (*zhuzhang*), the ritual knife (*jiedao*), the *cibu* (monastic administrative) cylinder, the bowl bag, the shoe bag (inside which a strip of cloth is placed to serve as a foot-cloth), the pillow, the bell-mouthed shoes with laces, and the front and back head-wraps.
A double-layered wrapping of white silk; a wrapping for the sash; a pillow bag; a covering bag; a small oil cloth; a persimmon-oil cloth; a cotton bedding cloth; a cotton quilt;
three pure towels (one for covering the quilt, one for eating, and one for general use); a small water flask; a bath towel; a bathing skirt; a chest or cabinet with a small lock;
and tea utensils along with other articles of clothing—all these should be provided according to the family’s means, whether abundant or modest.

Before packing, place the monastic robes (enshrined in handkerchiefs) inside the front pack, wrapped within the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). The *pian-shan* (side-garment), *jia-ao* (lined jacket), or *bei-xin* (vest) should be pure garments and placed in the front pack.
In the rear pack, place the bedding, cotton clothing, and undergarments; these should be contact garments (*spṛṣṭa-cīvara*).

For items of this kind, first wrap them repeatedly with white silk and place them inside a bag. Place the bath towel and bathing skirt within the pillow bag, and place the sacred image and scripture within the hat.
Regarding the method for packing such tea utensils and other items: one should fasten the skirt over the outer robe (*pianshan*).
First secure the front pack, next tie the pillow pack, then fasten the rear pack, and finally loop it over the right shoulder.
Hang the alms bowl under the left armpit with the opening facing the body; next, drape it over the left shoulder. Hang the shoe bag under the right armpit.

First, insert the ritual knife (kaṭhina-dhāraṇī) under the right armpit; next, insert the *cibu* tube under the left armpit (the *cibu* bag is secured over the shoulder with a cord or strap, and another strip of cord or strap is used to tie it horizontally around the waist.

If the rear pack has not yet been tied, secure it first with this [horizontal strap]. Then, turn the *cibu* tube upside down and lift it up before placing on the rear pack—this is even more convenient).

Next, fasten the carrying strap (then insert the pillow, tea cylinder, and water flask onto the strap. Place them on the left and right sides of the bundle in front). Regarding the method for wearing the rain hat: with the right hand, hold the brim of the hat palm-upward;
lift it, rotate it, and place it upon the crown of the head, wearing it level—this is best. One must not lean forward or backward, nor tilt it to the left or right.
The method for removing the hat is likewise to hold it palm-upward, rotate it, and lower it. Use only [the prescribed method].

With the right hand held palm-upward, grasp the brim of the rain hat and carry it over the right shoulder. Regarding the method for holding the staff: if it has branches, it is called the "defiled end" (chūtō);
if it is branchless, it is called the "pure end" (jittō). When walking, the pure end is placed in front, and the right hand carries it.
When lowering the hat, it is held within the left hand. When meeting people on the road, if one offers a brief greeting, one holds the staff with the left hand palm-upward. Palm-upward.
With the right hand, lower the *kasa* (straw hat). Fold the *kasa* and hold it against the chest. Regarding the method for leaving the temple:

after completing the parting salutations with one’s fellow practitioners (*tongpao*), place the *kasa* on top of the eaves outside the triple gate. Regarding the method for entering the temple: remove the *kasa* from atop the eaves outside the triple gate.

Carry the staff with the left hand, letting the tip of the staff hang down; with the right hand, hold the *kasa* level with the right shoulder. If one encounters a fellow practitioner, fold the *kasa*.

Approaching the chest [of the monk's quarters], one merely expresses respect. If one is immediately to register as a resident, then at the bed to the south of the front door of the Sangha Hall, one first places the hat face-up.

Next, the staff is placed on the bed directly above [the hat]. The attendant (jingtou) stands to the north. First, he takes the clean water pitcher, the tea cylinder, and the pillow, and places them inside the hat.
Next, he unties the straps of the bundle and places them inside the hat as well. He then places the shoe bag [inside].
On the ground: place the alms-bag atop the hat. After untying it, place both the inner wrapping and the pillow-wrap upon the bed.
Next, take down the front wrapping and place it inside the hat, or place it upon the rear wrapping and the single-layer mat. First, take out the *kāṣāya* and the sitting mat.
Then, place the pillow, the pillow-wrap, the cord-wrap, and the front wrapping all inside the rear wrapping and tie them securely. Finally, take the clean cloth and carry the shoes.
Wash your feet in the bag (the rear rack). Having put on your shoes and socks, place the straw sandals in the shoe-bag and set it beneath the bed.
After drying your hands with a cloth, don your *kāṣāya* and go to the Hall Office (*táng-sī*) in your *cíbù* robe to register.

Once you have completed the registration, if there is a chest or cabinet in the hall, place your luggage inside, lock it, and then take your rain hat and staff back to your quarters. If there is no hall...

There are no chests or trunks within for storing luggage. Upon arriving at the quarters and completing the formalities with the residents, follow the instructions given by the abbot or the head seat regarding your assigned location.
Once you have finished the inspection, hang your alms bowl and arrange your bedding inside the Sangha Hall. Place your tea canister and written documents on the table within your quarters.

Upon entering the gate, first inquire as to the location of the guest quarters (*danguo*). Once you have entered the hall and finished unpacking your belongings, assume a dignified posture and proceed to the guest seat, saying:

"I have arrived briefly to pay my respects. The Guest Master (*zhike*) comes out, and each person performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*). When taking leave, say: "I am passing through here at this moment."
Having had the good fortune to behold [the Abbot], the guest prefect says, "It was no easy matter to arrive here after such a long journey across rivers and mountains.
Thereafter, all the guest prefects go to the quarters to return the bow, just as one would when visiting the Abbot; those who wish to register for residence should do the same.
After resting for one or two days, go to the Hall Office (Tangsi) to register.

Prepare the formal requisites for entry; if there are two or more people, designate one person—preferably one who is experienced in social protocol or has a seniority of ordination (*śīla-varṣa*)—to act as the leader (*candana*). At the Hall Office, [proceed with the following].

They look at one another. The visitor seeks out an attendant to inform the *karmadāna*, saying, "The newly arrived person requests an audience. Upon meeting, they each perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*).
After finishing tea, the visitor rises, approaches, and says, "I have long admired your reputation for the Way; I have come specifically today to seek refuge under your guidance."
Furthermore, we look forward to your compassion. The Rector (Vina) says: "The mountain gate is most fortunate to receive your special visit.

Thereupon, each person presents themselves to the Archivist (Cibu) and the Rector according to the order of their seniority in ordination (*kaṣāya-lakṣa*). Once the Rector has received them, they are placed in order inside a chest. The newly arrived monk performs a prostration with touching the ground and says:
"At this moment, we are most fortunate; we deeply thank you for your warm reception. The Rector replies with a single prostration and says: "May the officials treat you with care."
[The Master] said, "It is sparse; for now, I hope you will take the Way as your primary concern and abstain from hot water. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) escorted him out.

The Hall Office said, "Please, Senior Monk, return to the hall to register your stay. The newly arrived monk entered through the southern side of the front door of the Sangha Hall (the *sanchou*, or leader of the group, enters from the northern side), stood before the Holy Monk, and performed three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*).
He then folded his sitting cloth, made one circuit of the hall starting from the seat of the Head Seat, and returned.
After completing the inquiries before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), they take their seats in order at the third position on the wooden platform beneath the southern wall inside the front gate.

Once the *Vina* has finished recording the names on the ordination register according to seniority by monastic age (*kṣetra-vaya*), he instructs an attendant to carry the *cibu* (ordination certificate) case into the hall.
(In some places, the *Vina* first burns incense before the Sacred Monk. The newly arrived monk rises and stands before the platform; they exchange formal greetings.

[The procedure] is finished. The *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) passes through the *ci-bu* (Department of Sacrifices) in order. At the head of the register, he performs a prostration with hands touching the ground facing southeast.

The newly arrived monk also performs a prostration with hands touching the ground. The *vinaya-dhara* assigns lodgings according to the sequence of seniority in ordination (*śīla-kalpa*) and performs a prostration with hands touching the ground.

The *vinaya-dhara* always occupies the upper seat: as before, if at the northern side of the front gate, he faces northeast; if at the southern side of the front gate, he faces southeast; if at the northern side of the rear gate, he faces northwest. As before...

The southern cheek of the gate is the southwest side of the face). Once the new arrivals have been settled, the *karmadāna* (Venerable Leader) emerges (in some places he exits through the front gate; in others, through the rear gate). He escorts the new arrivals (if he exits through the rear gate, the new arrivals do not cross the threshold;
if he exits through the front gate, they part outside the gate). The *karmadāna* says: "I request Venerable So-and-so to visit Venerable So-and-so at their respective quarters for a brief interview.
Having taken leave, the new arrivals return to their quarters and inform the head of the quarters (*shouzhu*), saying: "We have visited the new arrivals."

Upon seeing the head of the quarters (liao-zhu), each person performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths. When the tea service has ended, those from the head of the assembly (can-tou) downward rise and step forward, saying:
"The *weina* has given instructions for us to enter the superior quarters and take up residence here.

Thereupon, the head of the quarters examines the seniority of their precept years (*jie-la*) and directs those from the head of the assembly downward to proceed in order to inspect the beds and register for residency according to the seating chart. Each person then performs one prostration with unopened sitting cloths.

The newly arrived monk stands in order before the sacred image. Having completed his inquiries and finished his circuit of the quarters (*luoxia*), he seeks out the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) within the hall to meet him.
Each person performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*). He then takes up his luggage and consults the Hall Master (*liaozhu*), who arranges for the Head Seat to escort him.

Next, he goes to the Abbot’s hall to see the Attendant (*shizhe*) (without yet performing a formal prostration), saying: "I, the newly arrived, pay my respects to the Venerable Master. I trouble you, Attendant..."

[The attendant] reports [to the abbot] as when the Hall Master receives guests. If the guest is resting, he extends tea and soup to them. If there are no obstacles, he may lead the guest away immediately (at which point the formal serving of tea is not yet required).

The attendant then asks: "Is the Senior Seat (Upādhyāya) a disciple who has entered the inner chamber? Is he a kinsman of the Dharma? If he is neither a disciple who has entered the inner chamber nor a kinsman of the Dharma, they proceed with a single round of reception.
If he is a disciple who has entered the inner chamber, one must wait until the greetings of the newly arrived guest have concluded before proceeding.
They look at one another. The attendant first reports to the Abbot, saying: "So-and-so many are newly arrived; so-and-so many are入室 (入室) disciples;
so-and-so many are dharma-kinsmen. After they have prostrated, they are led inside. The two-fold unfolding and three prostrations for the newly arrived are as described above.
The dharma-relatives also perform two-fold unfolding and three prostrations; this is because they are returning the formal etiquette due to the public domain of the Abbot.

However, the abbot should not receive formal prostrations (*namaskāra*). Nor should one perform a touching prostration (*chuli*) to the abbot; instead, one should simply say, "I shall go to the quarters later to pay my respects. The abbot should then assign a nearby superior quarters for the visitor. When the abbot returns to the quarters, he performs a return prostration.

If the visitor is a close senior, they perform the full nine prostrations with wide unfolding of the robes (*dazhan jiuliu*). If this is waived, they perform two wide unfoldings and three prostrations. If waived again, they perform a touching prostration of three bows. If the Dharma relative (*dharmabandhu*) is somewhat more distant, they perform two wide unfoldings and three prostrations, or a touching prostration of three bows. If the Dharma relative is a close kinsman, it does not matter whether they are senior or junior.
The administrative officers (*zhishi*), heads of departments (*toushou*), junior disciples (*xiaoshi*), and practitioners (*xingzhe*) should all enter into service.
The入室 disciples (入室弟子) and the dharma-kinsmen (法眷) of humble conduct shall all perform nine prostrations with fully spread mats (*dazhan*), or two spreads and three prostrations (*lianzhan sanbai*).
The head attendant (*cantou*) steps forward with a slight bow and says: "I have long admired the Venerable Master’s reputation for the Way;

today I am honored to behold your august countenance. My humble heart cannot contain its utmost joy. He then withdraws to his position and performs another single spread, saying: "I inquire after your health. I humbly pray that the Venerable Master..."

I respectfully wish that Your Reverence’s health and daily activities remain blessed with myriad blessings. (In the first month, the beginning of spring, it is still cold; in the second month, mid-spring, it gradually warms; in the third month, late spring, it is extremely warm; in the fourth month, the beginning of summer, it gradually becomes hot.)

In the middle month of the fifth lunar month, there is scorching heat; in the final month of the sixth lunar month, it is extreme heat; in the first month of the seventh lunar month, it is still hot; in the middle month of the eighth lunar month, it gradually cools; in the final month of the ninth lunar month, it is cold with frost; in the first month of the tenth lunar month, it gradually becomes cold.

In the middle month of the eleventh lunar month, there is severe cold; in the final month of the twelfth lunar month, it is extreme cold. A close disciple says: "I have long been separated from the Master’s compassionate instruction; today I am honored to behold your venerable countenance.

A dharma-relative says: "I have long received the Master’s dharma-protection; today I am honored to behold your venerable countenance. My humble feelings are beyond measure. They exchange greetings as before.
After the tea and soup are finished, one then examines the letters from the attendants, the administrative office, and the head seat.

The Registrar (Kizō) and the Guest Master (Chikaku) say: "On this day, we are most fortunate to have you as our guest. They briefly exchange greetings of the season (each performing three prostrations with touching the head to the ground;
however, if one has already served as a temporary Guest Master elsewhere, these prostrations are omitted). They inquire after [the guest's] long-term residence.

If the Bath Master (Yokushu) has prepared refreshments, they go to see the Bath Master and inquire after his dharma-relatives and brothers, exchanging prostrations. For three days, [the guest] shall remain constantly in the quarters.
One must remain on duty within the Sangha Hall while waiting for the invitation to tea or soup; one must not wander about idly to avoid being sought out.

One should rise early at dawn, fearing that those who invite [the assembly] might disturb the community. (In some places, when the Abbot, administrators, or heads of departments return to their quarters on the same day, newly arrived monks merely bow and withdraw, rather than taking their seats.

When administrators or heads of departments visit various quarters, they all occupy guest seats; only the Abbot may occupy the host seat. Newly arrived monks must both go out to welcome and see them off. If one wishes to leave, one must first ensure the hall is properly guarded.

[The] ritual: Having finished the half-monthly tea service in the quarters, or upon returning from the imperial audience following a sacred festival, one must inform the head of the quarters (*lǎozhǔ*) as well as those of the upper and lower ranks before proceeding.

If a person of renowned virtue enters the monastery to take up residence, the abbot (*zhùchí*), the rector (*wéinà*), and the guest master (*zhīkè*) shall jointly escort him into his private quarters (*dúlǎo*) for settling in; thereafter, the rector shall escort him [to other locations], or as the case may require.
When moving out from the communal quarters—whether due to one's own retirement as an abbot, head seat, or library curator—one must go to the Head Monk’s quarters to express thanks for the lodging.
This may be done by performing a full prostration (*daizhan*), two prostrations with three bows (*liangzhan sanbai*), or a simple touching-prostration (*chuli*) three times.

The ritual procedures are to be adjusted according to the circumstances. Next, one thanks the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina). One may either inquire after his well-being or perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*).
Upon the day of departure, one withdraws from the quarters at the Abbot’s residence (*fangzhang*) and the *vinaya-dhara*’s quarters; the ritual procedures are as before, adjusted as appropriate.
The door-hooks and keys must all be presented face-to-face to the *vinaya-dhara* before one may depart. If a newly arrived monk has previously resided in this monastery...
Those serving as heads of administrative affairs (*kaji*), chief masters (*shushu*), or transformation masters (*kechizu*), shall all be drawn from the former quarters (*zenziryō*).

Those from various regions who possess the talent and virtue for administrative duties, as well as those who have served under a master for a full term, shall all be assigned to the upper quarters (*jōryō*). From two people upward, there shall be no further formal bowing (*sai*) or withdrawal from the quarters (*tōryō*).
If there is a truly urgent matter requiring attention before the summer retreat has concluded or the hall protocols (*dōgi*) are complete, one must inform the Hall (*baitō*).
The official shall request leave; one must not depart on one’s own authority, for the mountain gate shall impose a heavy penalty.

If one requests leave to travel the mountains and exceeds half a month, one must submit a report to the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu). One must again observe the regulations of the Hall. The form for the certificate of authorization is as follows:

[Name of Monastery], Bhikṣu [Name] in Brown or Purple Robes, Right [Name]. Regarding the account books of [Year] held by this person, they were submitted to [Name of Temple]. Now, I hold my original name.

The three complete copies of the *dùdié* (ordination certificate) and the *jiuniàn jiédié* (precepts certificate for the six recollections) have been presented for inspection at the Prefectural Office (*shìyá*).

We seek to obtain an official warrant (*gōngpíng*) to travel to [place name] for pilgrimage as designated leaders (*dītóu*). We respectfully entreat Your Honor to graciously issue a written decree for its execution.

We await your instructions (or orders). This memorial is respectfully submitted. Dated [Month and Year], stamped with the Monastery Seal. Submitted by [Name], former office-holder. [Format for the Official Warrant (*pípíng*) is provided below.]

The rank is as before. This petitioner, [Name], humbly submits that on such-and-such day of such-and-such month, at such-and-such place, he executed a public warrant (*gōbyō*) to travel to such-and-such place for the purpose of pilgrimage.
However, due to the onset of a respiratory ailment, he has been unable to proceed and fears he may violate the time limit stipulated by the public warrant.
He respectfully requests a formal endorsement (*hikaku*). He dares not act on his own authority and awaits Your Majesty’s decree. Respectfully submitted, [Month and Year].
(No seal required) Daily Record. [Name] of the preceding rank, in such-and-such capacity.

When attending the morning gruel or midday meal, seating must follow the order of seniority according to one's *kaṣāya* (precept years). After the morning period of seclusion has ended, three strikes of the bell signal the time for the meal.
Prior to this, when first taking one's seat during the meal period, one waits for the long board to sound and for three strikes on the wooden fish;

immediately upon these sounds, one rises and sets down the bowl (according to the old teachings, one must not pass beyond the third seat). When setting down the bowl, it must be placed upon the upper shoulder.

After the wooden fish has been struck, no one may enter the hall. As for the method of entering the hall: those who enter through the front gate do so from the southern side (first lifting the right foot). This is why one does not [enter] from...

Regarding those who enter by the northern side: these are persons of honorable standing who maintain the office. (As for those who enter through the rear door: if they sit in the upper section, they enter by the northern side; first lifting the left foot. If they sit in the lower section, they enter by the southern side.)
First lift the right foot). Having finished the inquiry after the noble Sangha, one sits down. Regarding the method for ascending the platform: inquire after those in the adjacent seats.
First, with the right hand, gather the sleeve of the left side and press it down under the armpit; then, with the left hand, gather the sleeve of the right side and slightly lift it.
After that, take hold of the front of the *kāṣāya* with both hands, and next grasp it together with the left hand. That is—

Step onto the bed and sit near the inner edge. Then, discard your shoes. First, support yourself with your left hand on the bed; next, draw up your left leg first to mount the bed, followed by drawing up your right leg.
Sit upright with your entire body, pressing the left foot over the right. Spread the *kāṣāya* robe to cover your knees, ensuring that your undergarments are not exposed.
Furthermore, you must not let the robe hang down while sitting on the edge of the bed; you must withdraw your body by the distance of one *bō* (a bowl’s length).

The site is authorized. To clarify the protection and purification (the three purifications being: first, placing the *kāṣāya*; second, spreading out the alms bowl; third, the direction in which the head is turned):

the *jianyuan*, *weina*, *zhisui*, *shizhe*, and others shall stand in the upper section outside the hall; the *zhike*, *yuzhu*, *tantou*, *fangjie*, *tangzhu*, and others shall stand in the lower section outside the hall.
After the drum is struck three times, the Abbot proceeds to the hall, and the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and heads (*tou-shou*) take their respective seats.
Upon the sounding of the bell before the hall, the assembly descends from their seats together. The Abbot enters the hall;

having finished bowing to the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), he bows to the assembly, after which he takes his place. Once the Abbot has completed his bow and taken his seat, the assembly may then ascend their seats.
The attendants and śrāmaṇeras follow the Abbot outside the hall and stand in a row, awaiting [the next instruction].
The assembly sits. At one time, they exchange greetings. Thereafter, the attendant enters the hall, bows before the table, and exits. Next, the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) enters the hall;

having finished bowing before the Sacred Monk (*ārya-saṃgha*), he burns incense and stands by the side of the mallet. The assembly spreads out their alms bowls. (At Hongji Monastery, it is added that the mallet is struck once, and it is said:

"The assembly shall each recite three fascicles of the Heart Sūtra and dedicate the merit to [Name]. This single strike of the mallet occurs only when land-granary porridge is served at various monasteries. If the meal coincides with an occasion of auspicious or inauspicious significance, the same applies.

When the distribution of incense has concluded, kneel before the incense burner and strike the mallet once, saying: "Homage to the Bhagavān, the perfect Sūtra, and the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Saṃgha; their merit is inconceivable. Alternatively, one may say:

"The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha is the most supreme field of merit. All who take refuge in it shall manifest a response. Or one may say: "As the autumn moon appears in clear water, so do blessings arise through earnest prayer to the field of merit. Only the Buddha’s Bodhi is the true place of reliance."

Generally, one must not recite long verses while striking the mallet at the edges [of the ritual space]. This morning’s preparatory service includes a memorial; I respectfully face the Cloud Hall to represent you all in proclaiming this petition.

I humbly pray that your compassion will bear witness. Having finished proclaiming the memorial, he says: "The preceding written memorial has been fully proclaimed. May your holy eye, being impartial, graciously grant its clear inspection.
He then looks up toward the assembly and chants for a long while: "Pure Dharma Body... etc. If the mallet is struck too hurriedly, it immediately...

When striking the mallet, if it is struck too high, one strikes the Buddha’s head; if it is struck too low, one strikes the Buddha’s feet. When performing the ordinary *xian-shi* (filling-in) ritual, one simply announces the mallet-strike, saying:
"I reverently entreat the Triple Gem to grant their seal of approval. One does not further chant the name of the Buddha. After the ten recitations of the Buddha's name have concluded:

After a long pause, he struck the mallet once. The Head Seat offered the food (for gruel, it is said: "Gruel has ten benefits that profit the practitioner; its karmic retribution is rebirth in heaven, culminating in eternal bliss"). He spoke again, saying:

Congee is a most excellent medicine; it can eliminate hunger and thirst. By giving and receiving it, one attains refreshing clarity and together accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way. Regarding the *zhāi* (fasting/consecration): "With the three virtues and six flavors, I offer to the Buddha and the Sangha;

may all beings of the Dharma-realm, humans, and devas, universally partake in this offering. Regarding the *zuàn fàn* (stirring the rice): "May both giver and receiver equally attain the Five Constant Virtues; may they obtain physical vigor, long life, peace, and unimpeded eloquence. (The above are all recited with a loud, resonant voice.

When the food distribution is finished, the practitioner calls out for the food to enter. (In calling for the food, the words must be distinct and the names must not be mistaken. If there is an error, the ritual of receiving the food is not accomplished and must be recited again. If the food is distributed too quickly, the recipients will be flustered; if distributed too slowly, they will sit for a long time and become annoyed.)
The food is distributed. The *vinaya-dhara* strikes the wooden mallet once. The head seat (*shouzuo*) receives the food and completes the visualization; only then does the assembly begin to eat.
The *vinaya-dhara*, turning behind the curtain of the Holy Sangha (*shengseng*), bows to the head seat (thereby requesting the head seat to bestow wealth).

He then returns to his own position and strikes the mallet once. The head seat bestows wealth (exclaiming: "The two gifts of wealth and Dharma are equal and without distinction. The *dānapāramitā* is fully perfected"). [The *kudou* or the *vinaya-dhara*...]

Regarding the sequence for placing the offerings: one should lay them gently upon the mats before the monks (with the intention of showing respect). The assembly of monks shall receive the offerings with palms joined; they must not look at them, nor may they toss the offering money onto their seats or make any noise.

(At the conclusion of the meal, collect them). The method for unfolding the bowl (*pātra*) is as follows: first, perform a greeting; then, remove the outer cloth (*upadhāna*), take the bowl, and wipe it.

Fold it small and place it horizontally before you, close to your body, together with the pouches for the spoon and chopsticks. Next, unfold the clean towel (*śucimukha*) and spread it over your knees.

Open the outer cloth and fold it into a triangle with the edges facing inward, ensuring it is neat and orderly. Let one corner hang over the edge of the bed. First, open the bowl with both hands and cover it to the right.
With his hand, he holds the edge of the robe toward his body to cover the bowl. Then, with his left hand turned upward, he takes the bowl and places it upon the robe.
With both index fingers of his left hand, he grasps the rim of the bowl and unfolds it from the bottom up in sequence, without making any sound.

If the seating space is somewhat narrow, one should only unfold three bowls. Next, open the bag and take out the spoons and chopsticks (when taking them out, the chopsticks first; when putting them in, the spoon first).
Lay them horizontally behind the front edge of the bowl, with the tips of the spoons and chopsticks pointing toward the upper shoulder.

Place the bowl-brush at the lower shoulder, with the outer edge of the brush facing outward and the handle pointing away from the body, awaiting the serving of food. Regarding the method for distributing food, it should be performed by a lay attendant (*karmadāna*); the monastics themselves do not.
One may take food with one's own hands. When a layperson serves food—such as rice, soup, or congee—one must not soil the hands or the rim of the bowl;
rather, one should dip the ladle two or three times and serve it after a short pause. One should bend the body and clasp both hands together at the chest.
Regarding the quantity of rice or congee, each person follows their own inclination. As for the method of receiving food: hold the bowl with both hands and keep them low.
Setting aside the alms bowl, receive it with the bowl level; one should receive only what is measured and must not have any remainder.

Until the *karmadāna* has announced the signal by striking the wooden mallet (*gandi*) throughout, one must not lift the bowl to first perform an offering. Wait until the sound of the mallet has been heard throughout, then join the palms and bow before eating.

Next, perform the Five Contemplations: (1) Calculate the labor involved and measure the distance from which the food has come; (2) Reflect upon whether one’s own virtue is complete or deficient to determine if one deserves the offering; (3) Guard the mind against transgressions, making the abandonment of greed and other passions the primary principle; (4) Regard the food as excellent medicine for treating the emaciation of the body; (5) [Receive it] for the purpose of attaining the Way.

Therefore, one should accept this food. Only then may it be brought forth (if the five contemplations have not been performed, it is not one’s portion of food and may not be brought forth). As the verse says: "O assembly of ghosts and spirits, I now bestow upon you this offering;
this food pervades the ten directions for all ghosts and spirits to share. Regarding the method of eating: hold the bowl up to the mouth; do not bring the mouth down to the food.

Regarding the exterior of the alms bowl: that which is more than halfway up is called "pure" (śuddha); that which is less than halfway up is called "touched" (spṛṣṭa). Place the index finger inside the bowl;
apply the second and third fingers to the exterior of the bowl. The fourth and fifth fingers are not used. The same applies to the small bowl (kaṭacchu).
When picking up or setting down the bowl, and when handling the spoon or chopsticks, one must not make a sound. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "Receive food with a focused mind.
Receive soup and rice with the bowl held level. Eat both the soup and the rice together, eating them in sequence. One must not scoop from the center of the bowl to eat.
Unless one is ill, one must not ask for more soup or rice for oneself. One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more. One must not... [continue].
One should not give rise to a mind of aversion while looking at the bowl of a fellow monk. One should eat with the thought that one is merely binding the bowl.

One must not take large mouthfuls of food. One must not open the mouth wide in anticipation of the food. One must not speak while food is in the mouth. One must not throw morsels of food into the mouth.
One must not let food fall and scatter. One must not stuff food into the cheeks. One must not make noise while chewing food. One must not slurp the food while eating.
One must not lick with the tongue while eating. One must not shake the hands while eating. One must not eat by grasping scattered grains of rice with the hands.
One must not hold food vessels with soiled hands. All of the above rules from the Vinaya text should be strictly observed.
Furthermore, one must not scratch the head so that dandruff falls into the bowl or saucer. Nor should one sway the body, grasp the knees while squatting, yawn, or make sounds by pinching the nose.
If one wishes to sneeze or spit, one must cover the nose. If one wishes to pick at teeth, one must cover the mouth.
Vegetable scraps and fruit pits should be placed behind the bowl in a secluded spot to avoid offending those in neighboring seats.
If there is leftover food or fruit in the bowl of a neighbor, one must not take it even if offered. Furthermore, if a neighbor is someone who fears drafts, one must not [allow wind to reach them].
[Hold] a fan (as if you yourself were afraid of the wind; the white *vina* eats outside the hall). If there is anything required, point it out silently;

do not call out loudly to have things brought. When the meal is finished, wipe the remains from the bowl with the bowl itself and eat them. Receive water in the primary bowl (*toubō*) and wash [the bowls] in sequence.
Furthermore, do not wash the ladle (*tetsushi*) inside the primary bowl. Wipe the bowls and the ladle in sequence until they are perfectly dry.
Wash the spoons and chopsticks and place them inside the storage bag. Do not let the remaining water from the bowl drip onto the floor beneath the bed.
The mantra for discarding the bowl-water is: *Oṃ ma-hū-ra-se svāhā*. Place both thumbs inside the bowl with the palms facing upward;
hold the bowl with the left hand and place it in the center of the folded cloth (*pātra-kośa*). Cover it with the right hand held close to the body, palm facing downward.
Place the lid of the alms bowl on the edge of the bowl. Then, with both hands, stack them single-layered and rest them at the mouth of the bowl.
Cover the bowl with the corner of the cloth facing the body. Next, take the corner of the cloth hanging from the edge of the bed and cover it toward the body.

After that, stack the clean towel, along with the bags for the spoon and chopsticks, and the bowl brush upon the cloth. Cover these with the bowl-wiping cloth. Once the bowl has been nested, hear the mallet signaling the departure from the hall, and recite:

After finishing the meal, [the verse says]: "The meal being finished, physical strength is restored; majestic power shakes the ten directions, the heroes of the three periods of time. Turning causes toward the fruit is not a matter of thought; all sentient beings shall attain supernatural powers.
The abbot rises from his seat, hangs his bowl, and orders the bedding of the newly arrived monks to be neatly arranged.

He squats down, sits upon the bed, and then with his left hand gathers the lower robe behind him, using it as a cushion against his body and covering the edge of the bed. He then slowly lowers his feet; he must not straddle the bed.
Below. As for the tea service during the formal sitting in the hall, entering and exiting the hall, ascending and descending from the platform—all follow this same procedure.
After the congee, the session is dismissed (*fangcan*). The abbot then exits the hall and strikes the *fangcan* bell three times. If it is the morning session (*zao can*), the bell is not struck.
If acting on behalf of a donor, one ascends the hall after the third strike; in such a case, the *fangcan* bell must also be struck. Great.
When the tea service has concluded, the abbot bows before the Holy Monk and exits; immediately thereafter, the hall bell is struck three times.

If the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) or the Head Seat (Shouzuo) enters the hall to prepare the tea, they escort the abbot out, then return to the hall to bow before the Holy Monk at both the upper and lower ends.
Once the tea bowls have been cleared, the hall bell is struck three times, and only then does the assembly [proceed].
One may descend from the platform. The deportment for exiting the hall is identical to the rules for entering the hall.

When proceeding to the tea or soup hall, the ceremony is performed specifically for the tea or soup; the ritual protocol is solemn and weighty. Those who have received the invitation should not be negligent or casual. Once the invitation has been accepted...
Having been invited, you must know that you shall first proceed to such-and-such a place, next to such-and-such a place, and finally to such-and-such a place.
Upon hearing the sound of the drum or the wooden board, arrive there in a timely manner. Clearly remember your seat according to the seating chart to avoid confusion or disorder.

For instance, when attending tea or soup service in the Hall, once the assembly has gathered, the attendant bows and invites the Abbot to enter; the Head Seat then follows him, standing in his assigned position, while the Abbot [takes his seat].
After the person has bowed, one should gather up the *kāṣāya*. Proceeding to the seat with composure, one must ensure that the shoes are not placed unevenly.

When withdrawing the feet, one must not allow the chair to creak. Sitting upright and straight, one must not lean back against the chair. The *kāṣāya* should cover the knees, and the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) should hang down in front.
With a solemn expression, one joins the palms and bows toward the host. One should always keep the inner robe (*pāṃśukūla*) covering the sleeves. And...
One must not expose one’s wrists. When it is hot, cross the hands with the palms facing outward; when it is cold, cross the hands with the palms facing inward.

Furthermore, press the right thumb over the left sleeve and the second finger of the left hand over the right sleeve. The attendant shall perform inquiries and burn incense, acting on behalf of the abbot in these ritual matters.
One should always remain respectful and solemn while attending to him. When receiving the cup, take it with both hands in a composed and dignified manner.
Hold it at chest level. Do not let go of it to bring it too low, nor hold it too high. If it is held at the same height when looking up or down, it is considered most excellent.
One must observe this specifically for those who are specially qualified; only after the host has returned the bow should one bow to those above and below.
When drinking tea, do not blow on the tea, do not swing the cup, and do not make grunting sounds.

Make a sound when taking up or setting down the cup; do not let it clatter against the tray. If you set down the cup before others, place it at the rear of the tray. Arrange them in order one after another without confusion.
With the right hand, receive the tea or medicinal decoction and hold it up. Wait until it has been served to all and everyone has bowed before drinking.
Do not open your mouth wide to toss the liquid in, nor bite into it so that it makes a noise. When the tea is finished, leave your seat and set [the vessel] aside.
Having carefully lowered his feet and finished the inquiries after one's health, he follows the assembly out.

One who has been specially treated must step forward one or two paces to inquire after the host’s well-being, thereby performing the ritual of thanking them for the tea. His gait must be dignified and orderly;
he must not walk hurriedly with large strides, nor slip off his sandals to tread upon the ground and make noise. If the host sees him off, there is an exchange of inquiries.
Having bowed respectfully and withdrawn, one then proceeds in order to the storehouse and the various quarters for tea and soup.

If the Abbot specifically provides tea or soup, one receives it but does not attend the assembly (if one is suddenly afflicted by illness, or pressed by the need for urination or defecation, one should entrust the matter to a fellow attendee to inform the attendant). One’s proper etiquette is to withdraw from the position.

If one were to allow them to leave the monastery, the Dharma would perish and there would be no community. Furthermore, it is inappropriate for the abbot to display anger or resentment before the assembly.
(In the guest quarters and all other locations where tea and soup are specially served, speech and laughter are strictly prohibited.)

The invitation for the *in-yuan* (causal conditions) or the conclusion of the fortnightly hall ceremony, or the conclusion of the tea service on the first or second day, shall each be established according to the incumbent abbot.

Prior to entering the room, one shall be received by the attendant; the attendant shall inquire and request a conversation. Once the attendant has reported this, one may then enter for the formal interview (*chan*).

Having bowed with their heads to the ground, they stand facing north in formation. Once the incense has been burned in succession, the head of the assembly steps forward from the ranks and performs a formal greeting (*monshin*) facing the master.
Turning toward the southwest corner of the meditation chair, he performs another greeting and says: "For us, the matter of birth and death is of great importance, and impermanence is swift."

We humbly beseech the Venerable Master’s compassionate instruction regarding the *yinyuan* (causal conditions). If the Abbot grants permission, the *can-tou* (head of the assembly) returns to his position and performs three full prostrations with the sitting cloth (*zuojù*) fully spread.

Rising from the prostrations, he folds the sitting cloth. The assembly turns their bodies toward the west side of the meditation chairs, facing east, and stands in succession performing *wenshen* (greeting) bows.
Once the request for the *yinyuan* is concluded, the *can-tou* and those below him perform three full prostrations in their original positions.

After performing prostrations and inquiries, one departs (in some places, there are three prostrations for the inquiry and six prostrations for the expression of thanks, totaling nine; in other places, there are six prostrations each for the inquiry and the expression of thanks, totaling twelve).

The words for the inquiry are: "I humbly receive the compassion of the Venerable Master, who has graciously granted my request. I am filled with the utmost joy. The words for the expression of thanks are: "We have been fortunate in our past lives to have already received the compassionate instruction on causes and conditions from the Venerable Master. Our hearts are moved by your profound kindness beyond measure.
Then, returning to the quarters, one expresses thanks to the attendant, either by performing a single prostration with the forehead touching the ground (*chuli*) or simply by making a bow of inquiry.

[And so it ends. (In some places, when standing in meditation before the assembly, only the *canshou* [lead participant] burns incense. Having made his inquiry, he returns to his position and performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan*) together with the assembly.

Then, after the mutual inquiries are concluded, they turn together. Once the request for discourse is finished, the *canshou* and the others burn incense in succession. They stand facing the master according to their positions and perform three or six prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths).

Such rules as these vary according to local custom; one must consult the attendant and act accordingly. One must not harbor fixed views or act with obstinacy, causing the master to feel resentment or anger. (For those newly admitted to the monastery...)

As was previously done when offering greetings, at the time of entering the room, one burns incense and makes this request: "I beseech the Master’s compassion; I pray that you permit me to enter the room as before. If permission is granted, one performs three full prostrations (*daizhan sanbai*) and says:

"I humbly receive your compassionate special grant of permission. My inner feelings are beyond measure of gratitude. Then, withdrawing, one performs three prostrations (if the request is declined, one simply performs three full prostrations).

The entry into the hall may take place in separate corridors or separate quarters; it may occur on alternate days or consecutive days; and it may be held in the morning or the evening—each according to the regulations established by the abbot.
When the time for entry arrives, the attendant instructs the acolytes to prepare incense and sets up the seats for prostration facing the [abbot] (in some places...).
No prostration is made, nor is the mat spread again. When the procedure is finished, one consults the abbot.

If there is an instruction to enter the room, then the "Entering the Room" plaque is hung, and either the drum is beaten, the wooden board is struck, or the "Entering the Room" plaque is tapped to alert and assemble the great assembly.

Once the abbot is seated, the attendant stands with hands folded at the eastern side outside the abbot’s quarters. When the assembly has gathered slightly and is standing in formation, perhaps in a single row facing [the abbot]—
In the east, the two rows may face each other. The attendant enters the abbot’s quarters and bows in greeting directly opposite him.

Turning, he stands facing south behind the incense altar at the eastern side of the meditation chair. He first bows, offers incense with his left hand, and after completing the bow, bows again directly opposite the abbot before exiting to bow before the assembly.
He then requests permission to enter the room. The attendant returns to the monks’ hall. The one entering the room turns slightly.

The attendant shall inquire after the health of the assembly on behalf of the abbot. Proceeding in proper sequence with palms joined, one must not cut ahead so as to cause the assembly to be disturbed in mind.

One enters through the right side of the abbot’s quarters door, first lifting the left foot. Having completed the inquiry before the abbot’s face, one turns around, joins the palms, and stands making an inquiry at the southwest corner of the meditation chair.
Furthermore, one must first make the inquiry and only then disclose the news. Do not...
One may engage in conversation for a considerable time, yet must not speak of worldly or idle matters so as to cause long delays for the assembly.

Once the discourse is concluded, one should inquire after their well-being and withdraw. One should perform a prostration directly before them (in some places there is one prostration, in some three; in some places there is a full prostration [dazhan], in some a touching prostration [chuli]).
Turning toward the east with hands clasped, one exits from the left side, lifting the left foot first. This is done to avoid those who follow behind and to prevent any accidental collisions.
Exiting from outside the abbot’s quarters, he pays his respects to the incumbent and departs. Upon reaching the assembly, he again pays his respects and exits.

Sometimes they form two rows; upon entering the room, they immediately divide into two directions, proceeding east and west in succession (in some places, whether it be for raising a koan, general discourse, or requesting instruction, each is conducted at its own time and not permitted to be intermingled; in other places, these are performed together). When the assembly has finished entering the room, the attendant enters.

In the room, he should still roll up his mat and withdraw (for the ritual of entering the room, it is proper to burn incense. Regarding the method for burning incense: upon first entering the abbot’s quarters, one should perform a formal greeting facing him. Having finished, turn around and place one's hands together in prayer behind the incense stand; then proceed toward the abbot to perform a greeting.

Offer incense with the right hand, perform a greeting facing him again, and stand at a right angle to the corner of the meditation chair. Nowadays, because this takes time and hinders the assembly, incense is not burned. At some places, a mat is set outside the door for a single prostration before withdrawing; this too is likely due to a concern for not hindering the assembly.

Those who enter the room must always ensure their clothing is clean and free of stains or grease, and that their deportment is orderly and their movements are composed, thereby manifesting an attitude of reverence). He then instructs the attendant.
Unless it concerns urgent guests or matters of vital importance, one must not announce oneself upon entering the hall.
Furthermore, attendants must not speak aloud, make noise, or create a disturbance that distracts the assembly.
