When ascending the hall, it is conducted as if for a formal public assembly. After the morning gruel, the period for private retreat (*fàngcān*) is not granted; at dawn, the silence is lifted. The Head Seat (*shouzuo*) leads the assembly into the hall.
Upon hearing the first roll of the drum, the Head Seat and the assembly enter the Dharma Hall, arranging themselves in single file in successive order.
They stand to one side. Those who serve as the head seat near the Dharma Hall throne stand in their respective positions.

The secretary (*shuji*), storekeeper (*zangzhu*), guest prefect (*zhike*), and bath master (*yuzhu*) form their own group and stand in sequence before the assembly. All other heads of departments (*tou-shou*) follow the general order of the community.
If there is a retired elder (*chuanyuan*), he stands two seats apart from the head seat, slightly turned to the side, facing south. First...

The second round of the drum signals that the four administrative officers (zhishi) shall attend the assembly. They proceed in order to the interior of the Dharma Hall door and stand near the southern side of the seating mats facing the Dharma seat;
the Prior stands to the east. Upon hearing the first round of the drum, the novices (tongxing) line up and wait in the storehouse hall.
At the second round of the drum, they follow the administrative officers to the assembly and perform a formal greeting (wenxun) before the Dharma Hall.
The assembly in the hall passes to the east side and stands facing west, with those in the north as the seat of honor (novices attending the *can* must wear shoes and socks).
When the third signal drum is struck, the attendant reports to the abbot. The abbot emerges, and the assembly bows in unison.

The abbot ascends the seat and stands before the meditation chair; first, the attendant bows (the incense-bearer attendant immediately moves to the east side of the Dharma seat, standing nearby to the west).
Next, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) and the assembly turn their bodies to face the Dharma seat directly to offer greetings, and then return to their positions.
Next, the administrative officers (Zhishi) approach to offer greetings; it is considered superior for them to stand facing the Dharma seat in alignment with the Head Seat and others.

Then, the novices (Shami) and probationary practitioners (Tongxing) turn before the Dharma seat to offer greetings and stand according to their respective positions. (At Mount Lu, the Tongxing of Yuan Tong enter the Dharma hall alone to offer greetings at the eastern section.)

They form three lines and stand according to their rank. The administrative officers (zhishi) stand after performing inquiries of courtesy. Three lines of novices proceed in succession from the south to the front of the Dharma seat and stand in place. Once the inquiries are finished, the leader at the eastern edge first proceeds next, following in succession back to their original positions to stand after performing inquiries of courtesy.
The guest prefect leads the patrons to stand on the shoulders of the administrative officers.

Those who oversee affairs above them stand in a side-by-side formation like a flight of geese, leaning slightly to listen for the abbot to descend from his seat. The entire assembly performs inquiries of courtesy together. The head seat (shouzuo) has already...
The assembly stands in their places as the abbot enters the hall; the administrators (zhishi) then conduct a circuit of the hall.

If there is tea at the mountain gate, they take their seats once in position, while the administrators remain outside the gate. When the tea is finished, the abbot rises and strikes the bell for the end of the session.
If no tea is served, the administrators conduct a circuit of the hall and exit to wait for the abbot, after which they perform a bow and withdraw. Alternatively...
After the three prostrations, he ascends the hall. In the morning, the *can* (meditation session) is dismissed according to custom; after the session, there is no further circuiting of the hall.

Whenever the abbot ascends the hall, all must attend, with the exception of the *liáozhǔ* (hall master) and those on duty in the hall. Those who fail to attend shall be subject to severe punishment by the monastery and should strictly avoid such negligence.
If one has urgent matters due to other circumstances and is not being indolent, a slight delay in attending the session is permissible, as in the case of the *zhùchí* (abbot).
Once the master has ascended the seat, you must no longer enter; you should likewise withdraw from the abbot’s presence so as not to be seen by him.
When the assembly attends the formal inquiry, no one—including the abbot—shall wear a hat or have their sleeves rolled up.

If there is something humorous in the dialogue, one must not laugh loudly in the hall or even smile with an open face; rather, one should maintain a reverent and solemn attitude to listen attentively to the profound sound of the Dharma.
After the recitation for twenty-four days has concluded, the attendant of the Hall Office reports to the Abbot following the midday meal. Only then is the notice board hung.

When the time arrives, the main hall, the Great Hall, and the Shrine of the Local Deity (Jishin-dō) are swept clean and tidied; incense and lamps are prepared, and the bell is struck to assemble the assembly.
The assembly of administrators gathers. The abbot incenses the Land Deity Hall, the Great Hall, and the Sangha Hall in succession, performing three prostrations before the Buddha alone.
The abbot and administrators stand in the upper section, while the head seat and those below him stand in the lower section.
The rector strikes the bell to signal the commencement of the recitation, chanting: "May the imperial wind forever fan; may the Emperor... (and so forth).

May the Way flourish far and wide; may the Sun of the Buddha increase its brilliance and the Wheel of Dharma turn eternally. May the local deities of the monasteries protect the Dharma and bring peace to the people.
May the donors from the ten directions increase in merit and wisdom. For these reasons, we recite for the sake of the pure Dharmakāya and so forth... [as appropriate].

On the eighth, the eighteenth, or the twenty-eighth day, one recites the *śukla-varga* (White Recitation). O Great Assembly: Since the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entered Parinirvāṇa until the present day...

In the second year of the Yuánfú era of the Imperial Sòng dynasty, two thousand four hundred and seven years [since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa] have already elapsed (add the subsequent years accordingly).
As the days pass, life likewise diminishes; like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be? You all should exert yourselves with diligence as if your hair were on fire.
Mind only impermanence and be careful not to be negligent. May the local deities of this monastery protect the Dharma and bring peace to the people. Ten.
"May the donor’s merit and wisdom increase. [Recite] the aforementioned verses for the sake of mindfulness of the pure Dharmakāya, and so forth.
When the recitation is finished, the Abbot first enters and stands in his designated place. The Head Seat (Śrīmad-āsana) and those below him stand in procession through the hall.
The Attendant (Upādhyāya) follows behind the assembly and stands before the front gate at the empty space at the end of the aisle. The Administrative Officers (Karmadāna) stand last, separately.
The assembly proceeds in order to circumambulate the hall. The śrāmaṇeras do not participate in the circumambulation; they remain outside the hall, standing before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ).
When the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) or the abbot emerge, they bow with their bodies bent in salutation. Those who have arrived temporarily stand behind the assembly inside the gate.

Regarding the retired elders (*yuanzhang*), if they are registered as permanent residents (*guādá*), they stand in the position immediately below the Chief Seat (*shouzuo*); if they are not so registered, they follow the protocol for guests.

Taking one’s position (at the northern side of the rear door, facing the abbot). After the circumambulation of the hall is completed, the assembly returns to their quarters to exchange greetings and drink medicinal soup.

Once finished, they re-enter the hall, spread their mats, and lower the curtains (if in a mountain or forest monastery, the great bell is struck; the abbot descends from the hall, the rector stops the bell, and the assembly exchanges greetings while chanting in succession).

On the fifth day, the *xiǎocān* (informal sermon) was held in the hall to rouse and clarify the fundamental tenets. On the twenty-fourth day, the *niànsòng* (recitation) was performed to repay the kindness of the dragons and spirits.

Profound words were requested to elucidate the principles of the past and present. The *xiǎocān* serves as the family instruction that governs the monastic community. As for the method of the *xiǎocān*, it begins with the striking of the evening bell.

At the sound of the bell, seats are arranged in the dormitory hall, and the administrative staff and the assembly gather. The protocol for the exchange of greetings between host and guests is identical to that of the morning assembly (*zōsan*).

Beyond the formal recitation, everyone from the senior administrators and heads down to the novice monks and novices must provide admonition and correction regarding anything within the community that does not conform to the Dharma, regardless of whether the matter is great or small.
This is what is meant by the saying: "The various offices of the mountain gate each have their respective duties."

Do not cause disorder within the monastic community; rather, strive for peace and stability. The Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) shall attend the morning and evening sessions in the Hall, as well as the morning assembly and the two meal periods, arriving first.
The administrative officers (Karmadāna), unless there is urgent business that requires mobilizing the assembly, should likewise come together in unison.

Each should exercise his own strengths to jointly revitalize the monastery. For a time you are guest and host; for a lifetime you become teacher and disciple. Do not rely on your past diligence and secretly give rise to indolence.
Regarding pride: even those who are brothers in the Cloud Hall must be diligent in their spiritual practice.

Day and night you should consult one another and mutually refine yourselves, clearly understanding the rules and regulations and becoming thoroughly familiar with the monastic community. Only when you have traveled through various regions on pilgrimage should you pack your bags;

only when you have reached your destination should you carry your satchel. Manual labor should be performed in a secluded place; you must not soak your robes overnight, nor should you dangle them [to dry].
Do not swing your arms or jump about; do not walk with a crouching gait, sit with hands on hips, or dance with haughty gestures and frantic hand movements.
When walking, first lower the heels before placing the toes upon the ground. One’s gaze should always be respectful and limited to a distance of no more than one *vyāma* (a fathom).

Those passing by must strictly avoid cutting through the hall. One must not walk through the space between the upper and lower levels. When reciting sutras or mantras, they should be chanted silently. [Count] the number...

The *zhū* (bead necklace) must not make a sound. During morning attendance and evening petitions, one should simply remain solemn with hands joined in *añjali*. Beneath the outer robe (*piānshān*), one must wear an undergarment; it is improper to expose the body.
Regarding the mouth-clasp, sandals, and shoes, one must wear socks as a matter of propriety. Grass sandals are permissible, provided they do not strike the ground too low.

When the legs are bound beneath the skirt, the hem of the trousers must not hang down. When sitting in a squatting posture, one should tuck in the feet and always keep the hands pressed down while adjusting the lower garment.
Place the hands together at the chest with the right hand uppermost. When joining the palms in greeting, keep the fingers tucked in and facing each other.

Do not look at scriptures while wearing a robe open at the side or with a hanging sash. It is improper to spit, sneeze, or turn toward a stupa when defecating or urinating. When sleeping, one should lie on the right side with the sword fastened to the belt.

When entering for the morning service, one should stand like a crane and listen attentively by the side. One’s bedding and robes must always be kept neat and orderly. Unless it is one’s own single mat, one must not move another’s at will.
When opening a mat or folding a blanket, do so with low, careful attention. To turn one’s back toward others while mounting the bed is a laughingstock in the monastic groves (chónglín).
To walk or stand upon the bed violates the rules of decorum. When about to lie down, place a clean towel as a fold-undersheet beneath the *kāṣāya*. Never remove one’s upper robe before the pillow.
Be vigilant against thieves and robbers during times of urgency or relaxation. When sitting in meditation on a shared platform, do not lean your back against the wooden headboard.

While walking in meditation along the corridors, strictly avoid speaking or laughing loudly. When gathering for conversation in the hall after nightfall, remove your sandals; when lifting the curtain, do not let it hang behind you.

When washing your face, ensure the bucket and ladle do not make a clamor, and avoid making noise with spitting or blowing one's nose, as this disturbs the pure assembly. Do not wrap medicinal pills into balls or engage in frivolous play.
He speaks excessively. He leans against the balustrade in the venerable hall. He leaves himself nakedly exposed within the bathhouse.

He fails to fulfill his duty in overseeing the monastery gate. He spreads rumors and stirs up strife, creating groundless complications. When escorting deceased monks away, he lacks any sense of sorrowful compassion.

They harbor the intention of seeking surplus value when robes are auctioned; they discuss spiritual practice while failing to observe the precepts (*śīla*), yet vie for seating positions based on the seniority of their ordination age.
They are never satisfied with the gruel and rice they receive, speaking only of the provisions available elsewhere; when invited to tea or soup, they do not come.
I can only blame my host for his lack of propriety. Having received from him the entrustment of both clothing and bowl, he drew near and resided with me, yet he insulted those of venerable virtue;

he distanced himself from his teachers, monks, and parents. My original intention was to inquire after the Way and practice Zen; if there were no Buddha-Dharma within one's own body and mind, what would be the point?
How can one transcend the mundane and enter the sacred? If you possess even a fragmentary understanding, there is no need to thrust your nostrils toward the heavens.

Even if you have studied extensively and heard much, it is best to keep your heels firmly planted on the ground. Some people, like those leaning against a blade or dodging arrows, refuse to shoulder the burden of the monastic community;

since they do not share in "dying together and living together," they may be said to have failed their predecessors. This is especially so for those who have left the household life to travel as pilgrims.

When entering the assembly for Zen practice—whether partaking of porridge, rice, tea, or soup; attending morning and evening inquiries; or in speech, activity, movement, or deportment—one must conform to the regulations of the community.
You should provide detailed guidance and reminders on all such matters. If one remains silent and speaks not at all, the profound thread of the Dharma will gradually fall to the ground.

If those of later generations are to receive the medicinal teachings of the Dharma, they should engrave them into their bones and inscribe them upon their flesh, gathering even the slightest fragments of goodness.
Nothing is left out; even the slightest flaw is removed without exception. This is the intended meaning behind the establishment of the *xiǎocān* (informal discourse).

When a traveling monk (*yóuxíng rén*) wishes to join a monastery for the summer retreat (*jiéxià*), he must register as a resident (*guādá*) by half the day prior; this is for the sake of ensuring that he receives the tea and soup offerings.
Matters do not occur by chance. On the fourteenth day of the fourth month, after the midday meal, the plaque for recitation is hung.
By evening, the administrative officers prepare incense, flowers, and ritual implements before the local deity (Dongti), assemble the congregation, and perform recitations. (The liturgy states:

"We humbly observe that as the warm breeze fans the wilds and the Fire Emperor presides over the quarter, this is the time when the Dharma King observes the summer retreat and the day when the Śākyaputrīyas protect living beings. We have personally gathered the great assembly to solemnly proceed to this sacred shrine to chant and uphold the vast and majestic names of the myriad virtues, dedicating the merit to the true lords of this hall. We pray that they will grant protection so that our aspirations may be fulfilled."

For the *an-gu* (rainy season retreat), one relies upon the venerable assembly to chant [the liturgy] aloud, etc. It is further said: "The merit of this recitation is dedicated entirely toward the protection of the True Dharma and the local deities and dragons; we humbly pray that their divine radiance may provide assistance, manifesting deeds of benefit, causing the monastic garden (*brahman-vana*) to flourish, and bestowing eternal, impartial blessings.

Again, relying upon the venerable assembly, one chants "The Ten Directions," etc., at a low volume for the ritual proceedings. Upon hearing the low-voiced ritual, the drum is struck immediately. The administrative officers (*karmadāna*) shall have an attendant stand by in advance;
as soon as the low-voiced ritual is heard, they shall strike the drum. The Hall Office shall have the ordination seniority boards (*kaṣāya-piṭaka*) and incense and flowers prepared beforehand.
15. Offerings (These are set out before the Sangha Hall). One proceeds through the hall in order and takes one's seat.

A single administrative officer (*kaji*) performs the ritual duties (ordinarily this is the duty of the *jianyuan*, but in his absence, the *weina* acts on his behalf). Before the recitation begins, a notice is first written and presented to the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) to request his presence (the notice reads:

"The Kusi [Administrative Office] will tonight provide tea and refreshments in the Cloud Hall specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly, as a modest expression of the formal conclusion of the retreat. We humbly hope that the assembly will graciously deign to attend. Respectfully submitted by the bhikṣus of the Kusi, so-and-so, etc."). 15.
Before the morning gruel, the administrative officers (*karmadāna*), heads of departments, junior disciples, and Dharma relatives first come to the Abbot’s quarters for formal greetings.

If the Abbot has already performed these greetings on the preceding night, they are exempt from doing so again; furthermore, they need not go up to the Abbot’s quarters at all. Once the ascent to the hall (*shengtang*) has concluded, the administrative officers approach, perform two prostrations with hands opened (*liangzhan*) and three full prostrations (*sanli*).

(For the first opening of the hands, one says: "At this time of the summer retreat, when the feet are restrained, we have the honor of serving as your attendants; we rely solely upon the Venerable Master’s power of the Dharma for support, praying that there may be no difficulties. For the second opening of the hands, one expresses greetings regarding the weather.")

[The guest] greets warmly and performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). The Abbot says, "This is a great fortune; we have been able to dwell together in this *an-gu* (summer retreat). We also hope that the spiritual power of [Name] and others will provide mutual support, so that there may be no difficulties.
The Chief Seat (*shouzuo*) and the assembly all follow this same form. Next, the Chief Seat and the assembly perform two displays and three prostrations before the Abbot.

At this time, junior disciples, attendants, those of lower standing, Dharma relatives, and *śrāmaṇeras* stand to one side; they are not yet permitted to join the assembly in these formal greetings. The assembly...
When the rites are concluded, the Ritual Master (Zhishi) returns first to the Library Hall (Kutang) to take his place.

The Head Seat (Shouzuo) leads the assembly to perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*) before the officers of the Library Administration (Kusi). At this time, junior monks, attendants, and Dharma relatives go to the Dharma Hall to pay respects to the Abbot.

Next, the Head Seat proceeds to the front of the Sangha Hall and stands facing south, while the assembly faces north; each performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths. They then take their positions within the hall according to their seniority in ordination (*jiala*). The Ritual Master... [text continues].

The attendant enters the hall. Before the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ), he performs three prostrations with the robes fully spread out (*dazhan sanbai*), then rises and performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*) before the Head Seat (*śuōzuò*).
The assembly returns the prostrations. He then circumambulates the hall and exits. The Abbot enters the hall to burn incense;

rising after performing three prostrations with the robes fully spread out, at which time the junior disciples (*xiǎoshī*) stand aside behind the Holy Monk, while the Dharma relatives follow the assembly. He performs a prostration with the head touching the ground before the Head Seat, who returns the prostration. He circumambulates the hall as previously described (the junior disciples wait for the...).

The assembly bows in response, rises, and returns to their respective positions to stand [waiting and exchanging greetings]. The abbot exits the hall; the head seat and those below him perform three prostrations with raised hands in return and say:
At this time, we are fortunate to dwell together in retreat. Fearing that our three karmas may be unwholesome, we look to you for your compassion.

Once the Chief Seat (Shouzuo) and those below him have returned to their quarters, they shall wait as the various quarters and their masters do. The Chief Seat and those below each perform three prostrations with hands touching the ground (chuli) to express the dharma of being in the same hall.
The Abbot (Zhuchi) then rises from the Library Hall (Kutang) to inspect the quarters, followed in succession by the assembly, who escort him to [the end of the tour].
The abbot and the assembly then withdraw. Thereafter, each of the monks performs the customary rites of courtesy according to their rank.

The abbot, the head of the administrative office (kusi), and the head seat (shouzuo) proceed in order to the hall to prepare the tea service. Subsequently, the abbot specifically invites the administrators and heads of the various offices to join the head seat and the assembly for a meal.
On the following day, the administrative office specifically invites the secretary and the heads of the various offices and below to join the head seat for a meal.

After the assembly has gathered together, the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) proceeds to his quarters specifically to invite the administrative officers (karmadāna) and heads of departments (śreṣṭhin) to join him.
All other officials from the Rector (Karmadāna) downward, as well as the retired abbots (vṛddhasthavira), the standing elders (sthavira), and the Monastic Head Seat (Saṃghasthavira),
each go to their respective quarters to prepare tea specifically for the administrative officers and heads of departments.

On the evening of the fourteenth day of the seventh month, the summer retreat ends; the chanting is performed and medicinal broth is prepared. On the following day, the abbot ascends the hall. The protocol for receiving guests, the rounds through the quarters, and the preparation of tea and broth are all identical to the ceremonies for the commencement of the summer retreat (*kṣetrasaṃvāsa*), differing only in the wording of the notice posted by the administrative office (*kośavāra*). This serves as a brief expression of the ceremony for the conclusion of the retreat). Recitation at the Hall of the Local Deities: "It is considered that the golden wind fans the wilds and the White Emperor presides over the quarter. This is the time when the Buddha, the Awakened King, concludes the retreat; it is the day when the year of the Dharma reaches its full cycle."

The ninety-day summer retreat has passed without difficulty, and the entire assembly remains at peace. By reciting the great names of all Buddhas, we pay our respects to the true masters of this hall. We rely upon the Great Assembly (the same as the recitation for the closing of the summer retreat).

Words of Thanks from the Administrative Officers (*zhishi*): "We are deeply gratified that the year of the Dharma has been completed without any obstacles. This is surely due to the protection and grace of the Venerable Master’s spiritual power. We are overwhelmed with a sense of profound gratitude. Words of Thanks from the Abbot (*zhuchi*):

"I am deeply gratified that the year of the Dharma has been completed. I thank those such as [Name] for their contribution of the power of the Dharma. I am overwhelmed with a sense of profound gratitude. [The Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and those below him in the Hall; the Chief Attendant (*liaozhu*) and those below him in the Quarters.]

The following is the expression of thanks: "For nine months we have lived together, yet our three karmas were unwholesome and we disturbed the assembly; we humbly pray for your compassionate forgiveness. The administrative officers and heads shall announce:

"Brothers among the assembly who are traveling on pilgrimage must wait until the tea and soup service has concluded before departing as they please" (unless there is an urgent matter, in which case this restriction does not apply).
On the day before the New Year’s holiday in winter, the Abbot is exempted from receiving formal greetings (renshi). A notice is posted in advance on the front of the Sangha Hall.

By evening, the Kuosi (Storehouse Office) serves hot soup within the hall. (The Winter Notice states: "To briefly express the ritual of offering congratulations upon the arrival of this season. The Yearly Notice states: "To briefly express the ritual of offering congratulations upon the change of the year. The beginning and end are identical to the preceding. The Abbot proceeds to the Sangha...

The Hall serves tea and refreshments (the wording of the notice is the same as before). On the following day, within the Abbot’s quarters, the Abbot specifically invites the assembly to accompany him for tea and refreshments on behalf of the administrators and head officers.
On the next day, the administrators serve tea and refreshments specifically for the Head Seat and those below him at the Treasury Office.

The Head Seat and the Rector then serve them in succession, each at their own quarters, specifically for this purpose (if social visits cannot be avoided, then the junior disciples and others shall visit prior to the morning gruel; after the formal lecture in the hall has concluded, the assembly and others [shall follow]).
Regarding the Inspection of the Quarters (xúnluó):

A plaque for the inspection of the quarters is hung above the hall. Within the quarters, the head of the quarters (luózhǔ) and the Head Seat (shǒuzuò) arrange seating and offerings of incense and flowers. Whether it be tea or...

When the Abbot (Tang) is about to visit, the resident administrators approach and strike the wooden board to assemble the assembly outside the quarters. They line up in order before the door of the quarters and perform a formal greeting (*wenshen*).
The attendants enter the quarters with the Abbot. Once the Head of the Quarters has finished burning incense, the assembly performs a formal greeting.

Whether it be tea or soup, once the Abbot has finished discussing the matters at hand, as he is about to rise, the Head of the Quarters steps forward, spreads his sitting mat (*zuoju*), and offers his thanks.

(The verse says: "I humbly receive the Honored Master’s visit; my inner feelings are beyond measure for such profound gratitude. [Followed by: 'At this time, the weather is warm. If he does not accept the prostrations, the assembly performs *wenxun* (inquiries after his well-being), and they escort him out of the quarters.
[Note: This escorting is unnecessary if it is not the occasion for the formal opening or closing of the retreat, or if it is a routine inspection of the quarters.])

Upon approaching the arrival of a senior elder (zunsu) entering the monastery, the gatekeeper and the administrative officers (zhishi) assemble in advance to welcome him. The assembly ascends together to the Dharma Hall.

After the resident abbot, the administrative officers, and the assembly have completed their formal greetings in order, they escort the guest back to his quarters; the guest then proceeds to visit the resident abbot.

If the person does not enter the guest quarters, they immediately visit the host. The host accompanies them on a tour of the administrative offices (*liao*), after which they return to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to drink medicinal soup (*tang*) and disperse.
Thereafter, the host proceeds to the guest quarters to offer formal thanks. If the parties are not related by law (i.e., are unrelated), both guest and host use formal written notices (*menshuang*).

That evening there is an evening assembly (*wan-chan*); the following day, the guest ascends the hall (*sheng-tang*), and a special meal is prepared for them. This applies when the parties are of equal standing.

Below, consult the procedures for actual practice. Regarding the detailed protocol for receiving officials (when a Provincial Inspector, a Prefectural Magistrate, or a District Magistrate arrives with a retinue to welcome them):

the administrative officers (*zhishi*) shall stand outside the second gate; the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and those below him shall stand inside the third gate. In these cases, those further from the entrance are considered superior. Regarding the protocol for escorting officials:

the Head Seat and the assembly shall stand inside [the gates], with those closer to the entrance being superior. All must be orderly and uniform; no irregularities are permitted. As for the procedure when the Abbot escorts officials: [the same applies].
The person stands in the Dharma Hall and invites the administrative officers (*zhishi*),
the various *jianyuan* (in some places, the deputy *yuan* are also established), the *weina*, the *dianzuo*, and the *zhisui*. First, they invite the administrative heads (*zhishou*).
The former retired administrator was invited for tea. After the tea, the abbot announced: "A certain administrative official has requested to retire.
I request that the assembly deliberate together on who might be suitable to fill this position. After he had consulted them repeatedly, the assembly remained silent.
The Abbot then says: "I wish to request such-and-such a person to serve as a certain administrative officer (*karmadāna*). What is the assembly’s intention?

If the assembly consents, he orders an attendant to invite that person, along with those who are acquainted with them and others who should be invited in succession. After serving tea once more, the Abbot stands up and says:
"Such-and-such an administrative officer has requested to resign. As we cannot allow this position to remain vacant, I wish to request such-and-such a person."

The Head Seat shall serve as the [Name] Administrative Officer (zhishi). We hope that the assembly will join in the formal invitation; we trust you will not refuse, but rather keep the Buddha-Dharma in mind.

Having completed the invitation, perform two prostrations with the hands extended and three full bows (*li*). [First prostration with hands extended: "This newly ordained monk has but recently entered the monastic community and is inexperienced in all matters.

Having been most graciously appointed by the Venerable Master, I am filled with the utmost trepidation. [Second prostration with hands extended, expressing greetings: "I humbly pray that the Venerable Master’s health and daily life are entirely auspicious. Then, perform three prostrations touching the ground (*chuli*). The various administrative officers and others shall offer their congratulations.

The Abbot performs two full prostrations and three bows (the first prostration says: "It is a source of great fortune for this monastery; we rejoice that the newly appointed administrative official [Name] has received your compassionate command. We, your humble servants, feel a boundless sense of joy and exultation.")

Furthermore, they exchange greetings and perform the *chuli* (touching the ground with the forehead) as before. Next, the new *shishi* (administrative official) and the others exchange congratulations and thanks, each performing three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*).

[The words of thanks say: "We are deeply grateful for your recommendation; we are overcome with shame and trepidation. [The words of congratulation say: "We are indebted to the assembly’s worthy talent; we humbly pray that you may rejoice. They turn their chairs to face one another and drink the medicinal soup.
They inform the assembly, ring the bell to gather them, and enter the hall to stand in formation. The *weina* burns incense before the Sacred Monk and then makes a private report to the Abbot.

The person circumambulates the hall once, and after completing the inquiries, strikes the mallet once and says: "I inform the assembly: Formerly, the administrative officer [Name] requested to retire.
This office must not be left vacant. Recently, we received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, who commanded that I be invited to serve as the administrative officer [Name].
I respectfully inform you. He strikes the mallet once again. Then, the former administrative officers, heads of departments, and retired masters...

The former [monks] together approach and request [the candidate]; once it has been accepted, they perform two prostrations with hands extended and three full prostrations (the words of thanks are the same as before).

At that time, the *vinaya-dhara* strikes the mallet once and says: "It is now announced that such-and-such a person has been requested to serve as the administrative official for such-and-such a post. He strikes the mallet once again.

The *karmadāna* leads [the candidate] before the *seng-seng* (the sacred image) to perform two prostrations with hands extended and three full prostrations, then withdraws the sitting mat and touches [the feet] before the *śraddhā-agra* (head seat).
He performs three prostrations, and the assembly returns the bows. The Guest Master leads him out while touring the hall. The Rector announces:
"I request the assembly to escort the administrative official to the storehouse. If it is the Rector who is being invited, the Guest Master (or the Head Attendant) announces:
"I request the assembly to escort the Rector to the Hall Office. The Abbot and those below him escort him to either the storehouse or the Hall Office. The Abbot [then proceeds].

Established according to the position of the presiding master: the newly appointed administrator performs two prostrations with both knees and three full prostrations before the incumbent abbot, escorts the abbot out, and then returns to his own station to perform three prostrations with touching heads to his colleagues.
Next, he performs three prostrations with touching heads to the Head Seat and the assembly, escorts the assembly out, and then the attendant collects the robes and bedding in a chest and returns.
The arrangements for this occasion are as follows: The guest prefect leads the tour of the quarters, first proceeding to the Abbot’s hall where they take their seats and drink soup.

The retired officials (qinjiu) accompany them, and after the tour of the quarters is completed in due order, the Abbot, the administrative officers (zhishi), and the heads of departments (toushou) shall jointly hand over the funds, silks, and recorded ledgers to the new and former administrative officers.
Whether on that same day or the following day, tea and hot water shall be served, after which they retire. Next—

The day before, the administrative office (Kusi) specially prepares a meal for them. (Those newly appointed as administrators shall temporarily follow the established regulations; they must not arbitrarily alter them or boast of their own achievements.

If they have personal views, they should wait for a private audience to discuss them with the Abbot and their colleagues. What can be implemented should be put into practice, and what should be halted should be stopped. They must not disregard the public interest for private gain or disturb the assembly.

On the following day, the Abbot personally serves tea in the Hall specifically for the new and former administrators. (The tea notice reads: "This morning, after the midday meal, the Abbot will retire to the Cloud Hall to serve tea, specifically for the new and former [Name] administrators.")

This matter expresses the ritual of congratulations and thanks, and also requests the Head Seat and the assembly to graciously join as honored companions. On this day of this month, the attendant [Name] respectfully informs you. The tea notice shall be posted outside the hall, on the upper section.

After the new *jianyuan* (superintendent) has finished serving tea and soup to the *tangtou*, the *shouzuo*, and the others, he enters the hall to prepare and serve the tea with the *shouzuo* and the assembly.

(The Tea Notice states: "The Kusi office, this morning after the midday meal, has come to the Cloud Hall to prepare and serve tea. We specially invite the *shouzuo* and the assembly, as well as all the administrative officers (*zhishi*), to join us. We humbly hope that the assembly will graciously deign to descend and attend. On this day of this month. )

[The administrative monk so-and-so respectfully informs: Before the midday meal, having prepared the tea casket and tray, present the tea notice to the Head Seat [with these words]: "We have heard that the Head Seat will retire from the midday meal this morning specifically to prepare tea for the hall;

we humbly hope you will deign to descend in your compassion. Either perform three prostrations (this is for inviting the venerable elders residing in the monastery and the Head Seat who has been ordained), or simply exchange formal greetings and withdraw.
Immediately have an attendant post the tea notice outside the hall in the lower section, and have an attendant invite [the guests].

The various head officers of the quarters then proceed to the Hall to formally invite the Abbot to serve as the presiding master. They perform two prostrations with hands opened (the first prostration is made while saying: "This morning, following the meal, we have specially prepared tea in the hall for the Head Seat;

we respectfully request that you, the Venerable Master, join the assembly. We humbly hope for your compassionate favor and grant us your permission"). After the second prostration with hands opened—during which they exchange greetings regarding the weather—they perform three prostrations with hands touching the ground.

Having thus requested their participation, the officers enter the hall to join the assembly. On the following day, within the Kitchen Hall, they specifically conduct the formal handover of duties to the administrative officers and head officials.

Please request the head of the assembly to accompany you. Thereafter, the administrative officers (zhishi), the head seat (shouzuo), and others shall take turns specifically preparing tea for the new and former administrative officers.
If it is the deputy director (fuyuan), the kitchen steward (dianzuo), or the year-steward (zhisui), they shall proceed to the storehouse hall (kudang).

If it is the rector (weina), they shall proceed to the office of the hall administration (tangsi). Specifically for the handover between colleagues, tea shall be prepared (note: only the abbot, the director of the monastery [jianyuan], and the head seat enter the hall to prepare the tea).

Chief Administrator.
The position of *jianyuan* (Superintendent) oversees all affairs of the monastery gate. This includes providing official services, receiving and offering salutations, congratulations, and thanks;

presiding over incense offerings when the monastic assembly gathers and hosting visiting dignitaries; attending to the auspicious and inauspicious events of patrons, such as celebrations and mourning; managing the lending and borrowing of funds;

and overseeing the annual budget of the monastery’s cash and grain, including the collection of income and expenditure for preparation, as well as the annual provisions of rice, wheat, and other materials for meals.

At the appropriate times, one should purchase provisions; likewise, the preparation of sauces and vinegar must follow the seasonal requirements. Furthermore, tasks such as pressing oil and grinding flour should be attended to with care.

The monastic community should always maintain an excellent spirit regarding the provision of midday meals and morning gruel, attending to the four classes of visitors with hospitality rather than negligence.

This includes the Winter Retreat, the New Year’s Retreat, the Breaking of the Summer Retreat, and the Observance of the Summer Retreat, as well as the Great Eggplant Feast (on the fifth day of the fifth month, the seventh day of the seventh month, the ninth day of the ninth month, the opening and closing of the furnace, and the eighth day of the twelfth month and the fifteenth day of the second month). As it is said:
Regarding the superior *zhāihuì* (vegetarian feast assemblies), if the monastery administration (*jiànyuàn*) has the resources, it should organize them itself;
if its strength is insufficient, it should invite others to manage them. Matters that are minor for the monastery or routine procedures may be settled unilaterally.

However, if the matter is somewhat significant or involves a new precedent, the administrative officers (*zhīshì*) and head monks (*tóushǒu*) must consult together before reporting to the resident master (*zhùchǎn*).

Those who uphold the precepts should practice this. From the point of "abiding in one's own observance" downwards, if there are matters—great or small—that do not conform to proper rules or accord with human sentiment, one must present them through tactful explanation; one must neither remain silent nor speak with coarse or violent language.
Regarding the method for instructing junior practitioners, it is appropriate to employ skillful means to arrange matters in advance; one must not act recklessly.
Regarding the administration of the whip: if there is a need for punishment, it should be carried out in the library hall before the assembly, and shall not exceed ten or so strokes.
One must be cautious regarding unforeseen matters. For instance, when sending a practitioner out of the monastery, they must have committed a grave offense;
their confession of guilt must be obtained and reported to the Abbot before they are dismissed. In such cases, further corporal punishment is unnecessary. Should one act otherwise—

One must avoid official inquiries regarding the appointment of those such as the *xiangfang* (street alms-collector), *huazhu* (inviter), *zhuangzhu* (manager of estates), *tantou* (charcoal-head), *jiangtou* (sauce-head), *zhoutou* (congee-head), *xiangfang banruotou* (street Prajñā-head), *Huayan tou* (Avataṃsaka-head), *yutou* (bath-head), *shuitou* (water-head), *yantou* (garden-head), *motou* (mill-head), and *dengtou* (lamp-head).

Those who are to assist the monastery should be requested by the *toushou* (administrative heads) at the appropriate time, having first reported the matter to the *zhuchi* (abbot). One must not act otherwise.
One must not be negligent or dilatory. When a donor enters the monastery, one should arrange a guest seat and receive them according to the Dharma.
If a great vegetarian feast (dazhai) is to be held, one should consult in advance with the various administrators and heads of departments to ensure that no deficiencies occur at the last moment.

The character of the Chief Administrator (jianyuan) should be to honor the worthy and tolerate the masses; to maintain harmony between superiors and subordinates; and to provide security for his colleagues, so that the entire community may always remain joyful.
With a mindful heart, you must not rely on your power and status to treat the assembly with contempt, nor act according to your own whims to cause unrest among the community.

Unless ill or attending to official guests, everyone shall attend the hall; this is for the sake of the benefit provided during the two daily periods of practice. Practitioners should maintain a dignified and orderly appearance.
If the treasury lacks funds for expenditures, one should exert one's efforts and devise strategies oneself; it is inappropriate to trouble or disturb the master of the house.
When presenting these matters to the assembly, those who possess talent and virtue should be recommended and praised.
If there are those holding office who fail to advance or whose holy life is suspect, they should be privately and subtly admonished so that they may be inspired to renew themselves.

To ensure that the Dharma remains for a long time, if there is someone acting as a "great official" who commits transgressions or causes harm to the monastery, one should likewise inform the abbot so that he may take cognizance of it.
As for all other matters concerning appearance and communal affairs, one should simply observe their successful completion from a distance.

The term *vinaya* in Sanskrit is translated here as *yuezhong* (Pleaser of the Assembly). He presides over all matters arising within the monastic community. When new arrivals join the assembly to take up residence, they must be diligent and respectful in their observance of the rites.

Those who have come from various regions on official business, as well as persons of renowned virtue, shall be specially selected and assigned to the superior quarters (*shangliao*). Upon completion of their service, they shall retire.

The Head Elder shall arrange the seating for the morning gruel and midday meal at the three upper sections of the hall according to the order of seniority indicated in the Abbot’s official notice (*jūji-tō*) and the opening sermon (*kaidō-so*).
If there are renowned virtuous monks from other quarters present, they shall also be arranged in the sequence of their respective categories of precept seniority at the three upper sections.
Within the hall, woolen mats and straw mats shall be replaced between winter and summer, and cooling screens as well as warming screens shall be hung.

When the outer curtains are rolled up and the inner curtains opened, and the incense burners are prepared for the commencement of the summer retreat, the notice board for the retreat must be posted in advance.
One must ensure that the incense and lamps within the hall are properly arranged, the area before the hall is swept clean, and the offering vessels are set out before the guests.

Furthermore, the attendant of the Holy Monk, the Hall Superintendent, and the offering attendants must all maintain constant supervision. They shall prepare the quarters, ensuring that doors, windows, seating positions, bedding, curtains, and all necessary utensils are in order.

Objects must always be inspected, maintained, and kept in order. Should anything be missing, the storehouse (kūsi) and the year-round steward (chak-sui) must be notified so that replacements may be provided.
Regarding the porridge, rice, bedding, curtains, and attendants for the sick monks in the Yanshou Hall, these matters shall all be jointly supervised by the hall master (tángzhǔ).

Care must be taken not to allow the patients to be deprived of their proper accommodations. As for the various minor heads of departments within the monastery, they are to be treated like the attendants of the Hall Head (tángtóu).

The positions of the Abbot’s Attendant, the Master of the Hall for Extending Life, the Head of the Incense Burner, the Various Dormitory Masters, the Chief Seat Holder, the Tower Master, the Hall Master, and the Rector are all appointed by request.
If there is an abundance of funds and goods within the halls or towers, the Abbot shall request them [to manage them].

If one violates the rules of conduct, those who have committed major offenses shall be reported to the Abbot and ordered to leave the community; minor offenders shall merely be ordered to move to another dormitory. In the event of quarrels or disputes, [the appropriate measures shall be taken].
Furthermore, one should first exhaust all efforts to reach a harmonious settlement. Only if the two disputing parties do not submit should one proceed according to the established rules.

If an item is lost within the community and the owner insists on a search, one must inform the assembly and conduct a search of the quarters. If the item is not found upon searching, the owner may leave the assembly or move to another quarters.
If the lost object is of little value, one should immediately settle the matter amicably with the owner and allow them to desist, thereby sparing them further trouble.

This would cause commotion among the assembly and create stagnation within the monastic community. Funds designated for the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ) should only be used to purchase incense, lamps, and ritual implements;

they must not be diverted for other purposes. If the funds are withdrawn from the treasury and placed under the custody of the Hall Superintendent, they shall be recorded in the ledger and disbursed by the Holy Monk’s attendant.
If the funds belong to the general monastic accounts, one must await official instructions and notification before proceeding.

A notice shall be posted to inform all that foot-copies (job-se) shall be taken and the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu) shall verify them according to established precedent to collect the funds for the account books.

Although the issuance of official warrants (gongping) is handled solely by the Treasury Office (Kusi), matters involving the office of the Rector (Weina) must be further scrutinized and deemed appropriate.
For monks seeking formal registration (guada), the authenticity of their Ministry of Sacrifices warrants must be verified in every case. If they are not...

One must avoid being negligent. For instance, regarding the reporting of a monk’s illness to the authorities, the escorting of deceased monks, the auctioning of their belongings, and the submission of the deceased monk’s ordination certificate (*dudie*) or documents for purple robes and honorary titles (*shihao*), the *vinaya-master* (Weina) shall take exclusive and diligent charge.

He shall notify the treasury office and submit the official receipt and the deceased monk’s ordination certificate to the authorities, ensuring that they are not submitted after the official deadline. [Read.]

The *shu* (administrative official) shall strike the gavel with full deliberation and scrutiny, ensuring that the donor generates wholesome merit. Special tea and soup must be prepared for newly arrived guests;

no ritual courtesy may be omitted. Furthermore, one must report the new arrivals' seniority (*jìlà*) to the attendants (*shìzhě*), the administrative officers (*zhīshì*), the heads of departments (*tóushǒu*), and their own quarters for registration.

It is important to know the sequence of the *kṣānti-lakṣa* (years since ordination). [For a new arrival: "The Elder So-and-so has been ordained for X years and is ranked below So-and-so. You should instruct each of the communal quarters (*sālā*) to prepare two tablets:

one for the entry into the quarter and one for the sequence of the *kṣānti-lakṣa*. These must be adjusted at every session by drawing and replacing names. This is so that the seating arrangements for the tea service and the order of precedence among the *vāsaka-pati* (quarter masters) and *śālā-pati* (hall masters) shall not be confused.
When there is a general invitation for the entire community, except for the *vāsaka-pati* and those on duty in the hall, everyone must attend together. [Resident Master: ...reside.
Regarding the official in charge of removing illnesses who fails to attend when summoned: the attendant shall step forth from the assembly.

The duty of the *karmadāna* (steward) is to preside over the meals and gruel for the great assembly; he must exercise the mind of the Way (*mārgacitta*) and adapt according to the occasion to ensure the well-being of the community.

One should enjoy peace and happiness, and must not wastefully expend the provisions for the permanent monastic community. Furthermore, when inspecting the kitchen, one must not allow food to be carelessly scattered or discarded.
Those who are capable and experienced should be selected to take turns serving. The regulations governing these duties must not be overly strict.

If one is too strict, it will disturb the assembly; it should not be too lax. If one is too lax, one’s duties will be neglected. At the time of preparing food, one must personally supervise it so that it is naturally refined and pure.
Regarding the preparation of ingredients, as well as the types and quantities of the vegetarian meals and gruel, these must all be discussed in advance with the administrators of the storehouse.
Matters such as the brining, pickling, and storage of vegetables are the exclusive responsibility of the *diànzuò* (the cook). It is not...

Regarding gains and losses at the proper time, one must constantly and earnestly provide guidance. Firewood and torches should be distributed according to the schedule for the common benefit, ensuring they are allotted with strict impartiality.
If matters fall within the jurisdiction of the Chief Administrator, the Head of the Dormitory, or the Steward of the Storehouse, these parties may consult together as appropriate;

however, none should encroach upon the authority or duties of others. As for kitchen stoves, cauldrons, and utensils, if they are old or damaged, they shall be replaced by drawing from the offerings received.

Supplement: In instructing practitioners, one must strive to follow established rules and regulations. For instance, when distributing offerings to the various quarters, one must provide various instructions to ensure they understand the procedures.
Upon seeing the master or the senior monks, one must inquire after their well-being and stand respectfully to the side.

One should select diligent and sharp-witted practitioners to prepare for the distribution of offerings to the Hall Master, the administrative officers, and the head teachers, while constantly observing the conduct within all the quarters.

If there are those who are dull-witted or negligent and cannot keep pace, such as when an administrative head (zhishi-toushou) must retain a practitioner for a time, one should act with expedient compliance rather than insisting on strict enforcement or rotating assignments.
As for the kitchen steward (diansuo), he shall eat his porridge and rice within the kitchen; his food must not differ from that of the assembly.
When preparing meals for the two periods of the day, he must first go to the Sangha Hall to burn incense and perform prostrations before departing.

Food. The duties of the *zhisui* (the official in charge of annual provisions) include presiding over all manual labor within the monastery, as well as the construction and maintenance of the monastery gates and the monks' quarters.
The gates, windows, walls, and partitions, as well as all utensils and implements for daily use, shall be repaired, replaced, and adorned at appropriate times.

Furthermore, one must oversee the operation of the mill, the fields, the manor houses, the oil-press, the stable, the saddled horses, the boats, and the carts; perform sweeping and cleaning; engage in planting; patrol and protect the forests and mountains;

and maintain vigilance against thieves and bandits. Laborers shall be assigned and village residents shall be rotated for these duties, all of whom should act with public-mindedness, diligence, and a sense of timing.

There are other appropriate occasions. For instance, in the event of major construction or significant tasks, one must follow the plans and regulations of the abbot and consult with fellow practitioners;
one must not exercise one's own private views independently.

After one year as a junior administrative official (*gejishi*) or attendant official (*shikishi*), one enters the Abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*) at night to announce one's retirement. One performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloth (*sokusai*) and departs.

On the following morning, after the *weina* has announced the assembly for the morning gruel and the signal mallet has been struck, one enters through the rear gate. First, one strikes the mallet once and says: "Bi... (The remainder of the ritual follows).

"Venerable Abbot [Name], I inform the assembly: yesterday, I received the compassionate command of the Abbot of the Hall, ordering me to enter the storehouse office to serve as the mediator for such-and-such affairs.
Now, as my physical and mental strength are exhausted, I inform the assembly that I shall return to the hall. This is respectfully announced. (He strikes the mallet once more.
He turns behind the Holy Monk, comes before the Abbot, performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full bows. The Abbot first...
He instructs the attendant to move the dining table and respond with a bow. Next, he performs three full prostrations before the Honored Sangha and circumambulates the hall.

Upon exiting the hall, he performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*) for his colleagues. Once the request for the new administrative official (*xin zhishi*) is concluded, the Abbot, the administrative officials, and the Head Seat escort him into the hall to register his residency.
He performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground before the Abbot, who then escorts him to his quarters.
Before the abbot, he performs two prostrations with hands fully extended and three prostrations, then escorts him out the door. Next, he exchanges greetings with the assembly and disperses.

He provides special tea and soup for the newly appointed administrative officer as they tour the quarters. Subsequently, he prepares a special tea service for the new incumbent and the former colleagues together in the original quarters.
Please the head officials.

"Head officials" refers to the Chief Seat (Śayanāsana), the Scribe, the Librarian, the Guest Master, and the Bath Master. All shall follow the same procedure as previously established for the appointment of administrative officers (*karmadāna*).
The reception of their bows and the offering of congratulations shall be conducted exactly as prescribed. They are to be escorted by the assembly of fellow monks.

At the quarters, the abbot performs two prostrations with hands opened and three full prostrations before departing. He then performs three prostrations with the body touching the ground (*chuli*) before the assembly of monks.
The guest prefect leads the tour of the quarters according to the procedure for the administrative officers’ tour of the quarters. For three days, tea and soup are served along with food offerings.

If the Head Seat is being invited, the Abbot of the Hall proceeds to the hall to prepare and serve the tea (the beginning and end of the tea notice are the same as before; however, it is modified to read: "Solely for the newly appointed Head Seat, this is briefly offered to express our congratulations").

[Protocol: If there is an incumbent Head Seat (Shouzuo), one says: "Specifically for the new and incumbent Head Seats, we briefly perform this ceremony to express congratulations and gratitude; we also request that the administrative officers (Zhishi) and the assembly join us to grace us with their presence.

On the following day, the Head Seat, in turn, [performs the ceremony] for the Secretary (Shuji)—if there is no Secretary, then specifically for the next-ranking Head Official (Tou-shou). The assembly gathers in the Hall for the tea service (Jian-dian). [The invitation slip reads: "The Bhikṣu [Name], Head Seat, respectfully informs:

This morning, after the midday meal, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall (Yuntang) for the tea service, specifically for the Secretary and the assembly. We further request that all administrative officers accompany us. We humbly hope that you will graciously descend to grace us with your presence. Dated [Month and Day]. Signed by [Name] of the preceding position. The envelope reads: "Invitation Slip."

The stationery and communal requisites are hereby respectfully sealed by [Name] of the aforementioned office. This shall be affixed to the front of the petition box. Having presented this request, it is to be posted on the southern wall of the Sangha Hall. Next, the Abbot is invited to enter the hall to sit together with the assembly. Prior to the meal, the attendants are instructed to invite the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) and the heads of the various departments.

At the time of the meal, after the long board has been struck and the assembly is settled, the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) immediately rises before the Sacred Monk (*arhat*), burns incense, performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*daizhan sanbai*), circumambulates the hall once, and exits while maintaining a standing greeting (*wenxun*).

Monks remaining outside the hall stay outside. The Chief Administrator (*jianyuan*) and the Rector (*weina*) are provided with food, though they must first inform the Second Seat to act as their proxy for the blessing of the food (*zhoushi*). This applies to all those including the Scribe, the Librarian, the Bath Master, the Water Master, the Street Attendant, and the Charcoal Master. [End of Section]
Those invited by the Abbot (Dangtou) shall all attend to the preparation of tea and incense in their own quarters.

The Abbot’s attendant, the attendant for the Sacred Monk (Shengseng), the Hall Master (Dianzhu), the Hall Supervisor (Dangzhu), the Head of Purification (Jingtou), the Head of the Incense Burner (Lutou), and others are all appointed by the Rector (Weina).

For special tea and soup services held for three days at the monastery, the Hall Master, the Street-Walker (Fangjie), and the Ritual Reciter (Biaobai) of the Library (Zangxia) are all appointed by the Librarian (Zangzhu). Within the monastery...
The serving of tea and soup is specifically as described previously.

The Chief Seat (Shouzuo) serves as the representative of the assembly of monks, upholding what is right and correcting what is not. Within the hall, he oversees the seating arrangements, the hanging of robes and bedding, and the placement of alms bowls.
When spreading out the alms bowl to eat congee, rice, tea, or soup, one must always do so with refinement and composure.

Regarding all matters within the hall that are not in accordance with the Dharma, one should address the assembly with gentle words before the congee is served, ensuring that the speech is concise and appropriate. When eating, the head seat (śrāmaṇera) must not be too hurried;
he should take his time and accompany the rest of the monks in a relaxed manner. He must not finish first and then stand with his hands folded in a gesture of formality.
Observe the assembly and ensure that they do not act with haste or agitation, as if preparing gruel or rice improperly, or that their pacing is too fast or too slow and lacks regulation;
the Head Seat (Shouzuo) shall inspect all such matters and inform the administrators, so that the members of the hall may dwell in peace and comfort.

Prior to the dismissal of the session, the Head Seat enters the hall, burns incense before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), and takes his seat in position. The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi) then notifies the various [members].

The Chief Seat (shouzuo) announces: "The Hall is now open" (Huilin strikes the board before the quarters three times to notify the assembly). The assembly enters the hall and sits facing one another according to their respective positions.
The attendant of the Hall Office first reports to the Abbot to hang the "Evening Session" (fangcan) plaque, and then raises the curtain at the front of the hall.

The practitioner bows before the Head Seat and asks with a low voice, "Venerable Teacher, the session is over. Then, standing upright and bowing before the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni), he shouts, "Dismissal!
Thereafter, he strikes the bell for dismissal. Once the mats are folded and the curtains are lowered, he returns to his quarters to bow and partake of soup as he pleases.
If there is a recitation, he shall enter [the hall] only after returning to his quarters, bowing, and finishing the soup.
In the hall, one may spread out the sitting mat and hang the curtains beneath it. At dusk, when the bell tolls, one lowers the window curtains; at dawn, they are rolled up immediately.
Within the hall, before the assembly has opened for meditation (kaizō), one must not roll up the mats or fold the blankets to cover them with curtains, for fear of disturbing the assembly.

After the morning gruel and once meditation has been opened, and until the evening session has concluded, one must under no circumstances spread out the mats or cover oneself with blankets to sleep. In the early morning, [one attends] the long board.
At the time of the midday meal, one may only lower the alms bowl after the three strikes of the gong. When entering the hall or reciting the Buddha’s name, one must not cover the head.

After the final striking of the wooden mallet and the formal bowing for food by the Head Seat (Śraddhādeśaka), one may then engage in meditation. Upon concluding the meditation, one should emerge with composed dignity. One must wait until the Head Seat has finished eating before the assembly may eat.
Once the meal is concluded, all actions—from hanging up the bowl to descending from the platform—must be performed with careful deliberation and slowness. Do not [act hastily].
One may become coarse and impulsive. The above points are all matters for the Head Seat (Shouzuo) to investigate and point out.

As for the duties of the Secretary (Shuzhuang), he is primarily responsible for managing the correspondence and documents of the mountain gate; his calligraphy must be true and formal, and his language must be orderly and precise.

Seal the envelopes according to the proper method. Furthermore, one must recognize the distinctions between the noble and the humble, and what is appropriate for those who have touched [impure things] versus those who are pure, as well as for monastics and laypeople.

When writing letters to government officials, one must especially refrain from sending them recklessly. Each year, the fundraising master (huazhu) should arrange his correspondence in advance; it must be prepared immediately and carefully inspected.

This is done for fear that the sealing might be erroneous or that the donor’s name might be omitted, resulting in the donor’s clear resentment. As for writing letters on behalf of the monastery’s permanent property (changzhu):
The Head of the Monastery shall use his own permanent stationery and writing implements. For instance, when writing letters on behalf of the Abbot, one must use the Abbot’s stationery and implements;
it is improper to encroach upon these for personal correspondence. One should deeply guard against even the slightest dust accumulating into a mountain.

Special tea and soup offerings shall be prepared for newly arrived monks, and the rites must not be omitted. All official notices for the monastery gate and the formal petitions for vegetarian feasts and assemblies shall be carefully and skillfully composed.

One should compile and transcribe according to the Dharma all writings from ancient and modern times, such as letters, prefaces, and prose compositions; these must be read extensively to increase one’s erudition.
If one’s speech is dignified and formal, and one’s conduct accords with the Dharma, then one will be the eyes and brows for a thousand li, bringing splendor to the entire assembly.

However, one must not single-mindedly devote oneself to holding pens and inkstones while showing contempt for one’s fellow practitioners, nor treat the Buddha-Dharma as a mere matter of worldly affairs. — *Chanyueji* (The Record of Chanyue).
Ji himself was styled a "poet-monk. As for Jia Dao and Huixiu, their drifting through secular officialdom was surely not the original intent of leaving the household life.

The Abbot of the Tripitaka—Abbot, you who hold the golden scriptures in your hands—must solemnly set out the tables and desks, prepare tea, soup, oil, fire, incense, and candles, and carefully select and invite [the guests].
Regarding the method for requesting a desk (an-wei) for the Abbot, the lay attendants, the *biaobai*, those providing support, the residents of the quarters, and the assembly reading the scriptures:

First, one requests the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) of the Scripture Hall, inquiring whether a desk is available where one may reside. If a desk is available, one then consults the Librarian (*zangzhu*) regarding it.
After tea, the Librarian leads the applicant to the front of the desk in the Scripture Hall, where each person touches [the desk].

Perform one bow according to ritual. Escort the abbot’s steward (zangzhu) out. Before the sacred image, perform three full prostrations (dazhan) and rise. Perform a touching-bow (chuli) once to the Head Seat (shouzuo). Circumambulate the hall once.
Visit the Hall Master (dianzhu) and request that he conduct the sutra assembly (huijing) at the proper time; there are no bows for this. At dawn, the assembly rises.

Before the evening end-of-session bell (fangcan), the Hall Master strikes the bell to assemble the monks for the sutra session, during which the accounts of income and expenditure are settled. This is the sutra assembly.

The *saṃgha* should burn incense and pay obeisance within the repository. When carrying the scriptures with great reverence along the path, one must not engage in conversation or laughter with others.
Scriptures must not be piled upon desks, nor should pens, inkstones, miscellaneous items, or texts related to meditation manuals be placed there.
One should personally attend to lighting the lamps, replenishing the oil, and extinguishing them with meticulous care, for fear of defiling the holy teachings. Within the hall...
One may receive visiting guests; if someone comes to visit, one should silently bow and return to the quarters.

One must also not converse with others outside the window where the sutras are being read, for fear of disturbing the assembly. If there are clouds and mist, or if it is damp and humid; if the hands have been wiped and are still wet;
or if one is by a fire, or under the moonlight—these are all unsuitable conditions for reading the sutras. Regarding the method of rolling up the scroll: if it is too tight, it will be damaged.

Regarding the sutras: do not let them be uneven when placed before you. Do not lean against a desk with your body to press down on the sutras. Do not bite the sutra’s binding cord with your teeth. As for the method of opening the case:
grasp the top lid with both hands—the left hand facing upward and the right hand facing downward—and take hold of it together.

Place it gently upon the desk so that it makes no sound. As for the method of closing the case: the right hand faces upward and the left hand faces downward as you join them together. This, too, must be done with care and precision.

There are specific protocols for opening, folding, unrolling, and tying the cords of the sutras. Inquire with the Chief Seat (Shouzuo) who oversees the sutra-reading in the hall or with those experienced in these matters.
By the side of the sutra table, one must not untie or fasten one's robes, nor use a needle to pick lice.
If you do not recognize the characters, first consult the rhyming dictionary; only when doubts remain may you ask questions. If the inquiries are numerous...
Do not allow [the scriptures] to be exposed; if you must leave them for even a moment, they must be covered. Furthermore, you must not fold a *kāṣāya* robe and place it upon the scriptures.
When reading the scriptures, sit upright with the body straightened; do not make sounds, nor move your lips, nor attend to other matters.
When the evening session concludes and the lamps are extinguished, one must immediately follow the assembly back to the hall;
one must not leave the lamp burning, thereby disturbing the assembly and causing the Head Seat (śrāmaṇera) to become preoccupied with thoughts.

If, after the lamp-stand has been lowered in the evening and the oil has been replenished, an emergency arises such that one cannot attend the hall for the scripture recitation, one should take the lamp from the neighboring desk and lower the stand. If one wishes to withdraw from one's seat, one must first announce this as well.
The Chief Seat (Śrāmaṇera) of the Sūtra Hall and the Librarian shall return the scriptures to the canon before their wishes may be fulfilled.
All that has been stated above must be made known by the Librarian to the assembly. If they do not act according to the Dharma, he must provide skillful instruction.
All records of receipts and expenditures must be entered clearly and distinctly; these shall be subject solely to the signature of the Abbot.
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Three;
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Four: The Guest Prefect (*zhikè*).

When officials, lay patrons (*dānapati*), venerable elders, monastic officials, or persons of renown from various quarters enter the monastery for an inspection, the attendant first orders the *xingzhe* (attendant) to inform the Abbot.
Subsequently, the guest master (*zhike*) leads them up, ensuring they are escorted to their respective accommodations.
For ordinary guests, tea and soup are served at the guest quarters; however, if they wish to go to the Abbot’s quarters or the storehouse...
When visiting the various quarters, one should have an attendant lead the way. Within the *danguo* (guest) quarters, bedding, curtains, and utensils must always be kept orderly;

the resident monks and guests should be treated with hospitality. When receiving offerings from donors, whether for a meal or for the incense offering, these matters are all managed under the guidance of the *zhiké* (guest master).
When meeting with visitors, one must be respectful and solemn; one must not engage in idle or useless conversation.

One must always praise the master, the administrative head, the leaders, and all the members of the assembly according to reality, highlighting their virtuous deeds so as to inspire goodness in others;
one must never broadcast the family's internal failings to the outside world.

The duties of the *kūtū* (treasurer) consist primarily in managing the annual accounts for the receipt and disbursement of permanent funds, grain, and currency. All money and goods received must be immediately recorded in the official ledger and kept under strict supervision;
expenditures must be clearly accounted for. Furthermore, he must always maintain knowledge of the quantity and availability of rice and wheat used for ritual provisions.
Purchase items promptly upon their arrival and keep a record once every ten days; these shall first be signed by the Assistant Administrator (Tongzhishi).
At the end of each month, a general tally shall be made, signed by all members of the abbot’s staff and below. Precious metals and valuables must not be hidden away;
the quantity of cash on hand must always be known. One must not privately lend money to others. Should the Abbot or his colleagues act improperly, [the following shall apply].
Regarding the application of the principles of reason, one must resolutely adhere to them without yielding to personal sentiment.

Any property belonging to the permanent endowment (sthavira-vastu), even down to a single hair’s breadth, is the shared property of the Sangha of the ten directions. How could it be appropriate to use such property for private purposes according to one's own whims?
Unless it concerns the provisions supplied by the monastery gate to donors or officials who provide powerful protection, it is improper in all cases to employ the property of the permanent endowment.

Regarding the management of communal affairs: in matters such as lending or borrowing rice, wheat, money, or goods, one must not arbitrarily move any property belonging to the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*), except for the personal robes and bowls of the master or his colleagues which they may manage themselves.
The steward in charge of the storehouse must possess both mental acuity and physical strength, be proficient in calculation, maintain personal integrity and purity, and be truthful in word and deed;
only when he is thus esteemed and submissive by the assembly may he be entrusted with these duties. He should be like a mountain.

A temple in the countryside is somewhat distant from the city. One should prepare items for the use of the monastic community, such as medicine, honey, tea, and paper, and ensure these can be purchased when monks travel there.
One must constantly maintain mindfulness of the Way and not disdain the labor involved.
Supplies necessary for sick monks must not be lacking; they should be provided immediately whenever requested. If the storehouses are leaky, like those of a sparrow...
Rats cause damage and depletion; rice and wheat become damp and moldy. Constantly inspect the storage and placement of communal property and provide protection.
If matters are not handled according to the Dharma, they shall all be managed by the storekeeper in consultation with his colleagues.
The bath master (the aforementioned constitute the six head officials) prepares the bathing water by scrubbing and boiling the lye one day prior to the bath.
