On the actual day, before the midday meal, he hangs up a signboard indicating the opening of the bath, whether for washing away sweat or for cleansing the hair.
He then arranges the bathing stations for all the holy ones, as well as clean towels, incense, flowers, lamps, and candles; these are all prepared by the assembly of monks.

Regarding the wind-medicine tea service and the procedure for bathing in the bathhouse: After the midday meal, the wooden board is struck. Together with the donor, one enters the hall to burn incense and prostrate, inviting the sacred images to enter the bath.
After a long while, the board is struck again to signal the assembly; first, two sessions of the monks enter the bath, followed by one session of the attendants (*xingzhe*).
Finally, the abbot and the administrative officers (*zhishi*) enter the bath. This is the method for striking the board within the bathhouse.

One part hot water, two parts cold water, and three parts full [of liquid]. Regarding the method for entering the bath: when the senior monks ascend to the hall and the juniors descend from the hall, each must prepare a clean towel and bathing requisites.
One must not remain naked without shame, nor speak or laugh loudly, nor rattle buckets and ladles, nor spit or discharge filth.
When washing clothes, one must dry them over a fire or in the wind; furthermore, one must not run barefoot to the bath or allow the body to defile the clean path. All of these [are prohibited].
When the community of monks uses bathing water, one must always yield to those of seniority and must not act with impetuosity.

Should anyone violate these rules, the master of the bath must gently admonish and instruct them, never showing a countenance of resentment or acting in opposition to the assembly. One must ensure that the bath is provided for the residents of the quarters at the proper time and that no service is neglected.
On days when the bath is permitted, one should wait until the sweeping and the lighting of lamps are completed, and then together brush [the area clean].
The bathhouse must be cleaned before one may rest at will. The *wenli* (administrative calendar) is signed solely by the Head of the Hall (*tangtou*).

The various attendants include: the Water Attendant, the Charcoal Attendant, the Huayan Attendant, the Rice and Grain Attendant, the Vegetable Attendant, the Soy Sauce Attendant, the Water Attendant, the Charcoal Attendant, and the Lamp Attendant.

The *Yantou*, *Banzhou*, *Jingtou*, and *Mituo* [Sūtras] are all intended to externally encourage donors to increase their fields of merit and internally assist the monastic groves in sustaining the fruits of the Path.
Were it not for a mind that accords with the sages and stirs toward the Way, how could these hopes of the multitude be universally fulfilled?
The head of the Mòtóu Garden and the master of the monastery hold the office of the *mòtóu* (grinder).
The fine sieve is used for removing shards and rubble; the coarse sieve is used for removing dust and grit.
The fine sieve must use a fan-cart; the coarse sieve must be struck three hundred times. Fresh wheat does not require [the coarse sieve].
Washing: It is appropriate to wash the parched wheat. Mix two *dou* with eight *dou* of water. In the ninth month of the year, wash three *dou*;
increase by one *dou* each month until six *dou* are washed in the twelfth month. In the first month [of the following year], wash five *dou*;
decrease by one *dou* each month until two *dou* are washed in the fourth month. Soak and mix for one night so that it is neither dry nor wet. This is the general rule.

Thus, there is a proverb that says: "Coarse dust and fine leaks; wash the wheat according to the four seasons. Furthermore, observe the dryness or moisture of the wheat to adjust the duration of the soaking.
If the wheat is too dry or too moist, it is somewhat difficult to obtain flour. Regarding the first and second [stages], if they are not finely ground, flour will likewise be difficult to obtain.
The first and second are for making steamed flour (*mōmen*), while the third is for moist flour (*nimen*). The fourth... [and so on].
Fifth is washing the flour. The sieve must be turned and opened; it is not appropriate to kick it with one's feet. For grinding, use a cloth skirt so as to avoid dust and filth.

One should not allow waste to accumulate around the millstone; keep the path always clean, dry, and level. When feeding twice, ensure that the water and fodder for the first meal do not miss their appointed time.
During the long days of summer, the animals are often thirsty; provide an additional feeding for drinking water. Keep the neck-halter constantly [tightened].
Keep everything level and straight; when pulling fine threads, ensure they remain neat. Supervise the binding and securing of ropes to prevent wear and fraying.

Those who are ill should seek medical treatment early, and those who are weak or exhausted should be allowed to rest immediately. As for laborers and artisans, they must diligently cultivate the aspiration for the Way.
Regarding the duties of the garden master: clearing the ground, building ridges, sowing seeds until they sprout, watering, and weeding—all these tasks must be performed with care.

At the appropriate time, one should consult those who are experienced and well-versed in the matter. One must assess the seasonal conditions and the advantages of the terrain, ensuring that vegetables are produced in continuous succession.
The finest produce should be set aside for the community; only when there is a surplus may it be sold.

Household affairs should be maintained and renewed at all times, and one should always maintain harmonious cooperation with the *dianzuo* (the kitchen steward). To speak briefly: in early spring, one should plant lettuce, turnip, and *jün* (mustard greens).
*Gai*. Before the Cold Food Festival: eggplant, bottle gourd, cucumber, *jue-ming*, *kui* greens, and *lan-xiang*. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, plant radishes.
On the fifteenth day of the sixth month, plant autumn cucumbers. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, plant *tai-zi* and spinach (*bo-leng*).

The duties of the *zhuang-zhu* (village headman) consist of overseeing the two official taxes, plowing, sowing, weeding, reaping, and harvesting; as well as maintaining the fences, grafting trees, and compacting the earth with mud.

Repair walls and enclosures using broken tiles and soil; attend to these tasks personally and supervise them in a timely manner. Guard the boundaries of the grounds by clearly establishing their limits.
Provide fodder for the draft animals and minimize the use of the whip. Accommodate transient guests and select worthy families for residence.
Ensure that women who do needlework always remain in visible areas. Keep accounts of money and grain clear and distinct, and ensure that no alcohol, meat, onions, or scallions enter the premises.
Gate: Do not accept requests for the distribution or disposal [of property] that do not require immediate provision. Monks and laborers should be managed with skillful means;

neighbors to the south and north should be harmonized through tactful conduct. Be careful never to admit idle or miscellaneous persons. When welcoming visiting monks at the guest quarters, be respectful and diligent.

Do not misappropriate funds or goods belonging to the permanent endowment (sangha-ratna) for personal travel expenses. Regarding the monastic provisions: if cattle or donkeys should die, all [responsibilities]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
One must dig deep into the ground and bury [the items] securely. Bring the hides and horns to the authorities immediately so as not to cause the office to investigate or raise suspicions.

If there are instances of trampling seedlings or encroaching upon the crops, one may simply issue strict verbal instructions and warnings; do not resort to beating, scolding, or reporting the matter to the authorities.

Once the autumn harvest is gathered, the hosts and guests shall divide the shares according to the established accounts, ensuring the records are clear and distinct. Furthermore, provide them with generous leniency in many respects. As for...

When there is new construction, renovation, or repairs, one must first inform the administrators (*jishi*) of the monastery gate. The duties of the Monastery Gate Master (*xiayuanzhu*) include: overseeing the monastery gate;
managing the collection of grain and the buying and selling of goods; providing lodging and meals for visiting monks; gathering intelligence regarding local officials of the prefectures and counties;
responding to and reporting on official documents from the government; collecting offerings and financial contributions at the monastery gate; and welcoming donors from distant regions.

The Master of the Yan-shou Hall and the Master of the Jing-tou Hall must invite those who are broad-minded and patient, who maintain their practice of the Way with circumspection, who are skilled at caring for sick monks, and who have a thorough knowledge of cause and effect.
These include the firewood, charcoal, rice, flour, oil, salt, soy sauce, vegetables, tea, soup, medicine, ginger, and dates required for use within the hall.
The preparation of plum preserves and other household affairs shall all be managed through the fundraising efforts of the Hall Master (*tángzhǔ*).

If he lacks the capacity for this, only rice, flour, oil, and charcoal shall be provided from the monastery’s permanent stores. If a sick monk enters the hall for recuperation, the attendants (*xíngzhě*) shall prepare his bedding and arrange it according to the rules;
they shall also provide decoctions and medicines, serve gruel and meals, and inquire after him at every hour, ensuring that he remains comfortable and content.
Just as when a patient suffers much affliction and gives rise to anger; when porridge, rice, broth, and medicine do not agree with them;
and when they groan, cry out, and leave excrement and urine in disarray—one must in all cases regard them with compassion and attend to them, never allowing thoughts of aversion or contempt to arise.
It is like one who wishes to buy wine or administer medicine, using the pretext of soaking medicinal herbs to consume fish, meat, scallions, and leeks for the sake of seeking nourishment and benefit.

At that time, the hall master (*sāldhipati*) shall instruct [the practitioners] with wholesome words regarding the causes and effects of the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), causing them to maintain firm right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and not indulge in deviant thoughts.
He must strictly prohibit the offering of alcohol and meat. Those who perform the tasks of shaving, sewing, or mending are not permitted to remain hidden or to bring alcohol and meat into the hall.

(If medicine requires the use of alcohol, it must be soaked outside the monastery; likewise, pills may be made with alcohol-based glue. When decocting medicine, one may use scallion skins, but even liver, kidneys, fish, or meat must not be used.)

This is permissible; how much more so when it comes to eating and drinking to one's heart's content? If a sick monk is able to carry things himself or can eat some porridge and rice, you should encourage him to observe the fast and must not allow him to lightly violate the prohibitions and precepts.
No one shall be allowed to iron or wash silk cloths in the pots and pans within the hall, as this would interfere with the sick monk’s use of them.

Unless they are those specifically assigned to care for the sick in the hall, no guests shall be entertained with porridge or rice. (In some places, when a sick monk is in the hall, he is included in the aforementioned roster.)

[The expenses] shall be paid from the Treasury Office (and a vegetarian meal offering is also requested). If the sick monk becomes somewhat weak or gravely ill, the Hall Office shall be notified to conduct a census and transfer him to the Infirmary for the Seriously Ill.

Unless one possesses the keen and lucid eye of the Way, one should universally exhort others to single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and pray for rebirth in the Pure Land (it is most excellent to lead one's fellow practitioners to do so by striking the chime).

Among the eight fields of merit, caring for the sick is the foremost (the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; parents; teachers and elders; the poor; bridges; those in need of assistance; and the sick constitute the eight fields of merit).

How much more so for those who have left the household life, who wander like floating weeds—when illness strikes, who will show them compassion? One can rely only upon the compassionate care and support of one’s fellow practitioners.

This is truly a heavy responsibility; how could one treat it with a casual mind? Regarding the duties of the *jingtou* (sanitation officer): at the fifth watch, he lights the lamps; at sunrise, he collects the straw mats (*mao*).
He soaks the counting sticks (*chou*) and the cleaning cloths (*bu*) in water. Next, he brushes and washes the straw mat troughs and sweeps the floor.

He replenishes the straw mats, counting sticks, cleaning cloths, ash, earth, and soapberries (*zaojiao*). He prepares the water in the bathhouse. After the midday meal, he washes the counting sticks and cloths. In the evening, he boils hot water.
Apply oil [to the floor]. Always ensure that hot water flows continuously so as not to cause the assembly to be disturbed in mind.

The role of the *jingtou* (sanitation monitor) is extremely difficult for practitioners to bear and is deeply loathed by others; it can be said that no sin remains unextinguished, no ailment remains uncured, and no merit fails to arise.
When one’s fellow practitioners join their hands in reverence as they pass by the latrine, how could one possibly lack a sense of shame?

The Hall Master, the Bell-ringer, the Hall Attendant, the Pavilion Master, the Stūpa Master, the Arhat Hall Master, the Water-Land Hall Master, and the Zen Hall Master shall wipe away dust and arrange the primary offerings;
they shall sweep and clean at the proper times, adorn the incense burners and lamps, and spread out the mats after the formal sitting.
He waited for the assembly to pay their respects before transmitting the Dharma. It is said that King Zabingta died and was reborn as a thousand-headed fish;
his head was constantly severed by a wheel of swords, and the pain was beyond description. Whenever he heard the sound of a bell, the wheel of swords would not descend.

Thus, striking the bell at dawn and dusk was nothing other than an act of Buddha-work (*buddhakārya*). (According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, when the monk Shi Zhixing struck the bell according to the ritual, its sound shook the underworld, and all those suffering there attained liberation.)
The attendant of the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ), the incense burner attendant, and the hall steward provide the offerings of rice porridge, congee, tea, and soup, as well as incense, lamps, and candles.

Furthermore, the attendants of the Hall Office sweep the hall, wipe down the chests and cabinets, clear and arrange the desks and tables, and set out the formal offering implements for the midday meal. At the time of the meal, they present these offerings.

Conclude. Collect the *chèn* (undergarment) money for the Holy Monk and place it in the tube (the tube is to be placed on the pillar at the head of the Head Seat’s seat; present the *chèn* money briefly to the Head Seat and have him insert it).

Strike the hall gong twice during the two periods of the day (wait until the Abbot has finished with his bowl before striking the gong; immediately withdraw behind the Holy Monk’s screen to stand, thereby avoiding the Abbot’s salutation to the assembly).

As for the clothing, offerings, and benefits received by the Holy Monk, except for the *kāṣāya* robes and *chèn* money—which are collected and managed by the *Vina* to be distributed and used—[from this point]...

Other items, such as handkerchiefs, cloths, needles, thread, tea, medicine, money for sutra-copying, and materials for establishing karmic connections (*kyōzen*), are all obtained by the attendant of the Holy Monk (*Shōsō*).
Although the person appointed to the incense burner (*rozu*) is requested by the Rector (*Vinaya Master*), they are also selected through consultation with the charcoal master.

The burner is opened on the first day of the tenth month and closed on the first day of the second month. The burner is prepared before the release of the evening meditation period (*hōzan*), and charcoal is added before the morning gruel; one must gauge the cold accordingly.

The warming fire: adjust the amount according to the season. If it is warm outside and there is much charcoal, one wastes the offerings of the faithful; if it is cold outside and there is little charcoal, the assembly will suffer from the chill.
Sweep and wipe the area constantly to keep it clean and orderly. When brothers gather around the brazier, they should take turns yielding space to one another.
One must not draw patterns in the ashes, poke at the fire, rattle the fire tongs, engage in idle chatter in groups, or take fire for personal use without permission.

For use in ironing, warming, and so forth, follow the procedure for the *zhítáng* (hall attendant): begin from the second seat of the upper section as the starting point, proceeding in successive rotation until the cycle is complete and begins again.
The *zhítáng* shall oversee the bedding, seats, robes, and bowls of the assembly of monks within the hall.
At dawn, during the time of the long board, when the great assembly has gathered, he shall take the *zhítáng* plaque and perform a formal greeting before the presiding elder of that day, saying:

The Senior Elder (Upādhyāya) shall occupy the Hall today. Once the plaque has been handed over, he shall perform a greeting and return to his seat. (If the seat for the meal and the seat for the bedding are far apart, one must record the location of the bedding;

otherwise, how would those who do not inspect it know where the porridge and rice are? This is so that when the time arrives, there will be no need for a tedious search. Even if they are only adjacent seats, one must still descend from the platform to receive the plaque; the person receiving the plaque merely performs a greeting and accepts it, and neither party descends from the platform.

The person on duty in the Hall shall remain constantly within the hall, supervising both the upper and lower sections. If there is any business to be attended to, one must request a trusted person to act on one's behalf.

Brothers shall take turns guarding [the hall] for short periods. None are permitted to attend the ascent to the Dharma Hall (*shengtang*), the Longevity Hall (*yanshoutang*), or to join external invitations for recitations or tea services at various locations.
If the entire assembly is entering or exiting, except when the *weina* (chant master) directs the locking of the hall, no one shall leave their assigned post without authorization;
only after the end of the evening recitation may they act as they please. Should anything be lost within the hall, it shall be... [it is]... [the responsibility of]... [the guard].

Prior to the dismissal of the evening session (*fangcan*), it is the duty of the person on watch (*zhitang*) to take responsibility (the period of watchkeeping is limited until the dismissal of the session).
If one wishes to open a chest or cabinet, or to take out robes or bedding, one must first inform the person on watch. If one does not report beforehand, they shall be interrogated.
Prior to the opening of the quiet period (*kaijing*) and after the dismissal of the session, the brothers in the assembly must not open chests or cabinets, nor may they take out robes or bedding.
Regarding bedding: if one is sent into the hall with bedding, it is not an impediment. However, if one has committed an offense, the neighbors and the assembly shall reprimand and stop them.
One must not seek to evade this by moving directly to the bedding position in the hall beforehand, thereby causing the members of the hall to become disturbed in mind.

The Chief of the Quarters (Liaozhu) and the Head Seat (Liushouzuo) shall take turns serving as chief according to the order of their entry into the quarters—whether for one month, half a month, or ten days, as determined by local custom.

Each shall be responsible for guarding the robes and bowls of the assembly and for maintaining the inventory of the various utensils and furnishings of the quarters. All such items must be recorded in writing.
When taking over the quarters, the upper and lower sections shall be formally handed over. Special tea and soup shall be served for the newly arrived residents.

Both the new and the old occupants shall take turns boiling water and lighting the stoves. They must replenish the hot water, store fresh water, sweep and scrub thoroughly, and tidy and wipe down everything with diligent devotion to serve the pure assembly.
If there are any matters within the quarters that do not conform to the Dharma, they should be addressed with gentle words; one must not [act otherwise].

The abbot shall issue a reprimand to cause the assembly to take heed. Should there be a deficiency in the furnishings within the quarters, the resident superior may inquire after them during his rounds;
he should do so with tact and inform the authorities. Furthermore, one must not make frivolous requests.

Regarding the soup pitcher used for the community, brothers are not permitted to wash clothes or fumigate it for lice. All miscellaneous persons engaged in buying and selling must be barred from entering the quarters, lest there be [disorder].
Upon departure, the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) of the quarters shall invite a long-resident monk who is experienced in monastic affairs to serve as the attendant for the quarters.

This person shall stay overnight with the residents to guard the robes and bowls of the assembly. Furthermore, they shall provide special hospitality for newly arrived monks—though if the matter becomes burdensome, a single incense stick, a medicinal herb, or a cup of tea may suffice.
If the brothers become noisy, the attendant shall harmonize and exhort them; however, nothing [of this nature] shall be done before the period of silence has opened.
Allow brothers to enter the quarters. After the evening recitation has concluded, one must not enter the *lónggé* (the locked gate) or open the gate arbitrarily.
If there is an urgent matter, such as needing medicinal decoctions or obtaining clothing due to sudden cold, one must inform the *shouzuo* (head of the hall) or the *liaozhu* (chief of the quarters);
only after they have given permission may the gate be opened. Unless specifically requested by the *weina* (chant master), one must not allow anyone to stay overnight in the quarters.

The Hall Head Attendant (Dangtou Shizhe) is appointed in the same manner as the Attendant (Shizhe). He must be physically robust and youthful, possess clear and distinct speech, maintain pure cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), and have a mind capable of swift and skillful discernment.
In this way, all matters for the Hall Head will naturally be accomplished; he shall prepare and serve tea and soup according to the proper seasons. [He shall] go forth...
All arriving guests shall be permitted to observe the mind. Consequently, the venerable elders may transmit the Way in peace.

Although the invitation is extended by the *vinaya-dhara* (Weina), it must still be approved by the Abbot (*fangzhang*). When the external attendant prepares tea for the high seat, he must first report this in advance and then post the notice to invite the guests.
The seating arrangements, the burning of incense, and all ritual decorum must strictly conform to the Dharma. As for the guests...
When receiving visitors, one must know how to adjust the pace—whether responding immediately, or consulting at length, or having a subordinate present a letter to request an audience with the Master;

in all such cases, the Secretary shall provide the written reply. Furthermore, matters such as the special tea service for new arrivals, invitations to enter the room for recitation, the dismissal of the assembly, and the sequence of the summer retreat plaque, are all presided over by the Outer Attendant. The Inner [Attendant]... [text ends].
The attendant shall collect the head monk’s robes and alms bowl, the records of receipts and expenditures, and all items for the public use within the abbot’s quarters;
he shall also manage the tea and soup service, paper and brushes, and clothing for winter and summer, ensuring these are always kept in full readiness and that nothing is lacking.

If there is any deficiency, one must first inform [the abbot]. If one wishes to appraise the robes and utensils of the Hall Master (Dharmasvāmin), one should do so together with the Rector (Karmadāna).
Although the inner and outer attendants have distinct offices and assigned duties, they must always cooperate in providing tea and soup; do not distinguish between "self" and "other.
If one wishes to inquire about the evening "take care of yourself" (zhenzhong) or the morning gruel, one should report and ask whether it will be tomorrow or today.

There are matters concerning the preparation of tea and soup, as well as administrative arrangements. Apart from one’s assigned duties, one must not speak of the affairs of the *zhishi* (administrators), the *toushou* (heads of departments), or the merits and faults of the assembly.
One must likewise refrain from publicly proclaiming the words of the abbot within the assembly.
When hosting guests or managing affairs, one should take it as one’s primary intent to serve the master and provide for the community. One must not decline tasks out of fear of hardship or fatigue.

If you observe a fault in the abbot, do not speak of it behind his back; likewise, you must not emulate the conduct of an abbot by arbitrarily approving or disapproving of matters, nor suppress or exalt the assembly at will.
Instead, focus solely on serving with reverence and diligence to support the monastic community. In all matters, exercise extreme care, ensuring that your thoughts never disturb the abbot’s mind.
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Four;
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Five: The Ritual for the Master of Fundraising (*Huazhu*).
Alternatively, the attendants' quarters (shishōryō) may prepare a list of names from the prefectures and counties to issue invitations to those who have developed the aspiration [to serve].

Or, the administrative officers (chiji) and heads (toshu) may convene to perform the ritual of formal invitation, the etiquette for which is identical to that for the heads. Once they have entered the quarters, they shall organize the correspondence, tea, and medicinal decoctions.
Regarding items entrusted by donors for purchase, they must handle them with meticulous care and diligence, specifically preparing the medicinal decoctions for the handover.

Mark it. Inquire regarding last year’s precedents. It must be a document personally written by the Abbot, or one containing a formal letter of authorization, with the relevant seals and signatures duly attached for presentation and collection.
If items subject to taxation are being transported, they must clearly bear the tax seals.

As for those who transport them by manual labor, one must select individuals who are experienced and conscientious. All property belonging to the monastery and its offerings must be personally received and managed.

One must not rely entirely on human effort, for this serves as a precaution against divergent intentions. For instance, once a letter from a venerable elder has been presented and delivered, one should then perform a prostration.
If one encounters a formal petition from a high official or letters sent through the monastery gate, these should all be presented at once.

When visiting and paying respects to a donor, one should first inspect the formal documents, official notices, and correspondence to ensure there are no errors. Furthermore, one should prepare tea, soup, and items for social courtesy.
With a humble mind and patience, one should skillfully guide them with kind words. If they inquire about the affairs of the mountain gate, [one should respond accordingly].
You must respond with complete sincerity and truthfulness; you must not engage in false boasting or pretense, nor rely upon the authority or influence of officials.
Furthermore, you must not create unnecessary complications beyond the matters at hand, for fear that they may delay your departure and hinder the handover of responsibilities.
Since you have been dispatched by the monastery to act on behalf of the assembly in holding the alms bowl, you must exert your full heart and strength to increase the annual directory.

Except when ill and requiring rest, you may take temporary leave; however, you must not travel to mountains or enter summer retreats. Even if such activities do not hinder your affairs, they will inevitably prevent you from maintaining focused concentration.
Wait until the matter of fundraising is concluded, submit your report, and return to the assembly; only then may you follow [your own inclinations].
Furthermore, the names of donors must not be treated with negligence or omitted. All money and goods received must be clearly accounted for and properly stored.

Almsgiving from lay patrons is fundamentally intended as a field of merit; yet foolish practitioners treat it as their own private property. They may squander it on the expenses of wine and lust, or hoard it as capital for robes and bowls. Some use it to purchase ordination certificates or the titles of masters, while others give it to junior disciples to shave their heads.

Little do they realize that even a single coin and above belongs to the assembly of monks—a transgression for which no repentance is permitted even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world. Before one reaches heaven, hell will already have been established. Therefore, those who serve as stewards or administrators ought to uphold integrity and purity.

Truly so. Regarding the provision of medicinal milk for the Abbot and the personal provisions for the administrative officers and heads of departments, these should all follow the precedents of previous years and the customary practices of the assembly.
It is improper to seek special favors or manipulate human sentiments beyond what is due. If such things truly arise from the sincere resolve of a donor, then there is no harm.
Once one has departed from the meditation hall and frequented the doors of patrons, one gradually becomes submerged in worldly affairs. This is a constant [danger].
Reflect that you should return early to cultivate the Way; it is not fitting to remain idle abroad. You must take great care amidst wealth and sensual pleasures.

Regarding the ritual for seeing off a fundraising monk (*huazhu*) at the monastery gate: once the date for the monk’s departure has been set, the permanent residents (*changzhu*) shall specially prepare tea and food on the day before.
On the actual day, the Abbot (*zhuchi*) ascends the seat to see him off, further exhorting him with verses of praise.
Having inspired them toward the Way, the abbot shall escort them to the gate accompanied by the head officers (*śreṣṭhin*), where they shall partake of tea and take their leave.

The fundraiser shall return to the monastery to briefly perform the customary social rites (the administrators, head officers, long-standing associates, and fellow brothers shall go to the guest quarters to express their thanks and inquire after his safe return).

After the detailed arrangements for the distribution of offerings are completed, he shall seal the corners of the small registers, the catalogs, and the ledgers (these must be carefully received and handed over to prevent any omissions; when handing over the accounts, all matters must be explained with full candor). All of these [are to be done].

One copy of the Statement of Offerings and Profits (attached). [The form states: "This day, the bhikṣu who serves as the administrator of this monastery, [Name], having received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, has gone to [Place] to solicit offerings for the monastic community and other needs.

A detailed account of the items presented is set forth below: 1. Alms collected for the monastic community: [Amount], totaling [Value] in cash. 2. Alms collected for the Arhats: [Number of seats], totaling [Value] in cash. 3. Alms collected for gruel: [Number of servings], totaling [Value] in cash.

*Within this, items such as [Specific Goods] were received: [Amount], totaling [Value] in cash. *From these funds, expenses for tea, hot water, personnel, and travel costs have been paid: [Value] in cash. *Totaling the above, excluding all disbursements, the net sum is [Value] in cash. The aforementioned offerings and profits are not numerous. We humbly entreat the Abbot..."

Venerable Head Monk, various administrative officers (*zhishi*), Chief Seat (*shouzuo*), and the Great Assembly: I respectfully request your compassionate acceptance. This memorial is submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. Submitted by the monk [Name], Dharma Master for the Hall and Quarters. A postscript following the memorial states:

"Previously borrowed such-and-such an amount from the monastery’s permanent assets (*changzhu*). Now returned with this memorial, as evidenced by the receipt. One copy of the Memorial for Medicinal Milk (the form reads): "Monk [Name], a student of the Way: [Item Name], [Quantity].

Right here, I respectfully present this to the Head Monk, merely to serve as medicinal milk. I humbly entreat your compassionate acceptance. This memorial is submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. Submitted by the monk [Name], a student of the Way. (If it is a junior disciple, state: 'Junior disciple, monk [Name]'). To be reported upon placing it inside the inner box."
Regarding the procedure for the presentation of offerings (*shilu*): First, the donated goods are brought before the Dharma Hall. The Hall Attendant notifies the assembly.
Chairs are arranged facing the front, with incense altars placed beside them; the drum is struck and the assembly gathers. The Abbot stands before the chairs while the attendant burns incense.

The assembly merely bows in greeting from their respective positions (as the offerings have already been presented). Subsequently, the Guest Master presents the ceremonial items. The Guest Master approaches and bows in greeting before the Abbot.

[The abbot] says: "A fundraising master from such-and-such a route, [Name], has submitted this petition. He then leads the fundraising master before the abbot to perform a greeting and stand at attention.
The guest master takes the record of offerings from the chest and gives it to the fundraising master.

The fundraising master presents it to the abbot (the fundraising master performs a greeting, steps back, and stands to one side). The abbot fumigates the document with incense and hands it to the attendant (the attendant, together with the secretary, the *vinaya-dhara*, or the guest master, [delivers it] before the assembly).

[Having finished the proclamation. The guest master steps forward, stands facing [the abbot] to exchange greetings, and the guest prefect takes a letter of introduction from the box and presents it to the guest master.

The guest master presents it to the abbot (the guest master bows and withdraws to stand to the side). Without further inquiry or examination, the abbot hands it to the attendant (the attendant reads the letter aloud).
The guest master bows in thanks to the abbot, performing two prostrations with the robe opened and three prostrations with the robe closed.

[Prostrations] (One *zhan* [prostration with hands extended]. "The offerings are meager; we humbly touch upon the Master. Our feelings are filled with utmost trepidation. Another *zhan* to express greetings, followed by three prostrations with the head touching the ground). Next, the administrators (*zhishi*) pay their respects and offer congratulations to the Abbot.

(Next, the Head Seat and the assembly pay their respects and offer congratulations to the Abbot, performing two *zhan* and three prostrations. The congratulatory words say: "The fundraising master has returned; we trust he encountered no difficulties. We humbly pray for your joyous celebration. Our feelings are filled with utmost exuberance.
When the Abbot and the assembly offer congratulations, the junior disciples follow suit). Next, the Head Seat and the assembly exchange congratulations with the administrators.

Each person performs three prostrations (reciting: "May the Master of the Transformation return without encountering difficulties; we humbly pray for your joy and celebration"). Upon completion of the rites, the Abbot returns to his quarters.

The Chief Seat (Shouzuo) and the assembly below him return to their positions in the hall. The Guest Prefect (Zhike) leads the fundraising master (Huazhu) before the Sacred Monk (Shengseng) for three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (Dazhan Sanbai).

Rising, he performs three prostrations by touching the ground before the Chief Seat, saying: "This occasion of successfully raising funds without difficulty is entirely due to the protective power of the Dharma and the shade of the Chief Seat and the assembly."

The Head Seat and those below him respond with bows (the Head Seat says: "The assembly has returned from its almsround; we rejoice that the offerings were so abundant. We are overwhelmed with gratitude"). The Guest Prefect leads them out to tour the hall.

Next, they enter the Dharma Hall and perform nine prostrations with the cushions fully spread (three prostrations, saying: "That this recent quest for alms was free of difficulties is entirely due to the protection and grace of the Abbot’s spiritual power.

We are deeply moved beyond measure. Then three prostrations to exchange greetings, followed by another three prostrations before rising). They take their seats to drink the medicinal soup, and together invite the new and former fundraising masters.
The former administrators and long-standing veterans who accompany him do not exceed ten or so individuals. The guest prefect (zhikè) inspects the quarters in order;

the masters of the various halls (zhòngliao), the hall heads (liáozhǔ), and the head seat (shǒuzuò) attend to him for three days with tea, soup, and specially prepared meals. No one else is permitted to register as a new arrival. The rector (weínnà) escorts him into his quarters. In some places, he ascends the hall the following day to offer formal thanks.

In some places, after the *nàshū* (receiving the draft) and the *bàwèi rénshì* (concluding the human affairs) have been completed, the abbot ascends the seat first. In other places, the *huàzhǔ* (inviting host) performs the opening of the offering and the meal, followed by the ascent to the hall (if there is no invitation, he does not ascend the hall).
Regarding the subordinate head officials (*shoushou*), these are those appointed by the Abbot (*tangtou*). After one year, they should first seek to retire through skillful means.

Thereafter, before the morning gruel, they shall go to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to inform him of their intention. They perform three prostrations with full prostration (*chuli*) and then withdraw. This applies to those head officials appointed by the Hall Administration (*tangsi*).

In these cases, the dismissal is concluded at the position of the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) without regard for specific times. For the subordinate head officials (*zhoutou*), the dismissal is concluded at the position of the *zangzhu* (storekeeper).
When the six head officials announce their retirement, the tea and soup service in the abbot’s quarters is the same; the *vinaya-dhara*, *karmadāna*, and others escort them into the quarters.

After performing two prostrations with both knees on the ground and three full prostrations to see the host out, the others merely exchange formal greetings. This applies in order to the successive head officials.

They shall be combined with those previously assigned to the *zilaofu* (provisionary quarters) for the purpose of receiving their allotments. Only the *weina* (rector) shall be invited to tea and soup and escorted into the quarters.

For three days, tea and soup shall be specially provided with meals (if these are invitations extended by the various head officials under the *zang*, the monastery shall provide the meals; however, the *zangzhu* [treasurer] must also personally attend to them). Only the *laozhu* (head of the quarters) and the *laoshouzuo* (head seat of the quarters) do not receive special tea and soup.
The Hall Head (Dangtou) instructs the attendant for tea and snacks (*jiandian shizhe*) to report to the Hall Head during the night session or before the morning congee.

On the following day, it may be decided that tea and snacks shall be specially prepared for a certain individual after the midday meal. Prior to the meal, the preparer sets out the noodles (*tangbing*), changes the water, boils the broth, and arranges the cups, bags, and tea trays.
(Wash and polish until gleaming. Incense, flowers, seating, tea, medicine, and the notification plaque for the served tea are prepared.

Once all matters are settled, invite the guests with meticulous care. When addressing the invited guests, bow respectfully and say: "The Abbot has specifically prepared this tea for [Name] following his midday meal;
please attend upon hearing the sound of the drum. Having bowed, withdraw. The ritual must be conducted with solemnity; one must not joke or laugh with others. (Or, if specially brewed...)

Regarding the *tāng* (hot tonic): the attendant should also report this to the Abbot the night before or prior to the midday meal. After the meal, the attendant shall oversee the preparation; the ritual for setting out the cups and vessels and boiling the tonic is identical to the previous procedure. The formal invitation is as follows: "Tonight, after the evening session (*fàngcān*), the Abbot will specially prepare a hot tonic for [Name].
Upon the conclusion of the meal, the attendant first goes to the Abbot’s quarters to attend to the incense burner and its position.

Next, he prepares the tonic pitcher, the cups, and the vessels. Once the attendant has arranged the tea service in unison (note: on the incense altar, only the incense burner and incense case are placed; the medicinal tablets and tea cups are each set in their own place), he reports back to the Abbot.

Once the people have assembled, the tea drum is struck (if the drum is struck before the tea is prepared, the assembly will sit for too long and become annoyed; if the storehouse officials strike the drum, they must proceed to the quarters to strike the board—both cases require careful consideration of this intent and it should not be done too early).
When the guests have gathered, the attendant bows them in (only then may the drum be stopped).

The Head Seat and those following him advance in order and stand according to their respective positions (if someone is found to be absent, he should be requested to come again, so as to spare the Abbot from being disturbed in mind; the attendant likewise must not act with haste). They wait until the meal is finished at the appointed hour.

Please request the Abbot to come forth (if there are guests who have not arrived, the Attendant may withdraw the chair only after receiving the Abbot’s instructions; if the Abbot does not give such instructions, one must not unilaterally move or remove it.

If there are guests who have not arrived or for other reasons they are not present before the assembly, the Abbot should not show his displeasure in front of the crowd to cause them unease). Alternatively, the Abbot may first come out and stand before the chair to wait upon the assembly.
The Attendant bows to the guests and invites them to enter. It is also permissible for the host and guests to remain standing while the Attendant [performs his duties].

Standing outside the hall at the southeast corner, slightly forward, one bows to inquire after the guests' well-being and invites them to be seated. (The attendant who invites the guests to burn incense performs all inquiries and bows on behalf of the abbot;
those who receive the invitation must each act with utmost reverence and must not be negligent or disrespectful. After a long pause, the incense is burned. As for the method of burning incense:

facing the abbot from the east of the incense altar, one bows. Then, opening and closing the incense casket, one offers the incense (holding the casket up with both hands and using the right hand to take out the incense sticks and place them inside).

Insert [the incense] with the left hand. With the right hand, take the lid of the incense box and place it on the incense stand. With the right hand, offer the incense toward the person being specially honored and burn it. Then, cover the incense box with the right hand and hold it with both hands, placing it securely upon the incense stand.

In all cases, one must act with courtesy and gentleness, ensuring that there is no clashing or knocking, nor that anything falls to the ground. Without further bowing of inquiry, simply adjust the sitting mat, join the palms, and proceed to the person being specially honored to perform a bow of inquiry.

(In some places, once the assembly is seated, the attendant first stands beside the Abbot to request the sitting mat and the incense as a mark of respectful ceremony. Now, one performs a bow of inquiry toward the Abbot by the side of the incense stand.)

This is the ritual procedure for requesting incense. Turning around and joining the palms, one stands in position. Next, one requests tea first. Next, one inquires after [the preceptor's] health and encourages him to drink tea. Next, one burns incense and requests it again.
Next, one universally requests medicine and partakes of the medicine. Next, one again requests tea first. Next, one again inquires after his health and encourages him to drink tea.
When the tea is finished, one briefly approaches to inquire after his health, collects the bowl and its cover, then inquires after his health once more and leaves the position.

(The attendant instructs the attendants in advance to wait in readiness. As soon as the guests rise, the attendant moves the chair facing them forward. He steps forward one or two paces specifically to offer a brief greeting and then withdraws, thereby expressing the courtesy of thanking them for the tea.

The abbot escorts the guests out. The guests turn back and together offer a greeting before departing. Immediately, the attendant directs the attendants to remove the chair, collect the seating items or fans, fold the layered cloths and the incense-stand coverings, and put away the tea and soup vessels along with the fine cups and bags.

They then hand over the keys and clean the original [vessels]. Only after the attendant and the serving attendants have finished their own tea may the guests act as they please; this is merely to spare the abbot the trouble of giving further instructions. Or, in the case of the local province...
The Provincial Governor, the Local Inspector, and the County Magistrate (all of whom are to be welcomed and escorted by the assembly; the Abbot shall occupy the seat of honor).

If they are within the jurisdiction of the county, the Abbot shall receive the Magistrate personally, while for all others this is unnecessary). After the Attendant has finished burning incense, the Abbot rises and says:
"I wish to offer coarse tea (or broth); please grant me your permission. Only if permission is granted may the tea be served. If they graciously express their appreciation, the Abbot simply—
The coarse tea is offered merely to express one's devotion; it is not appropriate to treat it with levity.

When officials enter the monastery, they must all be received with equal hospitality regarding tea, soup, and food. Unless they inquire about the Buddha-Dharma, one must not specifically respond to them (as if they were *dānapati* or patrons).
If officials or guests visit one another, incense is burned only once. The attendant’s duty is solely to inquire after the health of the Abbot. This is the required ritual.

One serving of tea and one serving of hot water. If the abbot summons someone to receive a separate serving of tea and hot water, no incense is burned (as when a lay donor enters the monastery, they likewise receive one serving of tea and hot water, and incense need not be burned).
○ When the Abbot of the Hall is not making a general invitation for monks to drink tea, he invites them on the spot as needed.

The attendant shall have the acolytes arrange the seating, the incense burners, and the tea and medicinal herbs; once this is finished, he shall invite them. The guests take their seats. The attendant...

The person facing [the master] performs a formal greeting while burning incense (offering the incense with the right hand). Then, withdrawing, they perform a general greeting with the entire assembly.
If fine tea has been served, no hot water is offered. If one has sat for a long time and requests hot water, the attendant does not burn incense again.

For those who have newly arrived, those visiting briefly, or visiting monks from other temples, incense is burned only once, followed by a general greeting; in all such cases, there is one serving of tea.

When a servant first encounters official guests, he should perform a formal bow with hands clasped; he need not withdraw to avoid the host. Under ordinary circumstances, monks and laypeople alike must not exchange bows or greetings with one another in the presence of the host.

Regarding the method for serving tea and refreshments within the Sangha Hall and the Tea-Serving Hall: the Abbot’s Office (Kusi) issues a notice, while the Head Seat (Shouzuo) issues a formal document. An attendant (xingzhe) carries these on a chest lined with cloth.
The Attendant (shizhe), the Supervisor (jianyuan), or the Head Seat presents them to the person being specially honored. Once the invitation has been formally extended, the document is posted.

Regarding the plaque for the Sangha Hall (the *tangtou* plaque is hung in the upper section; if it is an administrative officer or the Head Seat [Śrāmaṇera], it is in the lower section): An Administrative Officer (*karmadāna*) or the Head Seat shall formally invite the Abbot from the Abbot’s Quarters (*vihāra*).
After the long gong has sounded and the assembly of monks has gathered, they enter the hall to burn incense and perform three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*).

They then circumambulate the hall to invite the assembly. Once everyone is seated following the tolling of the hall bell after the midday meal, the person performing the ritual first goes to the front gate.

Facing the Southern Cheeks [of the altar], one stands to the side with palms joined; having offered a slow greeting, one leaves the original position and offers a greeting facing the Honored Monks (Seng-seng).
Next, one proceeds to the incense burner and offers a greeting. Having opened the incense casket and offered incense with the left hand, one steps back slightly and completes the greeting.
Next, one goes to the special area by the rear door and offers a greeting. Turning to face south, one then returns to the Honored Monks.
One should first exchange greetings with the Sangha members face-to-face. Then, turning northward, one exchanges greetings with the abbot.

Following this sequence, one proceeds through the hall until reaching the northern side of the rear door, where one bows by curving the body; upon reaching the southern side of the rear door, one likewise bows by curving the body.
As when one performs the ritual inquiry (wèn-xùn) outside the hall according to the seniority of the ranks, one returns to enter the hall and performs the inquiry before the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ).

Stepping back to one’s original position, one performs the inquiry again and stands with hands joined in *añjali*. When the tea has been served throughout and the hot water poured, one returns to stand near the front, facing the assembly, to perform the inquiry;
this is the invitation to first drink the tea. Once the tea pitcher is removed, the server proceeds through the hall to exhort the assembly to drink tea, as in the first round. Thus it is asked.
During the *xun-tang* (hall inspection), no incense is burned; this is all that differs. After the tea has been consumed, the bowls are collected specifically for the individual [the guest].
The assembly sets down their bowls on the platform and sits with hands folded. As before, incense is burned and the *xun-tang* concludes with the specific service for the individual.

They then return before the *sheng-seng* (sacred monk) and perform three full prostrations (*da-zhan san-bai*), circumambulate the hall once, and stand in their respective positions. When the distribution of medicine is finished, they approach the front.

He bows to inquire after [the guest's] well-being and requests that he take medicine. Next, tea is served with hot water poured over it; he again bows to inquire after his well-being and requests that he first drink the tea.

When the kettle of boiled water is brought out, he bows as before and circulates through the hall once more to encourage everyone to drink tea. When the tea is finished, they stand in their respective positions.
As for the attendant’s ritual duties: after the tea is finished, he first offers his greetings. He collects the cups at once, places them in the carrying case, and steps forward before the Abbot.
Making one formal bow, he says: "I am especially honored that the Venerable Master has prepared this tea for me;
I am moved beyond measure by your kindness. Making another bow, he inquires after the weather, saying: "I humbly hope that the Venerable Master’s health is flourishing."
Saying, "May you dwell in myriad blessings," he performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloth (*chul-li*) and escorts the abbot out of the hall.
The attendant, having performed inquiries before the Sacred Monk at both the upper and lower levels, strikes the bell for the end of the session.
Once the administrative office or the Head Seat has finished preparing the tea and soup, they first collect the abbot’s cup; then, the various administrators or the Head Seat stand before the abbot.
[The attendant] unfolds [the letter] and says: "On this day, we have received the humble tea (or, as some say, the humble soup) out of the Venerable Master’s compassion and honor;

your subordinate feelings cannot endure the height of our gratitude. He unfolds it once more to exchange greetings of the season, saying: "We humbly pray that the Venerable Master’s health and daily life are blessed with myriad blessings.
Thereupon, he performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). At the third prostration, the abbot does not return the bow, but simply asks:
He bows to the assembly to express his profound respect. Having completed the prostrations, he escorts the abbot out of the hall.
The officiants re-enter the hall and perform the ritual of mutual bowing before the Sacred Monk at both the upper and lower levels. Once the bowls have been withdrawn, they bow once more.

When the bell is struck, they exit the hall. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) also exits the hall and performs three prostrations with touching of heads (*chuli*) before the various administrative officers (*zhishi*).

If the Head Seat has specially designated the Secretary (Shuji), the Secretary likewise first exits the hall and performs three prostrations with touching of heads before the Head Seat, after which they disperse.

The notice for the Summer Retreat Tea Service (the Head Monk shall, this morning after the midday meal, proceed to the Cloud Hall to prepare tea specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly, briefly expressing the commencement of the retreat).

[Protocol]. Also invite all the administrative officers (zhīshì) to serve as honored guests. On this day of this month, the attendant [Name] respectfully announces. Tea Notice for the Abbot’s Summer Retreat Conclusion (The beginning and end are the same as above; however, change the wording to: "merely to manifest the protocol for concluding the retreat").

Tea Notice for the Administrative Office’s Summer Retreat Commencement (The Administrative Office shall, this morning after the midday meal, serve tea in the Cloud Hall (*yúntáng*). This is specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly, merely to manifest the protocol for commencing the retreat.

We humbly hope that the assembly will graciously descend in person. On this day of this month, the monk [Name] of the Administrative Office respectfully announces). Tea Notice for the Administrative Office’s Summer Retreat Conclusion (The beginning and end are the same as above; however, change the wording to: "merely to manifest the conclusion...")

The Protocol for the Opening of the Summer Retreat (Jie-zhi Yi). The Petition of the Head Seat for the Summer Retreat (Shouzuo Jie-xia Zhuang): [Name], Head Seat Bhikṣu. To [Name], Right. This morning, following the midday meal, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall to serve tea. We do this specifically for the Secretary and the assembly to briefly manifest the protocol for the opening of the retreat.

We also respectfully invite all the administrative officers (zhishi). We humbly hope that the assembly will, out of compassion, deign to grace us with their presence. Respectfully submitted. [Date]. Submitted by [Name], Head Seat Bhikṣu. The Envelope reads: "Petition to the Secretary and the Assembly; respectfully sealed by [Name], Head Seat Bhikṣu.

The Petition of the Head Seat for the Closing of the Summer Retreat (Shouzuo Jie-xia Zhuang): The beginning and end are identical to the above; however, change the wording to: "to briefly manifest the protocol for the closing of the retreat. If the Abbot (Tangtou) specifically prepares [the ceremony] for new and former [monks]...

The administrative head (zhishi shouzuo) and the administrative head serve tea; the formal notice for this is as previously requested regarding the administrative heads and senior officers, as clarified in the preceding section.
The administrative heads and senior officers serve the tea.

The administrative officials and various heads specifically perform the following: the tea-tray gong is struck; the presiding host stands according to his position and bows to the assembly to invite them to be seated.
The host also takes his seat, merely placing his feet down. After a long while, he bows to request that they withdraw their feet.

Shortly thereafter, he rises, performs a greeting, and leaves his position to offer incense (offering the incense with the right hand). Having completed the greetings for the specific person [the guest], he returns to his original position. On one side, the assembly acts in unison.
Inquire after the well-being of the assembly (one must by no means inquire before the chair of the presiding seat). Then, having inquired at one’s own seat, sit down. Pour two or three bowls of tea.
Holding the tea cup, bow toward those facing you specifically for their sake (bowing only to the head monk), as well as to those of higher and lower rank.

Then drink the tea. When the tea is finished (or when the cups are removed, remove only the host’s cup), rise and inquire after the assembly's well-being. Leave the seat to burn incense, then return to the seat and inquire once more.

The same as before. Next, the medicine is offered for all to partake; then, tea is offered first. When the tea is finished and the cups have been cleared away, one bows in greeting, rises, and escorts the guests to the gate.

If the *liàozhǔ* (abbot of the quarters) specifically hosts the assembly of the quarters, he shall invite the *shǒuzuò* (head seat) of that specific quarter to preside over the ritual proceedings himself.
If it is specifically for newly arrived monks, the etiquette is the same as that for the *zhìshì* (administrative officers). This does not apply when the head is currently in office.

The Head (Shu) shall not request the administrative officers for tea or hot water (fearing it might interfere with their official duties and avoiding the appearance of suspicion). ○ Regarding the protocol for the various heads of the storehouse office (Kusi) to welcome new arrivals:
there is morning tea after the midday meal and hot water at the conclusion of the evening session (Fangseng), accompanied by the burning of a single stick of incense in both instances.
If they do not request hot water for the evening, the tea following the midday meal is served while seated.

Regarding the method for serving tea according to the seniority of one’s time in the *lao* (monastic quarters): After the incense has been burned, one bows in greeting (*wensun*) starting with the *Liaozhu* (Head of the Quarters). Next, one bows in greeting starting with the *Shouzuo* (Head Seat).
Having finished bowing, one pours tea and makes a complete circuit of the *lao*, encouraging everyone to drink. After a short while, one steps forward, bows, and says: "Tea."

"Forgive this coarseness; we shall not exchange cups. Then, burn incense and invite [the guests] again. Next, make rounds through the quarters to inquire after their well-being. Following that, distribute medicine, then tea.

Next, offer a toast of tea (for both instances of burning incense and inquiring after well-being, as well as the final expression of thanks for the tea, one must follow the sequence of the first round. For the second round of offering tea, proceed as convenient; simplify the rounds of inquiry by making only one circuit.

For the first round of offering tea, simply inquire after the well-being of those in the upper and lower sections; it may also be done collectively). Next, express thanks for the tea, saying: "On this day, we have received this coarse tea, having been graced by the compassion and honor of the Abbot, the Head Seat, and the assembly."

Perform three prostrations with full prostration (chū-ri). Next, circumambulate the quarters once and collect the cups. Rise after performing a greeting. This is as when inviting [the assembly] for tea.

When the monks within the quarters have taken their seats, first burn one stick of incense, saying: "Tomorrow we respectfully invite the Abbot, the Head Seat, and the Great Assembly to graciously accept this special tea service. We humbly hope you will deign to honor us with your compassionate presence. Perform three prostrations with full prostration and circumambulate the quarters.
Once the greetings are concluded, the person responsible for serving tea on that day then performs the ritual procedures.

For those specially invited from among the assembly for morning tea, the invitation is made the night before; for post-meal tea, the invitation is made in the morning; for evening soup, the invitation is made after the meal.

If one is inviting a person of high standing and great respect (such as the Head Seat who has been ordained, elders from various quarters, or Dharma relatives such as uncles, cousins, or elder brothers), one should perform the full prostration with three bows.

Prostrate. If there is no space for this, perform three prostrations with touching (chuli). If one requests [a seat] from a person of successive respect (such as fellow practitioners, those whose years of ordination (*śīla-varṣa*) or spiritual practice are venerable and emulated, or generally those who are senior to oneself), perform only three prostrations with touching.

If they are peers or equal in years of ordination (such as dharma-relatives, younger brothers, or nephews), simply inquire after them and request [a seat]. Once the seating arrangement, incense, flowers, and the name plaque have been prepared, proceed to...

At that time, the guest is welcomed at the entrance and invited to take a seat. The attendant bows and says, "Please rest your feet. The incense is burned and another bow is made; this specific ritual is omitted for the guest.

Another bow is made and the attendant says, "Please dispense with the sitting mat. Furthermore, if it is hot during the summer, one says, "Please use a fan"; if it is cold during the winter, one says, "Please cover your head.
Tea is served, approximately three to five bowls, and the attendant bows again, saying, "Please first drink the tea. [The same applies to] the soup.

As soon as the tea pitcher is brought out, one should inquire after the person of special honor and offer tea. When the cups have been collected (if the cups are not collected, say: "The tea was coarse; please forgive me for not exchanging the cups.

If serving hot water without exchanging cups, say: "The hot water was coarse; please forgive me for not exchanging the cups"), one should burn incense again and inquire after the person of special honor.

Next, distribute the medicinal herbs throughout and inquire, saying: "Please take the medicine. Next, serve tea to wash down the medicine and invite [the guest] to drink the tea first, offering tea to all in the same manner.
Before the tea ceremony, after the tea has been served, he offers his thanks, saying: "On this day, the tea (or, as some say, the hot water) was prepared specifically for [Name] and [Name].

The tea was coarse and the seating arrangements were inconvenient. Your humble servant is filled with boundless gratitude. If the person addressed is of high rank or great respect, he performs three full prostrations.
In the evening, before or after the end of the *zaṅ* (the meal), he goes to the quarters to offer formal thanks. If the person is of intermediate rank or respect...
When meeting with peers, one should offer thanks, saying: "On this day, the tea (or, as some say, the boiled water) was specially prepared for [Name] and [Name].
Furthermore, it was not appropriate for me to rise to accompany [Name]; therefore, I prostrate twice in the *chuli* manner. One should further say:

"Fearing that my presence might trouble you, I dare not visit your quarters again this evening to offer formal thanks. Then, one prostrates once more, after which one exchanges greetings with all those who accompanied [Name] in the same manner.
After a long pause, he bows to inquire after [the guest's] well-being and collects his cup. Next, he bows again to leave his seat, then steps out the door first to see the guest off.

Among the assembly, one may specially prepare tea for a senior, such as for one’s own teacher, or for those who are like one’s own immediate paternal uncles, maternal uncles, or elder brothers. This is conducted as one would do while seated in one’s own quarters.

If one’s position is inconvenient or obstructs others, one may borrow a private room for the tea ceremony (the ritual procedures have already been explained). This is performed specifically for a single individual.
The head of the monastery (*shoushu*) occupies the central seat. For the person being honored, a seat is prepared facing the front;

they offer incense with their left hand (prostrating directly before the seat). If there are two or more people, they occupy the *zhao* seats, facing the head of the monastery, and offer incense with their left hands.
(At the incense table, perform prostrations outside the hall. The words, gestures, and all other matters are identical to the method for serving tea at the Head Seat (Tangtou).

However, after the final prostration, one approaches to inquire after [the guest’s] well-being (without bowing specifically to individuals; the guest rises first), then performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (chuli) outside the hall to express gratitude.
The accompanying attendants then inquire after [the guest] in succession and rise. They escort him out the door. In the evening, go to pay respects to the Venerable [Abbot].
Regarding the formal expressions of gratitude and inquiries by the *chángliáo* (senior resident):

if the *liáozhǔ* (head of the quarters) already possesses his own quarters, he should occupy the central seat specifically for the person [visiting], burning incense and performing prostrations entirely within the hall. (If one consults the general principles: since the quarters have already been lent to another for the purpose of providing tea and refreshments, it is appropriate to decline on some pretext and avoid the seat;
one must not occupy the head position oneself, as this would cause inconvenience for the other person’s prostrations and various duties.)
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Five;
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Six:
The Special Tea Service for the Dharma Relatives and入室 (入室, "entering the room") Disciples Prepared by the Abbot.

In the morning, assuming the proper dignified demeanor, he first goes to see the attendant and says, "I wish to trouble you to inform the Abbot that after the midday meal, I intend to go to the Abbot’s quarters to offer tea specifically for the Head of the Hall. Once the attendant has reported this, he leads him in to have an audience.

After the Head of the Hall has offered his greetings, [the visitor] says, "Please, Abbot, take your seat" (if the host is already seated, it is unnecessary to say "please be seated"). First, he performs three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*), then steps forward.

He bows his body and says: "This morning, after the midday meal, I wish to go to the Abbot’s quarters to serve tea specifically for the Head Monk (Dharmasvāmin). I humbly hope that you will look upon me with compassion and grant your permission.

The Resident Master (Zhuchi) replies: "I respectfully comply with your request. There is no need to perform a bow. [Alternatively, whether he returns the bow or not depends on their respective ranks. [The visitor] then performs three prostrations. Alternatively, having merely stated the purpose of the visit, he performs three full prostrations (*dazhan sanli*).
Or, having finished the invitation, he performs three *chuli* (touching prostrations), each according to their relative status. Thereafter, he withdraws and performs a formal inquiry (*wensun*).

Exit. Consult with the attendant to arrange the seating and the name tablets. Personally invite companions (one must invite high-ranking heads of the community, close dharma relatives, or former residents of long standing to accompany you).
After the meal, first go to the Head of the Monastery to supervise the incense, lamps, tea, medicine, cups, and the hot water pitcher, ensuring that no matters are neglected.
When the guests have gathered in order (without striking the drum to assemble the assembly), bow to the guests as they take their seats. Once the full number of people has assembled:

Thereafter, he enters the abbot’s quarters to invite the Abbot to take his seat at the central position. Once the Abbot has withdrawn his feet, the guest approaches to perform a formal greeting (*wensun*).
Turning westward, he passes to the east of the incense altar and performs a greeting outside the seating area at the southwest corner.

Having finished, he stands with hands folded at his sides (this indicates the guest's position; if the attendant in charge of the tea service burns incense on behalf of the Head of the Hall, he stands at the southeast corner outside the seating area to represent the host's etiquette). Great.

When the assembly has taken their seats, he inquires after their well-being at a leisurely pace. He leaves his position and stands upright beside the incense altar, bows toward the host, and offers incense with his left hand.
Having covered the incense casket, he does not bow again; instead, with palms joined, he turns and passes to the east side of the incense altar.
Having finished the inquiry before the abbot facing north, turn around and return to your original position to stand and inquire.

Distribute the tea throughout; about three or five cups of hot water should be poured. Approach and inquire (this is the invitation to drink tea first). Step back and stand according to your position.

The tea pitcher is brought out (or, if it is for the Master or the Senior Teacher to prepare the tea, the attendant pours the hot water and personally serves the tea to express special respect). Inquire before the abbot and offer encouragement.

Tea. [The procedure] is established according to rank. When the tea service is finished, the cups are collected (if one has personally served the tea, one must personally collect the cups). The host waits for the collection of the cups and the clearing of the table.

Following the previous procedure for burning incense, perform three full prostrations before the Abbot. Approaching him with a bowed body, say: "I wish to invite the Honored Elephant-Drawn Chariot to partake once more of this coarse tea;
I humbly beseech your compassion and grant me your special permission. Again, perform three prostrations or unfold the sitting mat for a full prostration.

First, state the purpose of the invitation as before. Withdrawing, perform three prostrations. The Abbot says: "Since you have already shown such diligent courtesy, why need there be further repetition? [The guest] bows once in response; if there is no response, each party returns to their respective positions of honor. Wait for the Abbot...

The Holder of the Staff withdraws his feet and offers greetings. He turns and stands in his place. The Medicine Master approaches and offers greetings (thereby requesting the medicine). He then withdraws and stands in his place.
Tea is served with three or five bowls of hot water (or he personally serves the tea). Again, he offers greetings (thereby requesting that the tea be drunk first).
When the tea pitcher is removed, he again approaches and offers greetings to encourage the drinking of tea. He turns and stands in his place, awaiting the tea.
[The ceremony] concludes. First, collect the abbot’s cup (or collect the cups yourself). Perform three full prostrations before the abbot.

Stepping forward with a bowed body, say: "On this day, we have received coarse tea; we are deeply grateful for the Venerable Master’s compassionate condescension. We are overwhelmed with emotion. The abbot replies: "I have prepared this tea out of deep respect; I am likewise moved beyond measure."

Whether the abbot returns the bow or not depends on his rank. Then, withdrawing, he performs three prostrations. Alternatively, he may spread out his sitting mat (*kaṣāya*), approach with a bowed body to inquire after his well-being.
First, he offers words of thanks as before. Withdrawing, he performs three prostrations.

If the abbot does not return the bow, once the person serving tea has finished his prostrations, the attendant approaches again to inquire after his well-being. Having withdrawn, he stands to the west with hands folded at his side. The abbot—

The person who prepared the refreshments leaves their seat. When the assembly enters the abbot’s quarters (at which time the assembly does not rise), the person who prepared the refreshments follows them in.

After offering greetings, they withdraw. If the abbot returns the bow, when the person who prepared the refreshments has performed the third prostration and has not yet risen, the abbot does not return the bow;
instead, he joins his palms and greets the assembly to express the etiquette of profound respect.

(As when the administrative officers and the head seat serve tea within the Sangha hall, the Abbot likewise follows this same etiquette). The person serving the tea does not withdraw from his position;

he escorts the Abbot back to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), bows in greeting, and then retires. He returns to his original station and stands there, thanking the assembly, saying: "This day’s tea is but a coarse offering."

Specifically for the Abbot: "I humbly receive the compassionate presence of [Name] and [Name]. Your subordinate feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. (Perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground. Then, inquire after each other’s well-being in succession and stand at their respective positions.
When the cups are withdrawn, perform an inquiry and rise. When seeing off guests, go only one or two steps outside the banquet hall to signify that there is no custom of escorting guests further.
However, one must express thanks to the attendant at the attendant’s quarters.)
The method for the communal preparation of tea and incense in the Dharma Hall:
For the large seat [of the Abbot], prepare the tea before the meal and enter the hall to pay respects and make the invitation; offer only one stick of incense.

After the meal (or when evening approaches), inquire about the hot water. For the first round of tea, offer two sticks of incense. For the second round, offer one stick of incense (the Head of the Hall and the Head of the Storehouse).

For all monastic quarters, special services performed at their respective locations shall follow this same protocol (with the sole exception that there is no formal invitation or prostration). For tea and soup offered outside of regular occasions, only a single stick of incense is offered.

Regarding the method for setting out food for a special service: once the invitation has been completed prior to the meal, the long board is struck to assemble the community. When the guests are seated in unison, the tables are brought in and incense is burned.
Inquiries are made specifically for those who are specially designated; for all others outside the immediate circle, inquiries are conducted collectively.

Once the serving of rice has been completed throughout, incense is burned again to inquire after those who are specially designated. After the money for the under-lining has been distributed, one again performs an inquiry before them.
The sequence is the same as previously described. The Hall Attendant (Dangtou Shizhe) performs the ritual duties, and the Head of the Administrative Office (Kusi Zhuxi) performs the ritual duties.

The Tea Master (Chadang) shall cease the special provision of food and tea. If the person is of lower rank, they shall immediately perform three prostrations with the sitting cloth spread out before the Abbot;
if this is not permitted, they shall perform three prostrations with the sitting cloth folded. If the person is of equal or higher rank, they shall...
In the evening, go to the Head of the Hall (Dangtou) to offer words of thanks, saying: "On this day, we have humbly received your gracious hospitality and the special preparation of tea.
We, your inferiors, are overcome with the utmost gratitude. (As the ancients said: "One thanks for the tea, not for the food.
