Regarding the formal prostrations, when the administrators (*zhishi*) or heads (*toushou*) provide special tea and soup on the occasion, it is not necessary to go to their quarters to offer thanks. This applies even if they are of equal standing among the assembly.
Regarding the fried snacks (*jiāndiǎn*): one must visit the quarters to express thanks before or after the end of the meditation session (*fàngcān*).

When viewing the Tripitaka, if a donor invites the assembly to view the Great Canon (*Dàzàngjīng*) either in the library or in the Dharma Hall, the *zhísuì* (the officer in charge of the monastery) shall arrange [the seating].

The seats and tables are arranged. The *diànzuò* (chief cook) supervises the setting out of the offerings. The *xíngzhě* (attendant practitioners) and the *zàngzhǔ* (library master) prepare tea, soup, incense, flowers, lamps, and candles.
The *wéiná* (chant leader), according to seniority in ordination (*jièlà*), issues the notice for the distribution of scriptures and seating placards, and requests the performance of ritual services.

Furthermore, he prepares the formal documents for the *fànlǎo* (Dharma Master) and writes the opening announcement. He also distributes the written petitions and the large notice for the scripture reading. The *zàngdiàn zhǔ* (temple library master) oversees these matters.
When it is time for the recitation of the sutra, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) strikes the bell to assemble the assembly and requests them to take their seats according to rank.

During the ritual, conch shells and cymbals are sounded. The guest prefect prepares the incense burner. After leading the patrons in the offering of incense, they kneel before the burner at the altar. The *vinaya-dhara* offers words of praise and proclaims the opening petition.
The *ācārya* leads the recitation of the Buddha’s name and chants the *brahmā-svara*. Once the chanting has ceased, the assembly may then open the sutra. If there is a sick person present...

When the patient’s condition improves and various conditions exist externally, the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) shall collect the funds along with the case and its label, wait for the assembly to enter the hall, and upon their return, distribute them for recitation.
This matter is most excellent. If a sick monk insists on taking the funds for the sutras, they must be handed over.
If there are remaining fragments of sutras that cannot be fully distributed to the assembly, they shall be handled according to the usual order of seniority based on years of ordination (*kṣapaṇa*).

The distribution of the tablets: If the donor has established a vegetarian feast for celebration and repentance on the day the sutra-recitation is completed, one must further read the prose memorial (san-wen shu) after the recitation is finished.

The donor’s funds for the sutras shall be collected and managed by the Hall Office (tang-si) for distribution (excluding the benefits for the permanent residents and the novices; the Rector [weina] reads the memorial).

The Secretary shall write out the formal petitions; the Librarian shall provide incense, candles, tea, and soup; and the Guest Master shall perform the rites of offering incense and chanting the *brahman* chants. Beyond these, the funds shall be distributed according to the current inventory, after verifying the available amount of money.

The Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) shall oversee the general affairs and personally attend to the reception of donors; the Librarian (Zangzhu) shall supply tea and soup for the assembly and constantly ensure that the sacred teachings are protected and cherished.
The method for reading the scriptures is detailed within the section concerning the Librarian; examine it thoroughly. If [the procedure] is not...

If one is able to read the scriptures, one should immediately resign from the duties of the Hall Office. If one has already received the scriptures, one must carefully and according to the Dharma examine them;
it is best to finish them as soon as possible. Not only will this fulfill the donor’s aspirational vow, but it will also ensure that one does not incur a debt for the scriptures at a later time.

Regarding the Middle Hall Feast (*zhōngyánzáì*): If a feast is held in the Middle Hall upon the arrival of a donor, the Chief Administrator (*jiànyuàn*) first inquires as to how many monastics and lay guests have been invited from outside, as well as the amount of each person’s meal contribution.
He then informs the Abbot, who, together with the Cook (*diǎnzuo*), determines the menu. Next...
To prepare the provisions for the memorial feast, the *zhisui* (yearly steward) shall arrange the seating, whether in the storehouse office (*kusō*) or in the Dharma Hall (*hōdō*).

Incense, flowers, and ceremonial canopies shall be provided according to the family’s means, whether abundant or frugal. The secretary shall compose the formal petitions (*monsho*) in accordance with the specific intent of the auspicious or inauspicious feast.

The *wina* (chant leader) shall arrange the seating and oversee that the abbot occupies the presiding seat (in his absence, the head of the administrative office [*kansō*] shall act as his representative). The head seat (*shuso*) shall divide the seats among the senior monks (*sokusoku*) of renown and virtue.

The seat facing the assembly shall be occupied by the Head Seat (the presiding officer, seated with his left hand toward the center). The Librarian and those below him shall take their places according to rank. Lay donors and guests shall be seated in the "mirror-position" (zhào-wei).
The Chief Administrator, the Rector, and the Age-Manager shall sit beneath the drum. All other senior officers and venerable elders shall be assigned positions as deemed appropriate.

If the seats are distant, they illuminate one another from east to west; if they are close, they face one another with their mats joined. In both cases, the position to the south is considered superior.

The *yugu* (fish-drum) gathers the assembly, and the bell is struck as they take their seats. Both guests and hosts perform the ritual salutation (*wensun*) together upon entering the hall. Before the sacred image, the ritual service is first announced.
The guest master (*zhike*) prepares the pure water and leads the patron (*shizhu*) to offer incense, starting from the abbot’s seat and proceeding to the southeast of the central dais.
[The incense] reaches the southwest corner of the central dais. For all other [paths], it is best to proceed directly as convenient.

When the offering of incense is finished, the patron kneels before the image for the ritual service and chants the liturgy. The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) proclaims the memorial text (*sūtra*), and they recite the Buddha’s name ten times.
The patron returns to his place. If the offering of incense does not employ the ritual service, then one person from the head of the ritual service is requested [to perform it].

First, chant "Prostrations with Reverence" (the abbreviated Sanskrit title for "All Pay Homage with Reverence to the Ever-Abiding Triple Gem"). Proceed in sequence from the invocation of the Buddha to the offering of incense.

Upon concluding the ritual service, chant the "Tathāgata Sanskrit" (from "The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body" to "therefore I take refuge; I pay homage with faith to the Ever-Abiding Triple Gem"). Kneel before the incense burner, read the preface, recite the Buddha’s name, and sit as before.
If there is no ritual service, or if the Buddha is not invoked, the preface is likewise not read. The Rector (Vina) [performs these duties].

The chime is struck and the ritual is intoned with reverent bows. Once the donor has finished distributing the incense, he kneels before the image and offers incense from the burner. The *vinaya-dhara* chants the "Brahma-sound of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgata-brahmasvara*).

The donor then recites the prayer for the vegetarian feast (*bai-zhai*) while maintaining mindfulness. The donor takes his seat; the chime is struck again to mark the conclusion of the seating arrangement. Finally, the chime is struck once more.

The Head Seat distributes the food. Next, the incense is passed and the signal to eat is given, circulating throughout [the central seating area; the attendants at the outer seats do not give the signal to eat, but simply pass the food item by item as it circulates, standing outside the central seating area].
A single strike of the chime is made. The assembly bows slightly and remains silent in meditation before the formal offering of the meal.

Once the rice has been distributed and eaten, the Rector strikes the chime. The Head Seat distributes the monetary offerings, either provided by the patron or distributed by the administrative officers. Great.
When the communal meal is finished, at the beginning of the ritual, the *karmadāna* strikes the *qing* (gong) and recites, "The worlds are like empty space," and so forth.

Briefly extracting the essential meaning from the commentary, one performs the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). After reciting the names of the ten Buddhas, strike the *qing* once more and rise (or strike the *qing* twice:

the first to mark the conclusion of the verse on the completion of the meal, the second to signal leaving one's seat). The midday great vegetarian feast should be prepared early; if it passes noon, it becomes an improper time (*akāla*).

When entering or leaving for any matter concerning the entire assembly— whether to attend a meal offering, to perform recitations, or to receive a venerable elder— if one departs after the morning gruel,
the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) shall announce it to the hall before the gruel; if one departs after the midday meal, the *vinaya-dhara* shall announce it during the meal.

The Hall. The Procedure for Announcing to the Hall: After the striking of the mallet has been completed following the distribution of gruel and rice, or after the distribution of alms has concluded, strike the mallet once and say:

"I announce to the assembly: this morning, after the gruel, upon hearing the sound of the bell, each of you shall assume your dignified demeanor and join us in a communal invitation to the meal at [name of location]."
The heads of all the various quarters (liaotou) shall roll up their curtains and proceed together. This is respectfully announced. [The bell] is struck once.
The Rector (Weina) then bows before the Holy Monk (Shengseng), bows again before the Abbot (Zhuzhi), and makes one circuit of the hall.

If there are monks outside the hall, he should also bow to them, with the exception of those in the Rear Hall (Houtang). When the time arrives, the bell is struck; everyone assembles beneath the Main Gate (Sanmen). The Abbot...

Proceed in order: first the Head Seat (Shouzuo), then the Registrar (Shuzhuang), the Librarian (Zangzhu), the Guest Master (Zhike), and the Bath Master (Yuzhu), followed by those of renowned virtue and long-standing service, all according to the sequence of their ordination seniority (jilao).
The Steward (Zhishuai), the Cook (Dianzuo), the Rector (Weina), and the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) follow behind the assembly.
They should proceed in a dignified and orderly manner without causing confusion. One must not look left or right, speak, smile, or recite scriptures aloud. Let them maintain a composed demeanor.
Lower the arms and let the hands hang loosely. Upon reaching the designated place, calmly remove the *kasa* (head-covering).

Wait until the abbot, the administrative officers (*zhishi*), the heads of departments (*toushou*), and the assembly have gathered in one place; once they have together bowed to the patron, you may then take your seat. You must remain solemn and silent throughout.
This shall cause them to give rise to a heart of reverence and respect. If one wishes to relieve oneself, one must not fold the *kāṣāya* and stand upon a seat, stool, or desk;

rather, one must go outside the assembly and place the *kāṣāya* in a clean location. Upon finishing the task, one should wash the hands and put it back on, so as to avoid inadvertently disturbing the pure assembly.
When a donor offers incense for purification or distributes offering cloths (*cīvara*), one should always receive and welcome these with singular care and diligence. Do not...
One must not be arrogant or casual. One must not view books or paintings. One must not play with children.
Regarding all objects of sensual pleasure, one must not cast a glance upon them. Upon finishing the meal, one shall accompany the abbot back to the monastery.

Under no circumstances shall one remain behind to handle affairs, as this will provoke the ridicule of others (whether by purchasing clothing, or buying medicinal herbs, or visiting patrons, or sightseeing at famous scenic spots, or returning to a separate residence to pay respects to teachers and monks; as for other matters...).
It is impossible to exhaustively describe this in words). If there is any administrative duty to attend to, one should request leave from the Hall Office on another day.

If attending a recitation service or receiving a venerable elder, the general principles shall follow this precedent. Whether the heads of the various quarters attend or not depends on the specific circumstances of the occasion.

The assembly should always be aware of the purpose whenever they hear the bells, drums, fish-shaped gongs, or wooden boards. When the large bell is struck at the fifth watch, it serves as an alarm for those who are sleeping.

Next, when the small bell is struck before the kitchen, it signals the opening of the "small period of stillness" (at which time all practitioners and attendants in the various quarters must rise first). Next...

Striking the cloud-board (*yunban*) in front of the kitchen signifies the opening of the Great Stillness (*dajing*); at this point, the assembly of monks rises together, and they may then fold their mats and bedding and enter the mosquito-canopy rooms (*wenchu*).

Next, striking the long board (*changban*) signals for the monks to set down their alms bowls (the monks enter the hall all at once). Next, striking the wooden fish (*muyu*) indicates that the assembly has gathered and settled (those who arrive later may no longer enter the hall).
When the drum sounds three times, the abbot (*zhuchi*) proceeds to the hall. The small bell before the hall then rings.
[The term] "zhě" (者) refers to the members of the Sangha descending from their seats to attend upon and inquire after the well-being of the abbot.

When the *weina* strikes the wooden mallet once at the beginning, it signals for the assembly to open their alms bowls (as they recite the *Heart Sūtra* three times in accordance with the sound of the mallet).

Next, when he strikes the mallet once more, it announces the intention to serve congee (or expresses the chanting of the preface). Next, when he strikes the mallet ten times, it indicates the recitation of the names of the ten Buddhas. Next, when he strikes the mallet...
One strike of the mallet signifies that the Head Seat (Shouzuo) is distributing the gruel. Another strike of the mallet signifies that the gruel has been served throughout.
One strike of the mallet after the gruel is finished signifies that the assembly of monks descends from the hall (the Abbot [Zhuchi] must first leave the hall before the monks may take their bowls).
Three strikes of the small bell in front of the hall signal the conclusion of the morning session. If the session is not concluded, the drum is struck in the hall to signal the ascent to the dais.

When the formal sitting has concluded and the tea ceremony is finished, the sounding of three short strokes on the small bell before the hall signals for the assembly of monks to descend from their seats.

When the sounding of three strikes on the wooden board is heard before the midday meal, it signals for the assembly of monks to set down their alms bowls. The subsequent tolling of the large bell announces that it is time for the meal (in city precincts, the meal bell precedes the three strikes;
in mountain forests, the three strikes precede the meal bell). All other long boards, fish-drums, and small bells in front of the hall are struck by the *vinaya-dhara* (the ritual leader).

When the *chui* (striking) is finished, one descends from the hall; this follows the same procedure as for the morning congee (with the exception that when a donor provides a vegetarian feast, after the general *chui*, one strikes an additional *chai-chui* once).
Next, if one hears the head monk or the storehouse supervisor strike the drum, or if various quarters strike the wooden board, the assembly of monks proceeds to tea.

If one hears the drum sounding before the kitchen, it is for the assembly’s collective labor (*pingsheng*). If one hears the bell ringing before the hall, it is for the purpose of escorting or receiving a venerable guest.

The official (guan) may request the administrative officers (*zhishi*) or escort deceased monks away. When the drum sounds at the conclusion of the bath, it signifies the opening of the bath or the laving of sweat.

When the bell is struck three times before the evening hall, it indicates the dismissal of the evening *zhan*. On the third and eighth days of each month, when the great bell or the small bell before the hall is heard, it is for the purpose of recitation (*nianzhou*).

(In the City God Temple, the small bell is struck to assemble the multitude for Buddha-recitation; in mountain forests, the great bell is first struck to gather the assembly, followed by the small bell.)

When the large bell is struck at dusk, it signifies that the practitioners are ascending to the hall to recite the Buddha’s name. If one hears the drum sounding in the hall, it indicates a *xiaocan* (informal discourse).
From dawn until dusk, the bells and drums alternate; this serves not only to awaken the assembly but also to ensure that the teaching of the Dharma continues without interruption.

The eminent masters of the monastic community each know the proper time for themselves. This is the method for opening the small period of quietude (*xiaojing*): first strike the wooden board three times.
The sound gradually becomes louder and more resonant. From slow to fast, and from heavy to light, this constitutes one session. For the second session, the sound is muted (strike twice slowly).

This is the method for opening the Great Silence (the same as the method for opening the Small Silence, but with only one long session). The method for striking the long board and the wooden fish is as follows: (with a light hand, draw out the sound, gradually increasing its volume until the tone is harmonious and flowing;

thereafter, alternate between fast and slow while balancing lightness and heaviness. At each session, pause briefly; it is essential that the rhythmic divisions be distinct so that listeners do not err. For the third session, the sound is muted; strike three times slowly). Above.

The Method for Beating the Drum for the Small Assembly in the Hall: First, lightly tap the drumhead three times. Then, strike it with a heavy hand, gradually increasing the force so that the tension and slack, as well as the lightness and heaviness, correspond to one another.

The sound should be harmonious and flowing, rising and falling in a continuous chain, a deep and resonant roar like the thunder of spring awakening the hibernating creatures. For the first round, prolong the sound by striking continuously; at the end of the round, pause briefly. For the second round, the sounds should be connected and slightly more rapid, without any further pauses.

Even when changing the signal, at the third assembly one strikes the gong with a single continuous stroke. One waits for the abbot to ascend the seat before striking the drum; the double mallets strike three times in succession. Regarding the method for the *zhāi* (midday) and *zhōu* (morning congee) drums:

these are struck in three assemblies just as in the method for ascending the hall, differing only in that the intervals between assemblies are slightly shorter. Regarding the method for the bath drum, tea drum, and general labor (*pǔqǐng*) drum:

these are struck with a long, sustained roll for one assembly, and no further changes or signals are made. Regarding the method for striking the small bell in front of the hall: this is the "hall-entry bell," which is sounded with a light hand until the tone gradually grows louder as the abbot enters.

The bell for entering the hall (the hall is established immediately). The bell for ending the session (*fangcan*): first strike the wooden board three times, then slowly strike the bell three times. The bell for recitation (*nianzuo*):

as in the method for opening the minor period of silence, once the abbot has entered the hall and finished burning incense, he stands before the Sangha Hall; the *vinaya-dhara* strikes the bell, and after the ten names of the Buddhas have been recited, he strikes it twice, then stops. The bell for descending from the platform: without striking the wooden board again, strike the bell twice consecutively.

The bell for escorting and receiving the administrators and for escorting deceased monks: strike it only once. The method for the *vinaya-dhara* to strike the gavel: having first performed a formal greeting, he grasps it with his right hand, palm facing upward.

Place the handle of the mallet flat upon the surface of the sounding block (*āṣṭhīlā*), with the head of the mallet facing toward one’s body. Extend two fingers of the left hand upward to support the edge of the mallet. Slowly rotate the handle of the mallet to strike it; then, lower the two left fingers to meet the edge of the block and straighten the hand.

The descent of the mallet must not exceed five inches (*cun*). During a single rotation, the mallet must not leave its original position. The Method for Striking the Great Bell: First, lightly tap the bell three times to signal it. Then strike slowly eighteen times, followed by rapidly eighteen times.

Three sets of rapid strikes and three sets of slow strikes together constitute one hundred and eight sounds. The attendant practitioner shall burn incense, prostrate, and recite verses before striking it. The verse says: "May the sufferings and bitternesses of the three realms and eight difficulties be stilled. May all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm hear this sound and awaken to the Way."

Upon finishing the recitation, one immediately ceases it). The drum in the hall is presided over by the attendant (shizhe); the drum below the storehouse is presided over by the director of the monastery (jianyuan).

The wooden board for meals and the wooden fish for opening the period of silence are presided over by the chief cook (dianzuo). The small bell in front of the hall is presided over by the ritual master (weina).

As for the large bell, if there is no designated bell-head, the ritual master presides over it; the practitioner who strikes the bell is presided over by the chief cook. The aforementioned bells and drums are as follows:

If it does not accord with the Dharma, it will cause the balance between severity and leniency to be lost and the rhythm of urgency and relaxation to lack measure; all such matters should be clearly explained, making the smooth and harmonious quality of the voice the highest priority.
Dispatch this letter.
As for the procedure for the appointment letter and the farewell letter: before entering the monastery, the special messenger first dispatches a letter and arrives at the temple.
Once the guest master has arranged the seating positions, the proceedings in the Dharma Hall follow the same protocol as when a ritual master submits a memorial.

The secretary reads the document, and the special messenger performs two prostrations with hands extended and three full prostrations before the abbot (the first extension of the hands says: "This special message has been dispatched to pay homage to your venerable countenance; our humble feelings are beyond measure as we gaze upon you...").

Looking up [to the abbot] with the utmost reverence. Then, once again, they exchange greetings regarding the weather (this is followed by three prostrations). The administrative officers (*kaji*), the head seat (*shuso*), and the assembly offer congratulations or consolation to the abbot (having previously sent word of his arrival;

this constitutes the first section). The head seat and the assembly stand before the Sangha Hall (the head seat occupies the first position in the upper section outside the door, while the rest of the monks are lined up in the lower section).
Arrange the incense table. The special envoy passes the document (shu) to the Head Seat (Shouzuo). The Head Seat incenses it and passes it to the Rector (Weina), who reads it aloud.

Once the reading is finished, the special envoy steps forward to inquire after [the assembly’s] well-being. The Head Seat withdraws slightly and stands. The Head Seat and the assembly enter the hall and stand at the top.

The special envoy enters the hall, proceeding according to the ritual for a visiting master (huazhu) entering the hall (the letter, sealed as on its envelope, is posted outside the door in the lower section). The Guest Prefect (Zhike) [performs his duties].

The special envoy is led into the Kūtāṅga Hall, where he presents the letter to the Chief Administrator (Jiànyuàn). Xūnxiǎn requests the Rector (Wéinà) to read it aloud; only after this do the formal greetings and the serving of tea and soup take place.

(In cases such as the transmission of a successor’s message or the arrival of a former resident, one simply proceeds to the quarters of the Abbot’s attendants to present the letter from the Head Seat’s office. Letters from the Head Seat and the assembly are posted outside the lower section of the gate.

In the Kūtāṅga Hall, the letter is merely presented to the Chief Administrator; in all such instances, the contents are not recited aloud. The Guest Master leads a tour of the monastic quarters (as when a fundraising master or a junior disciple delivers a letter to a venerable elder). Upon arrival, wait...
Only after the letter has been presented may one perform prostrations. Regarding the method for drafting a letter:

the language must be orderly and refined; the calligraphy and coloring must be meticulous; and the trimming and sealing of the corners must be performed according to the proper rules. Thus it shall be done.
In human affairs, one should act with propriety and give rise to a heart of respect. If matters are handled with negligence, people will pay them no heed;
it will merely waste paper and ink, and hinder one's spiritual practice. When writing letters to officials, one should exhort them to reduce punishments, protect the Dharma, and cherish monasteries.
One should not record even minor faults of the Sangha upon official warrants; even if there are instances of coarse conduct, one should instead encourage their protection and care.
Regarding the *kāṣāya*: one should exhort fellow practitioners to engage in meditation and recitation, maintain the sacred fires, and awaken to impermanence.
Or, one may write letters to venerable elders, urging them to endure toil and hardship to transmit the Dharma and benefit sentient beings.

One may also write to patrons, encouraging them to cultivate goodness and perform meritorious deeds. In all such matters, it is inappropriate to discuss worldly affairs at length; in speech, brevity and urgency are paramount. [Seal]
Burn incense and send it away (if it is not unavoidable, one should not rashly dispatch letters). Upon receiving a letter,
as if it were a missive bestowed by a highly esteemed and venerable person within the Sangha, one should immediately burn incense and look toward the Honored One.
When one has finished bowing toward the person [to whom it was sent], open it. If it is from someone of successive rank or superior respect, it must likewise be incensed with incense before opening.
For those of equal status, have an attendant or a practitioner open the seal (using scissors to cut one end carefully;

do not tear the envelope, for this is not only a lack of decorum but also constitutes coarse behavior). Once read, place it in a designated location according to the proper method, always maintaining a sense of gratitude. Do not...

It is easy to attain mastery. Just as when receiving an official letter, one should read it with great reverence; immediately thereafter, one should recite mantras and dedicate the merit to adorn and perfect one's blessings and wisdom.
When the Abbot or the Head of the Hall is recuperating from taking medicine, if it is not a common illness, they shall recuperate in a separate quarters for more than three days.
The attendant should inform the Head Seat and the administrative officers (zhishi). This applies likewise when the administrative officers of the Kusi or the various heads of departments are ill.
He shall also instruct the attendant to inform the *weina* to request leave to go to the *yanshou tang* (some places refer to it as the *shengxing tang*) to rest.
If the illness is slight and does not interfere with communal duties, he may simply rest in his own quarters. If the illness persists, he shall inform the abbot to appoint a successor.
When the abbot recovers, he shall ascend the hall to express his gratitude to the assembly, inquire after their welfare, and then descend from the seat. The chief administrator...

The assembly seated themselves; for matters of both illness and congratulations, they performed two prostrations with the robes spread out and three formal bows. (For words of thanks, it says: "Our methods of self-care were discordant, troubling you with inquiries after our health. Fortunately, by virtue of the power of the Dharma, we have somewhat recovered and are at peace. For words of congratulation, it says:)

I prostrate with joy that the Dharma-seat of the Abbot is at ease. My humble sentiments are filled with an irrepressible sense of exultation. [The assembly] circumambulates the hall to pay respects to the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ) and the Great Assembly.

Next, they enter the Abbot’s quarters to serve tea for the High Seat. When an administrative official (Karmadāna) recovers from illness, he enters the Hall to offer his thanks to the Resident Master (Upādhyāya).

He then pays his respects to the administrative officials, the heads of the various quarters, and the brothers within the assembly. If the initial signs of illness appear, the master may either go himself...
Alternatively, one may dispatch a person to inform the Hall Administrator (*tángsī*) to request leave for recuperation and notify the Head of the Quarters (*liáozhǔ*).

Only then should one enter the *Yánshòu Táng* (Hall of Longevity). Upon recovery from illness, one should first go to the Hall Administrator’s office to pay respects. Thereafter, one proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters (*fāngwǎn*) for formal greetings (the words of thanks being:

"Recently, by virtue of the Dharma-protection you have bestowed upon me, I have somewhat recovered my health. My humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. The reply is: "I am glad to hear that your physical health is at ease. I trust you are rejoicing. Subsequently, one visits the various administrative officers (*zhīshì*) in order.
Inquiries are made at the Head’s Quarters. Tea and soup for the various head officials from the Hall Master downward may be served according to custom; there is no need for special arrangements.
*Re-engraved Supplement to the Chan Garden Rules*, Volume Six;
*Re-engraved Supplement to the Chan Garden Rules*, Volume Seven.
When wishing to go to the toilet for small or large excrement, one must go there in advance; do not wait until the last moment when you are pressed by urgency and act in haste.

One should then fold the *kāṣāya* and place it upon the desk in the quarters or on a clean bamboo pole, perform a greeting, and depart. Immediately thereafter, one first puts on the undergarment (*nivasana*). Then...
With a clean towel draped over the left arm, one must not pass through the area of the Honored Hall.
Having hung the hand-towel upon a hook near the exterior of the toilet (dōshi), one rolls up the skirt and folds the outer robe (hen-shan). These are hung upon a pole in front of the toilet;
the outer robe is then placed atop the skirt and secured with a waist-belt. This serves both as a marker and to prevent them from falling to the ground. The right hand then carries [the items].
When carrying the water jar to the latrine, one must discard the shoes in a neat and orderly manner. Close the door gently and lower the hand to release the jar.
Upon reaching the latrine, snap the fingers three times to warn off the spirits that consume excrement. One must not spit or snot messily, nor strain with forceful breaths to make noise.

While using the wooden scrapers to clean the ground, one must remain separated from others by the door or wall and refrain from speaking or laughing. Regarding the method of purification, cold water is best; as for its use...
Hot water may cause intestinal wind; therefore, hold the bottle with the right hand and take water with the left (while still protecting the first and second fingers).

One must not splash water onto the ground or the rim of the basin on either side. When using a cleaning stick (*śalākā*), do not exceed one stalk (if someone has finished using it, they should wash it themselves before leaving).
To wash the hands, first use ash and then earth. Proceed to the rear rack to wash with soap pods (*kṣāra*) and cleansing powder (*kaṣāya*) up to the elbow.

Having finished washing and rinsing the mouth (according to the Vinaya, one must chew a willow twig), return to your original place. Fold and hang up the hand-towel, inquire after the *kāṣāya*, and put it on.
According to the Vinaya, if you have not washed yourself clean, you must not sit upon a monastic bed, nor prostrate before the Triple Gem, nor receive the prostrations of others.
Upon first arriving at the door of the latrine, if there is someone inside, do not cough, snap your fingers, or speak.

Regarding "speaking when pressed": if one is already in the latrine and perceives someone outside, one must exit immediately (from the point of washing the tally until this point, it is not appropriate to remain).
As described above for urinating in the latrine: gather the sleeves of the shirt and the skirt-garment, squat with the body close to the interior wall, and do not spit, sneeze, or speak.
One must always avoid those of senior virtue (according to the *Vinaya*, one must also wash clean after urination; violators shall be treated as previously stated).
When a deceased monk’s condition has become somewhat critical, the Hall Master shall consult with the Rector, the Monastic Supervisor, the Head Seat, the Librarian, the Scribe,

and the Guest Prefect to jointly conduct the inventory, perform the oral farewell, and collect the *sību* (monastic certificate) along with the deceased's belongings, which shall then be received and managed by the Hall Administration.

The Head Seat shall seal and take custody of the keys. The Administrative Officer shall submit a report to the authorities. If the illness worsens, he shall immediately submit another report regarding the severity of the condition.

If the monk has already passed away, he shall again submit a report to the authorities requesting that funeral rites be performed. Within three days, the certificates for the Temple Department, the Purple Robe, or the title of Master must be surrendered.
Upon the initial death of a deceased monk, the bath attendant shall bathe him, place the ladder-head and the vestments upon him, and seat him in the tub.

Internally, he was enshrined within a shrine and placed before the Hall of Extended Life (*yǎnshòu táng*). Incense and lamps were established there for his veneration, along with the cutting and crafting of white banners inscribed with verses on impermanence (*mùcháng jì*).

Furthermore, funeral flowers for the Buddha were placed upon the shrine, with an inscription reading: "In memory of the spirit of the deceased Venerable [Name]. The assembly was gathered to perform recitations;
that night, the ritual involved the chanting of the *Prātimokṣa* and the dedication of merit (*huíxiàng*). On the following morning, a vegetarian meal (*zhāi*) was served.

Regarding the subsequent escorting: On the appointed day, after the *vina* has finished striking the gong throughout the morning gruel and meal services—or after the distribution of funeral offerings—she strikes the gong once and announces:

"Venerable assembly, following the gruel (or midday meal), upon hearing the sound of the bell, each of you shall assume your dignified demeanor for the communal task (*pup-ch'ŏng*) of escorting the deceased monk."
All heads and officers of the various quarters shall assemble together. This is respectfully announced. (A single strike of the mallet.
The Rector then bows before the Sacred Monk and again bows before the Abbot, circumambulating the hall once. If there are monks outside the hall, they should likewise be bowed to.
With the exception of the rear section of the Sangha Hall, when the time arrives, the bell is struck; all gather before the shrine. The Abbot—
Next, the incense is burned in sequence. Once the *weina* has finished the recitation, the drum is struck and the bier is carried forward.

The assembly follows behind, holding banners, striking the *ting*, and carrying incense burners, censers, and ritual implements. The administrative officers (*zhishi*) of the storehouse office have made prior arrangements for these matters.

The practitioners and the *zhisui* (the officer in charge of daily affairs) shall lead the procession of the bier accordingly. Fuel and firewood are prepared before the altar; all matters pertaining to this tradition are to be conducted in this manner.
The Master presides over the rite. Once they have arrived at the pagoda site, the Abbot and those below him perform the incense-burning and abbreviated chanting of the Dharma service.

After the lighting of the pyre is completed (there should be a Dharma discourse), they recite the ten invocations of Amitābha Buddha and again chant the Dharma service. Upon its conclusion, the assembly disperses; some may chant sutras, each according to their own inclination.
If the funeral takes place within a city wall, the procedures for escorting the remains must be orderly and well-arranged from beginning to end; no frivolous behavior is permitted.

[The abbot] laughs. In silence, he recites the name of the Buddha and the secret mantra (*mantra*) to dedicate the merit to the deceased. All must depart together and return together; no one is permitted to remain behind.
If there is some business to attend to, one must request leave from the Hall Office on another day.

On the following day, the Hall Master (*shangtangzhu*) and the Rector (*weina*) perform the ritual for collecting the bones, which are then placed in a communal stupa (*putongta*) or scattered in water. Regarding the method for the distribution of robes (*changyi*): a plaque is hung to notify the assembly, and the bell is struck.
When the bell enters the hall, one first performs recitations for the deceased monk. Next, the robes and bowl are brought forth and requested that the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) verify their seals;

they are then opened before the assembly (prior to the striking of the bell, the robes and bowl have already been displayed within the hall). Once the sequential appraisal and chanting are completed, the Rector (Karmadāna) again performs recitations for the deceased monk.
Neither the Abbot nor the internal administrators (Anta-karmadāna) shall chant for the deceased monk’s belongings; the distribution is handled by the Rector.

One must break through [selfishness] to accord with the sentiments of the assembly; one must not spend funds recklessly. Aside from necessary expenses, distribute [the remainder] to the great assembly for the purpose of reading scriptures, or for the temporary reception of visiting monks who have come to see off a deceased monk, as well as those attending the chanting of the distribution of robes (*cāngyī*). From this, they shall receive one-third. The same applies to donors who come to read scriptures.

If there are many robes and bowls, they shall be drawn [from the store]. Furthermore, provide gruel or vegetarian offerings. This continues until the end of the first seven-day period, at which point the assembly shall gather.

The sutras and dharanis recited by the assembly shall be displayed simultaneously on the rear rack so that everyone may know them (the various administrators shall sign to demonstrate that they have communicated this to the community without partiality).
Aside from their spiritual practice, those who have left the household life must always keep their robes and alms bowls neat and sufficient for their needs;
it is improper to accumulate goods or increase one's greed. On the day of the distribution of robes, [these items] shall be exempted.

This causes the great assembly to sit for a long time and become weary. Furthermore, one must not be entirely without robes and bowls, so as to avoid allowing [the property] to be encroached upon or damaged after death.
Whenever the belongings of a deceased monk are auctioned, it is intended to counteract the mind of stinginess and to establish a karmic connection with the deceased monk.

One must not disparage items while singing their value or sell them at an exorbitant price. If the price set for the clothing and goods is too high, one must not harbor such thoughts, lest the assembly laugh in derision.
When the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) chants the distribution of robes, he must know the relative value—high or low—of the items being sung.

If an item is new, he says it is new; if old, he says it is old; if worn, he says it is worn. He must fix the sound of the price (whether it be full, reduced, or according to the current exchange rate). As it is said:

If the assembly is unwilling to contribute additional funds, one must strike [the gong] even at a low price. If the contribution is excessive, the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) shall immediately say:
"You must be more circumspect; regret is difficult to remedy later. This is done to avoid causing agitation or trouble among the assembly.

Furthermore, one must not entrust the chanting to others or involve communal property (*sangha-vastu*), for fear of giving rise to suspicion. If the communal property or the Head of the Hall enters...

Regarding the communal chanting for robes (*zhòngchàngyī*): it is permitted for others to entrust one with the chanting. Before the sick monk, the recitation is performed (the *vinaya-master*, having finished praising the Buddha, says:

"This morning, there is a certain bhikṣu who is ill. On his behalf, we shall repent for the enmities of many lifetimes and the transgressions of kalpas. We specially mobilize our utmost sincerity to look up to the pure assembly to proclaim the holy names, thereby washing away deep calamities. We rely upon the venerable ones to recite the *Qīngjìng* [Sūtra] and so forth. Furthermore, the dedication says:

"We humbly pray that this person’s single mind may be pure, their four great elements light and at ease, their lifespan and wisdom-life extended, and their physical body and Dharma-body made firm. If the illness is severe, then perform the ten recitations of Amitābha Buddha.)

The Method for Recitation: First, conclude with praises to Amitābha Buddha. Next, address the assembly, saying: "For the sake of [Name], we shall recite the four sacred names of Amitābha Buddha in a long-drawn voice. Then, perform the dedication, saying:

"We humbly pray that although [Name]'s various conditions have not yet ceased, they may soon attain ease; though their great life is difficult to turn back, may they be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. After reciting the four sacred names, exhort them to collect the mind and recite with purity, without following after worldly affairs.

Recitation before the Shrine (When the deceased monk first enters the shrine, the Hall Administrator informs the assembly and strikes the bell to gather them before the shrine. Once the Abbot and those below him, along with the administrative officers, hall heads, and hall masters, have finished offering incense in order, the Rector strikes the chime and, after praising the Buddha, says: "It is essential to consider that birth and death alternate..."

Cold and heat alternate in succession. Their coming is like lightning flashing across the vast sky; their departure is like waves subsiding in the great ocean. On this day, the deceased Bhikṣu [Name], his conditions for birth having been exhausted, has suddenly passed away. Having realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, he has attained the bliss of nirvāṇa.

We respectfully entrust him to the Great Assembly and solemnly approach the funerary shrine to recite the sublime names of the various Sages, offering his pure spirit to the Pure Land. We rely upon the Great Assembly to recite the "Pure Dharma Body" and other mantras. Furthermore, the dedication prayer says:

"We humbly pray that his spirit may transcend to the Pure Realm and his karma be shed from the toil of the mundane world. May the lotus flower of the highest grade bloom, and may the Buddha grant him the prediction of Buddhahood in one lifetime. [Recite] again: "We trouble the venerable assembly once more to recite the 'Ten Directions and Three Times'... [Proceed with] the chanting while lifting the coffin.

(The liturgy says: "As we prepare to escort the sacred shrine to the grand ceremony of *te-p'i* [cremation], we rely upon the venerable assembly to recite the great names of the various sages. This serves to express our grief at parting and to provide spiritual sustenance for the path to enlightenment.

After ten recitations of the Buddha’s name, proceed. The Ten Recitations Before the Stupa (The liturgy says: "We consider that the deceased, [Name], having followed conditions to pass into stillness, now undergoes cremation according to the Dharma. We burn the body that spent a hundred years propagating the Way, entering the single path of *nirvāṇa*. )

We look up to rely upon the venerable assembly to assist our departed spirits. Thus, we recite the Ten Recollections. Upon completion, it is said: "The sacred names have been extolled above to provide for the rebirth of the deceased. We pray that the mirror of wisdom may reflect its radiance and the true wind disperse its colors;

that within the Garden of Bodhi, the flowers of awakening may bloom, and within the Ocean of Dharmatā, the defilements of the mundane mind may be washed away. Tea is offered in three libations, and incense is burned in a single burner, to commemorate this journey to the clouds. I pay homage to the holy assembly. Prior to the auction of robes, the chanting is performed.

When the assembly has gathered, the Rector strikes the chime once and says: "As floating clouds disperse, their shadows do not linger; as the remaining candle burns out, its light naturally fades. This present auction is used to manifest impermanence."

We rely upon the venerable assembly to act on behalf of the deceased, [Name], for the purpose of assisting their enlightened spirit in rebirth in the Pure Land. We recite the verses on the Pure Dharma Body, and so forth. Again, the *qing* bell is struck, and it is said:
"The method of chanting for the distribution of robes follows established custom; the new and old, as well as the long and short, must be carefully accounted for.

The money must be of full value (either seventy-seven *mo* or seventy-five *mo* coins), and no new coins shall be mixed with them. Once the sound of the *qing* bell has ceased, there shall be no subsequent regrets. This is respectfully announced."

The chanting for the distribution of robes is concluded. It is then announced: "The above recitations by the assembly and the chanting of the merits of the distributed clothing and goods are all dedicated toward the deceased [Name], to assist their enlightened spirit in rebirth in the Pure Land.
We further request the assembly to recite the names of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time with sincere devotion; do not engage in laughter, idle talk, or discordant behavior.

The recitation of the precepts, the boiling of medicinal decoctions, the chanting for the distribution of robes, and the serving of tea are all under the jurisdiction of the Treasury Office (*kusi*). According to the Vinaya, corpses and clothing must not pass beneath a stupa.
Furthermore, one must not burn corpses beneath a stupa.

Regarding the appointment of a monk to retire from the monastery, the venerable elder, the head seat, or the library director—whomever accords with the expectations of the assembly—may be nominated; this shall be the responsibility of the incumbent abbot.

Having ascended the seat and finished the formal announcement (*bai*), the administrative officers and the assembly go to the abbot’s quarters to offer their invitation (the words of the invitation being:

"The assembly turns its heart toward you; we have long contemplated your instruction. We humbly hope that, out of compassion, you will deign to grant us your permission"). If he does not grant it, they do not return the bow (saying: "If one cannot save oneself, how can one act as a teacher for others?").

If he grants it, they immediately return the bow (saying: "Since we have received your firm request, we dare not refuse"). Thereupon, he proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to express his gratitude, with the ceremonial protocols adjusted as appropriate. He then retires from the monastery, honoring those of senior rank.

[The Guest] says: "I originally intended to seek refuge in your noble treasury with my humble and decrepit self. Having received your invitation, I dare not disobey. [The Host] replies: "Now that the great elephant-vehicle has arrived, the Wheel of Dharma shall turn constantly. Although it is improper to trouble you, pray keep the Buddha-Dharma in mind. [Regarding the departure from the monastery and those of equal standing: [The Guest] says:

"I was just planning to sustain myself and then act for the benefit of others. The superior command is difficult to refuse, yet my humble feelings are full of shame. [The Host] replies: "It is improper to trouble you; simply keep the Buddha-Dharma in mind. [Regarding eminent masters from all quarters and junior disciples who have come to study:

[The Guest] says: "This is by the Venerable Master’s direction. Now I am to receive the inquiries of my brothers. Although I lack deep realization, I dare not flatly decline. My humble feelings are beyond measure."

I am filled with the utmost awe and gratitude. He replied, "Since you have already received this residual light, simply keep the Buddha-dharma in mind. They all looked upon one another and expressed their thanks to the administrative officers.
On the following day, the Head of the Hall and the stewards specifically prepared a special tea service (providing food at will).

Please request one person from among the Venerable Elders, the Chief Administrator (Kān-yuàn), and the Rector (Wéi-ná) to be nominated; one person from among the external Head Officers (Tóu-shǒu) to be nominated;

and several individuals from among those with prior service or current labor who are diligent, possess the necessary mental capacity, understand the monastic community (cóng-lín), and are experienced in administrative affairs. These shall be combined for the required purpose.
Regarding money, goods, luggage, porters, sedan chairs, and other items necessary for travel by boat or ship:

official petitions, monastic petitions, petitions from monastic officials, petitions from various heads and elders, petitions from lay donors, and petitions from retired officials must all be meticulously prepared.

Furthermore, the abbot’s notice, reports submitted to the local prefectures and counties, the documents sent to the prefectures and counties of the destination, official correspondence, the monastery’s gate notice, and the tea list must likewise be detailed and thorough.
Prepare everything and arrange it according to the Dharma. Regarding items such as money and goods, one must select a monk to oversee the income and expenditure;
he must neither be overly extravagant nor too frugal, so as to avoid official inspections.

In all matters, one must not display a grandiose appearance; it is best to act unexpectedly. A special envoy shall first proceed to the relevant prefectures and counties to submit the official notice. Then...

Afterward, he shall enter the monastery and settle there. If the local prefectures or counties refuse to dispatch him, he should immediately request a return document (*huídié*) and first have a dedicated messenger take this document back to report to the original prefecture or county; he must not return immediately.
If there is a further written request, he should again petition that prefecture or county to dispatch him as before. Only when there is no further written request may he return to the monastery.

If the provincial and county authorities grant their approval, one should immediately proceed to the monastery to perform the formal invitation according to the Dharma. First, the special envoy shall consult with the administrative officers (zhishi).
Once this is concluded, they ascend to the Hall for the formalities of the abbot; after the tea ceremony has ended, the envoy carries the written invitations to announce the request.

Only after three earnest requests may the candidate accept. (Master Fayan Wuantong [Fayun Yuancong] always waited until the messenger had been dispatched three times before he would accept such an invitation.)

Regarding the method for a venerable elder to accept an official appointment (shūsō): when such a person sees that the abbot intends to appoint them, they must first request three times at the abbot’s quarters. If the abbot shows signs of consent, he shall strike the drum to assemble the community.

The candidate must then further decline and yield; only when it becomes unavoidable may they accept. They shall then be honored with incense and a formal discourse (faryū) shall be delivered. This is the procedure for the invitation.

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) reads the proclamation. After the ascent of the seat and the formal exhortation are completed, he descends from the seat and offers congratulations and thanks to the administrators (*karmadāna*), the head seat (*śrāmaṇera-śīrṣa*), and the assembly.

He performs two prostrations with hands extended and three full bows. (The words of congratulation say: "Having moved to this eminent monastery, joy stirs throughout the community; the Patriarchs are further glorified, and both humans and devas celebrate together. We, your humble servants, cannot contain our boundless delight. The words of thanks say: "To have accepted the request upon my breast has brought disgrace to the ancestral tradition;

looking upward, I am ashamed before the heavens, and looking downward, I am humbled before the great assembly"). If the request was made by someone other than the current abbot, one must first go to his quarters and make three formal requests.
If there is agreement, the abbot ascends the seat and makes a formal announcement, after which he and the assembly perform the ritual invitation. Thereupon, they prostrate.
The abbot receives the memorial document (*shu*). If the abbot has not yet served at this monastery, the special envoy shall have prepared a set of Dharma robes in advance.

When the proclamation and distribution of the *shu* (memorial) are finished, the special envoy presents it. It is incensed with fragrance and displayed for all to see; upon opening it, there should be a discourse on the Dharma.
If [the deceased] has already passed into liberation (*nirvāṇa*), this is not required. Thereafter, the presiding seat on the Dharma-throne is pointed out; there should be a discourse on the Dharma.

Once the exaltation is complete, the officiant descends from the seat and pays respects to the abbot, performing either nine full prostrations or two full prostrations and three bows. The words of thanks are: "Throughout my life I have sought discernment, yet I look up with shame at the former sages. Three..."

The invitation is already earnest; it is difficult to refuse the command from above. My humble feelings are filled with the utmost agitation and trepidation. The words of congratulation state: "The needle in the bag has already been revealed; the falling flowers cannot conceal it. Fortunately, you have taken up this worthy task; I humbly pray that you may rejoice. Next, offer congratulations and thanks to the administrators, the head seat, and the assembly.
Perform two prostrations and three bows (the words of thanks state: "Having received this appointment, I fear I have brought disgrace to the ancestral tradition.

I look up to your support and encouragement, for which I am overwhelmed with gratitude. The words of congratulation state: 'Rejoicing at having accepted the invitation of devas and humans, we add glory to the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. My humble feelings are filled with the utmost exultation'). For one or two days, visit the various quarters in succession.
The special envoy specifically presents the tea notice (*chábǎng*) to the new abbot first. On the following day, a meal is prepared and tea is served.
Regarding the etiquette for the final departure, the ascent to the hall, and the small discourse (*xiǎocān*) to bid farewell to the assembly, each should follow local custom.
If one encounters an attendant receiving an invitation, one must by no means privately take along items used within the monastery. If there is an exchange of money or grain, it must...

This handover must be clearly defined. Furthermore, one must not transfer capable attendants from the monastery to the traveling party, nor accept excessive provisions for the journey from this institution.
Even when accompanying those on a joint mission, one must ensure that this monastery does not suffer any loss of affairs.
Only then may one request that the leading brothers be dispatched, along with a full list of the entourage; select those who are fit to carry the necessary correspondence ahead.
The subordinate official and the donor submit their letter of thanks and the formal document of arrival. Two people return to the monastery to clear out the quarters.
On the day of departure, the new abbot packs his belongings together with the assembly and leaves the monastery (the abbot follows behind the assembly;
the special messenger and the accompanying monks and laypeople follow behind the new abbot).
Regarding the method for a venerable elder entering a monastery: when the new abbot arrives, he carries his bundle in front while his attendants follow behind.

If they encounter a welcoming party, he may either remove his sunshade and lower his staff to perform a greeting, or slightly grasp the edge of the sunshade with his right hand and bow his body, or be invited to take his seat.

Regarding the tea service: simply remove your hat, lean on your staff, and take your seat. One must not remove one’s bundle (when visiting a venerable elder, inquire and say: "On my journey, I was unable to maintain full decorum for prostrations"; when meeting officials, merely bow and say:
"My attire is inconvenient for travel; I hope you will not hold me in fault"). Upon entering the monastery, burn incense beneath the Triple Gate (at which time there should be a formal discourse).

Proceeding to the front of the Sangha Hall, unpack your belongings. Afterwards, wash your feet at the rear rack. Enter the hall to pay respects to the Holy Monk, burning incense while the fellow practitioners follow along.

Perform three prostrations with the full opening of the robes and circumambulate the hall once. The *Weina* (Chant Master) requests everyone to take their seats; perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*).

Once the formal entry has been completed, the new abbot first proceeds to the Great Hall, then to the Earth Deity Shrine, and then to the True Hall, chanting the liturgical rites and burning incense at each.

The administrative officers (*zhishi*) then invite him to enter the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*). Having taken his seat and displayed the formalities, the administrative officers offer their thanks and briefly introduce him to the community.

The guests meet one another. After a short while, the drums are sounded and they ascend the hall. They perform the successive rites of courtesy, offering congratulations and expressions of gratitude according to the ritual for "untying knots" (the congratulatory words state:

"We humbly receive the news that the Elephant-Vehicle [the Master] has graced this Dharma assembly; our inferior hearts cannot contain our utmost joy. The words of thanks state: "I am ashamed of my own unworthiness, yet I have presumptuously occupied this famous monastery; our inferior hearts cannot contain our utmost trepidation").

In the evening, there is a small *sīmān* (small *cān*), following the standard three-day interval. On the following morning, the officials observe the ceremony, performing the successive rites of courtesy. A day is selected to open the assembly.

In the Hall. As soon as you arrive and formalities have somewhat settled, you should specifically conduct a private visit for the special messenger and his attendants, as well as for the invited officials, donors, and former abbots or veteran monks (regarding the etiquette for the attendants, it must be harmonized;
before entering the monastery, order them to first go and settle in a separate quarters, waiting until things are settled before dispersing to invite them to their respective quarters).

Venerable elders who serve as abbots propagate the teachings on behalf of the Buddha and manifest extraordinary wisdom in their affairs; thus they are said to "transmit the Dharma. Each residing in a particular locality to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom is called "abbot" (zhuchi).
When first turning the wheel of the Dharma, one is commissioned to appear in the world; because the succession of masters has a verifiable basis, it is termed "transmitting the lamp."
Having attained the title of the Venerable Elder Subhūti, you reside in the quarters of the Tathāgata Suvarṇaśālī.
Privately, you sweep and cleanse for the noble assembly to purify the site of enlightenment; officially, you are invited to perform rites of incense and meditation to extend the Emperor’s longevity.
Therefore, it is fitting that you exercise the great mind and expound the Great Dharma, embodying great virtue and great practice, and manifesting the great Buddha-work through vast compassion.

Great benefit is thereby accomplished. With the scales and weights in hand, one may bestow or withhold as the occasion demands; because these are the rules and standards, they are difficult to fathom or deliberate upon.

Nevertheless, regarding its fundamental principle, the issuing of commands and the prohibition of transgressions must rely on awe-inspiring authority. As the saying goes, "When the form is straight, the shadow is upright"; nothing is more effective than maintaining reverence.
Appointing officials according to their abilities serves merely as a rough guide; with folded hands, look up to the accomplishment of the task, and be careful not to let your own efforts interfere.

To maintain the strict regulations of the monastic groves and to care for the great monks who are like dragons and elephants, providing guidance tirelessly from morning until evening—this is precisely the eye and the lamp for humanity.

When a Venerable Elder passes away as if already seated in the state of nirvana, he is placed within the Abbot’s quarters and offered incense and flowers. A verse of final instruction is affixed to the name tablet and hung on either side of the funeral altar.
Among the assembly of venerable elders, one kinsman is requested to serve as the presiding mourner; if none is available, [the procedure continues as follows].
Regarding the legal heirs, one should first request other abbots and venerable seniors; thereafter, compose and dispatch a death notice to inform the officials, donors, and monastic authorities.
Request neighboring venerable seniors, dharma-heir disciples, and close dharma-relatives to send out letters on their behalf.

Three days later, the body shall be placed in the coffin according to the rites for deceased monks. At the time of placing the body in the coffin, one venerable senior shall be requested to preside over the funeral service.

[The Abbot’s] Seat (there shall be a Dharma address). A shrine niche is established in the western wing of the Dharma Hall; in the eastern wing, a bed, a clothing rack, and various implements for personal use are laid out.
The true likeness [of the deceased] is hung upon the Dharma seat. Within the Dharma Hall, offerings of plain curtains, white flowers, lamps, and candles are prepared.
Before the true likeness, the ritual arrangements for the *daochang* (meditation hall) are spread. The junior disciples remain behind the curtain of the shrine niche, beneath the screen. Fully...

The mourners maintain vigil at the shrine. Once the funeral rites have been arranged within the Dharma Hall and the presiding mourner and those below him have completed their worship of the remains, the administrative officers, the heads of the community, the sons of the deceased, and the assembly shall meet with the presiding mourner.
Following this, the presiding mourner and the others shall offer mutual condolences in due order.
If there are outsiders coming to offer condolences, the outer guest master shall lead them to the hall, while the inner guest master leads them before the remains.
After they have burned incense and performed their salutations, they shall meet with the presiding mourner (*sangju*), the administrative officers (*jisa*), and the head seat (*shuse*).

Thereafter, they shall go to the mourning tent to console the junior monks (*ksiao-shi*) in mourning, and then return to offer tea and soup to the presiding mourner. Finally, the outer guest master shall see them out. If there is a formal sacrifice (*zhai*), the same procedure applies.

These items shall be arranged before the portrait. If no one is brought to read the liturgical texts for the offering, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual director) and the *śāstrī* (scribe) of this monastery shall read them in their stead.

For the funeral rites, it is appropriate to prepare a large coffin (*mahā-kuṭi*), along with temporary decorations, the portrait pavilion, the incense pavilion, ritual implements, flowers, and banners.
On the day the coffin is raised, this monastery shall provide a grand vegetarian feast according to its means; the offerings should be substantial.
As usual. When the time arrives, one venerable elder is invited to lead the bier (there shall be a formal discourse). The filial sons and attendants surround the rear of the bier.
Next, the presiding mourner and those below him follow, with the mourners and the assembly of this monastery proceeding in succession along the middle path.
Officials and donors walk alongside the assembly on the left and right. The nuns and the family members follow at the end.
Subsequently, for the funeral procession, if by cremation, one shall invite a venerable elder to light the pyre (there should be a Dharma discourse).

If interred in a stupa, one shall invite a venerable elder to descend the coffin (there should be a Dharma discourse), and again invite a venerable elder to scatter the earth (there should be a Dharma discourse).

However, rites such as the ten recitations shall follow the protocol for deceased monks. This monastery shall distribute funds for the recitation of the Buddha’s name; upon returning to the monastery, one shall invite a venerable elder.

Hang the portrait of the deceased (there should be a formal dharma discourse). For the time being, arrange it within the *shindō* (sleeping hall). The presiding mourner and those below him shall pay respects to the portrait, offer mutual condolences, and disperse.

The administrative officers, the head monks, and the filial sons shall attend before the portrait morning and evening to burn incense, and during the two meal times—midday and evening—they shall provide offerings along with the assembly.
Once a date for the new abbot’s entry into the monastery has been set, the portrait shall be moved into the *shindō*.
Regarding the procedures for entering the shrine, lifting the shrine, lowering the fire, lowering the shrine, scattering earth, and hanging the portrait—all of these involve ritual offerings.

The presiding mourner must present further tokens of gratitude. The monastic administration should maintain a degree of order and stability. For venerable seniors such as those mentioned above, everyone must specifically offer their thanks.

Matters shall be deliberated in due order; a formal petition shall be submitted by the newly appointed abbot and the administrative officers to clarify the situation, and the various heads of the monasteries and elders shall be invited.
Once the monastic officials have submitted their certification, if the person so certified does not meet with the approval of the assembly,

the administrative officers of this monastery shall go to the authorities to lodge an appeal, and another person shall be selected. Furthermore, if the authorities insist on proceeding alone or require this monastery to provide a guarantee,
we must also act promptly to avoid a prolonged vacancy in the position of abbot.
Upon leaving the monastery, whether due to old age, illness, or some other circumstance, one must not harbor lingering attachments to the position of abbot.

One should first settle affairs in the abbot’s quarters, including one's robes and bowl, and prepare one's traveling staff and bundle. This also includes matters such as funds held by the monastic community or offerings provided for the Sangha.

One must clearly record in writing all transactions with the administrative officer (*kaji*). Furthermore, the public property of the Abbot’s quarters (*dōtō*) must be formally handed over and managed through written records.
These must be sealed with the temple seal and distributed for the administrator’s knowledge.
A separate person shall be appointed to guard the Abbot’s quarters and oversee its contents, who shall reside in the Attendant’s Quarters (*shisurō*). If the Abbot’s robes or bowl are somewhat...

Generally, before retiring from the monastery, one should appraise the funds for the communal meals and allocate the money and goods to the permanent assets of the monastery to prevent the faults of embezzlement or misappropriation.
When departing the monastery, one’s luggage should consist only of personal effects and ritual implements;
if the luggage is excessive, it will provoke public ridicule or give rise to further slander. Furthermore, gold, silver, and silk fabrics are subject to taxation.
Items subject to prohibition or monopoly shall not be carried along. Furthermore, one must not carry letters or travel documents for officials, nor may one pre-arrange a retirement residence.
If one intends to leave the jurisdiction of this prefecture to travel far away, one must first make appropriate arrangements and obtain a formal authorization.
Once all matters are settled, one should then have an attendant or a junior disciple [act on one's behalf].
The person submits a letter of departure from the monastery. The abbot and his attendants subsequently withdraw from the main quarters and proceed elsewhere, or settle in a separate lodging.
Once departed, when staying as a guest at various locations, one should bring only one attendant and one novice;
they must not be too numerous, for fear of causing disturbance or anxiety to the host’s household or monastery. All other necessities, whether fine or coarse, are to be shared with the community.

One must not involve oneself in the affairs of the *yūen* (the monastic community) or engage in light criticism of the master. One must not speak of the merits or faults of the administrative officers (*jishi*) or the heads (*shushō*), nor mention past events.
Regarding all the labors and achievements of the abbot, as well as all matters of personal pride or self-aggrandizement, one must remain silent.

Whether or not one accepts an invitation to ascend the seat or give a *sōsan* (informal sermon) at various locations where one has passed through depends on the circumstances of the time; however, if it is not the host who invites one, [one should decline].
When one is recommended by others or formally invited by the administrative assembly (*karmadāna*), one must not unilaterally accept such an invitation to enter the quarters.

If one has already retired from the main monastery, it is inappropriate to remain constantly at its side or to take up residence in the old quarters; such conduct is extremely discordant with the sentiments of the community.
One should strictly guard against this. However, if one is ill or elderly and cannot leave, then it is harmless to act according to one's own convenience.
[End of] the Seventh Volume of the Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules of the Zen Garden).
[Beginning of] the Eighth Volume of the Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*.

The *Guijingwen* (Text on the Turtle-Mirror) states: "Two cassias cast their shade; one flower manifests its auspiciousness. From that time forth, the establishment of monastic communities (*senglin*) was essentially for the sake of the assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).

Therefore, because of the need to instruct and reveal the assembly of monks, there are elders (*sthavira*); because of the need to serve as a model and representative for the assembly of monks, there are head seats (*śrāmaṇera*). To bear...
Because of the responsibility for the community of monks, there is the *jianyuan* (superintendent); because of the need to harmonize the community of monks, there is the *weina* (rector);

because of the need to provide offerings to the community of monks, there is the *dianzuo* (head cook); because of performing labor for the community of monks, there is the *zhisui* (steward); because of handling the receipts and disbursements for the community of monks, there is the *kutou* (storekeeper);
because of managing the calligraphy and documents for the community of monks, there is the *shuzhuang* (secretary); and because of guarding the sacred teachings for the community of monks...
There is a storekeeper to receive and attend to donors for the sake of the community of monks; there is a guest master to receive invitations on behalf of the community of monks;

there is an attendant to guard the robes and bowls for the sake of the community of monks; there is a dormitory master to provide service with medicinal decoctions for the sake of the community of monks;
there is a bath master and water-head to wash for the sake of the community of monks; [and there is one] to protect the community of monks from...
Because of the cold, there are those who serve as charcoal-heads and furnace-heads. Because they beg for the sake of the community of monks, there are street-wardens and alms-collectors.
Because they perform manual labor for the community of monks, there are gardeners, millers, and estate managers. Because they cleanse for the community of monks, there are sanitation officers.
Because there are *śrāmaṇeras* and *karmadānas* to serve the community of monks, the conditions for practicing the Way are fully provided in every way;
the necessities for sustaining the body are ready in all their varieties. With no anxiety over myriad affairs, one may focus the single mind on the Way.

Noble and honored within the world, yet leisurely and at ease beyond material things—pure, unconditioned, and supreme among all assemblies. Reflecting upon the strength of many people, how could you not know this?
To repay kindness is to repay one's debt of gratitude. Attending at dawn and requesting instruction at dusk, never wasting a single moment, is how one repays the Elder.
Maintaining order between the honorable and the humble, and conducting oneself with composure and dignity, is how one repays the Head Seat.

Complying with laws and regulations externally while observing the monastic precepts internally is how one repays the Steward. Gathering together in the six harmonies, blending like water and milk, is how one repays the Rector. For...
One attains the Way only to then receive this food; thus, one repays the *diànzuò* (steward). One dwells peacefully in the monastic quarters and guards the communal utensils;
thus, one repays the *zhísuì* (yearly supervisor). One does not violate even a single hair’s breadth of the property of the Sangha;

thus, one repays the *kùtóu* (storekeeper). One does not take up a brush in hand, as if extinguishing a fire on one's head; thus, one repays the *shūzhuàng* (scribe). [The text continues: "Bright windows and clean desks... (the ancient...)

To illuminate the mind through teaching is the way to repay the Abbot. To conceal one's brilliance and obscure one's traces, refusing to seek social companionship, is the way to repay the Guest Master.
To have a constant place of residence and to arrive first when requesting instruction is the way to repay the Attendant.

To dwell with only a single flask and a single bowl amidst the community like a mountain is the way to repay the Dormitory Master. To endure mental and physical suffering and to take gruel and medicine as appropriate is the way to repay the Infirmary Master.
To repay the Hall Master: one serves with lightness, slowness, and silent composure, never neglecting the cause of the water, thereby repaying the Bath Master and the Water Head.

To repay the Charcoal Head and the Stove Head: one maintains silence and stands with hands clasped in reverence, withdrawing oneself and yielding to others. To repay the Street Alms-collector and the Fund-raiser:

one reflects upon whether one’s own virtue and conduct are complete or deficient in order to receive offerings. To repay the donors: one calculates the amount of merit and measures the extent of their arrival.

Providing lodging is the way to repay the *yuántóu* (garden master) and *móutóu* (field master). Drawing water and managing affairs with circumspection, while possessing a sense of shame and integrity, is the way to repay the *jìngtóu* (sanitation master).
Being broad-minded so as to be easy to follow, and simple so as to be easy to manage, is the way to repay the *jìngrén* (attendants).
Thus, beneath the monastic groves, the work of the Way is ever renewed; those of the highest capacity attain discernment in a single lifetime, while those of middling capacity...
