The Elder nurtures the holy embryo. Even while one has not yet awakened to the source of the mind, he does not waste his time;

such a person is a true Jewel of the Sangha and a field of merit for the world. He serves as a bridge and a ford for the degenerate age, destined to realize the ultimate fruit of the two types of adornment.
If, however, the monastic groves are not well-ordered and the Wheel of Dharma is not turned, this is not what an Elder should do for the sake of the assembly. If the three karmas are not...
If one does not regulate the four modes of deportment with gravity, one is not fit to lead the assembly as the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera).
If one’s capacity to accommodate others is not broad and one’s heart of affection for the assembly is not profound, one is not fit to protect the assembly as the Chief Administrator (Karmadāna).

If practitioners are not at peace and those who disrupt the community are not removed, one is not fit to gladden the assembly as the Rector (Karmadāna). If the six flavors are not refined and the three virtues are not provided, one is not [fit for the office].

If the *diànzuò* (chief cook) does not serve the assembly; if the quarters are not maintained and the utensils are not provided, he is not fulfilling the duty of one who should bring peace to the assembly.
If he hoards the permanent property and embezzles from the monks, he is not fulfilling the duty of a *kùtóu* (storekeeper) who should provide for the assembly.

If his calligraphy is unskillful and his characters are crude and fragmented, he is not fulfilling the duty of a scribe who should adorn the assembly. If the desks and tables are not solemn and there is clamor...

To allow afflictions to persist without ceasing is not how a Zangzhu (Storekeeper) should treat the assembly. To loathe the poor and love the wealthy, or to value the laity while slighting the monks, is not how a Zhike (Guest Master) should assist the assembly.
To lack courtesy in one’s demeanor or to cause the distinction between the honorable and the humble to fall into disorder is not how a Shizhe (Attendant) should command the assembly.
To be negligent in tidying up or lax in guarding the quarters is not how a Liaozhu (Wardron Master) should dwell with the assembly. Not...
To attend to and disturb a sick person with idle service is not the way for a Hall Master (*tangzhu*) to show compassion to the assembly.
To provide insufficient hot water or to fail to regulate its temperature is not the way for a Bath Master (*yuzhu*) or Water Head (*shuītóu*) to cleanse the assembly.

To fail to prepare in advance so that the multitude is troubled by anxiety is not the way for a Fire-wood Head (*lútóu*) or Charcoal Head (*tàntóu*) to serve the assembly. To be unjust in handling wealth or to fail to exert one’s full effort is not...
The reason why lay donors provide for the assembly is that while the land yields surplus benefits, no single person can achieve complete merit.
It is not the duty of the garden head, the miller, or the estate manager to act on behalf of the assembly; they must eliminate laziness and lack of all necessary conditions.

It is not the duty of the sanitation officer to serve the assembly if prohibitions go unheeded and commands are not carried out. It is not the duty of the lay attendants (*karmadāna*) to follow the assembly if they do not comply with restrictions and fail to execute orders.
Furthermore, if the assembly of monks treats their teacher with contempt and the Dharma with disdain, following their own whims and circumstances, this is not how they repay the Elder.

If they sit and lie in disorder and their conduct is discordant, this is not how they repay the Head Seat. If they hold the royal law in light regard and show no concern for the monastic community, this is not how they repay the Chief Administrator.
If those above and below are not in harmony and strife becomes entrenched, this is not how... [they repay the community].
To crave delicious food and disparage coarse meals is not the way to repay the *karmadāna*.
To dwell in one’s quarters and enjoy them for oneself without considering future occupants is not the way to repay the *śayanāsana-vārika*.

To greedily covet personal gain and offerings while neglecting the monastery’s permanent property is not the way to repay the *koṣṭhāgārika*. To devote oneself to holding pens and inkstones and to indulge in literary pursuits is not the way...
To reply with mere written correspondence; to treat the golden scriptures with negligence while seeking out secular texts—this is not how one repays the Abbot.

To follow after worldly men and cultivate ties with the noble—this is not how one repays the Guest Master. To neglect summoning and seating the assembly of monks—this is not how one repays the Attendant.
To hinder others for one’s own sake and to store things carelessly, thereby inviting theft—this is not [how one repays the Steward].
To repay the *liaozhu* (head of the quarters) for this; yet to be prone to anger and lacking joy, disregarding the conditions of one’s illness, is not the way to repay the *tangzhu* (hall master).
To let buckets and ladles make noise and to use water without moderation is not the way to repay the *yuzhu* (bath master) or the *shuītóu* (water-head).

To keep oneself warm and comfortable while causing inconvenience to others is not the way to repay the *lútóu* (stove-head) or the *tàn tóu* (charcoal-head). To fail to contemplate spiritual cultivation and remain complacent—[is not the way to repay the masters].
To accept offerings without purpose is not the way to repay the street-wardens and those who lead the alms-round.

To eat one’s fill all day long without applying the mind to anything is not the way to repay the garden-head, the mill-head, or the estate manager. To leave snot and spittle in disarray upon the walls and in the latrines is not the way to repay the sanitation head.
To be preoccupied solely with imposing authority while lacking any prior instruction in virtue is not the way to repay the janitors.

For even a whirlwind circling a thousand times may still leave something incomplete; we simply wish to set aside our shortcomings and follow what is most excellent in order to collectively discern the affairs of the renunciant life.
It is our hope that within the lion’s den all shall become lions, and beneath the sandalwood forest there shall be nothing but sandalwood.
May they thus behold the assembly at Vulture Peak once again during this latter five-hundred-year period. Now, the flourishing or decline of the Dharma depends upon the monastic community.
The Sangha is a field of reverence and should be honored and esteemed. If the Sangha is held in high regard, the Dharma is held in high regard; if the Sangha is slighted, the Dharma is slighted.
Once internal protection is strict, external protection must necessarily be diligent.

Even if one happens to serve as the host for the morning gruel and midday meal, or briefly presides over the administration of the monastery, one should always treat one’s fellow practitioners with respect. One must not arrogantly exalt oneself.

If one is conceited and self-important, handling private matters as if they were public affairs, how can one maintain such status when all things are impermanent? One day, one will return to the common assembly.
How can one look upon this? Cause and effect are without discrepancy and difficult to evade. As a monk, you are a son of the Buddha; your right to receive offerings is no different [from others].
Honored by all in both heaven and the human realm, it is only right that your morning and evening meals be refined and abundant. The four requisites for support must not be lacking.
For two thousand years, the Blessed One’s lingering shade has covered us, his descendants; it is but a fraction of the light of his white tuft of hair.
The enjoyment of these merits is inexhaustible; one need only know how to serve the assembly and need not worry about poverty.

Since the Sangha comprises both ordinary and holy beings and gathers from the ten directions, and as it is said that all have a share in the "invited dwellings" (caityas), how can one falsely give rise to discrimination or feel contemptuous aversion?

Guest monks stay for three mornings in the lodging for overnight guests, where they are received with full courtesy and service. When they come before the Sangha hall for a brief meal, they should be treated with an impartial mind.
When making offerings, even lay guests still provide attentive care; yet in the monastic community, one might endure neglecting to welcome them.

If one lacks a limited, narrow-minded heart, there will naturally be inexhaustible merit. When the Sangha is harmonious and those above and below are of one mind, they cover each other’s shortcomings for one another.
One must not allow the family’s internal flaws to be heard by outsiders. Although this causes no harm to the matter at hand, it ultimately diminishes the reputation of others.
Behold! It is like the worms within a lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh; this is not something that external paths or celestial Māras can rejoice in.

If you wish for the wind of the Way not to fall and the sun of the Buddha to remain ever bright, if you desire to augment the radiance of the ancestral realm and supplement the sagely transformation of the Imperial Court, I pray that you shall take these writings as a mirror of guidance.
In the ritual for sitting meditation, all Bodhisattvas who study Prajñā should first give rise to the mind of great compassion and make vast vows.
They should diligently cultivate samādhi and vow to deliver sentient beings, rather than seeking liberation for themselves alone. Only then should they set aside all external forms and rest.
In all matters, let body and mind be as one, with no interval between movement and stillness. Regulate your food and drink so that they are neither too much nor too little;
adjust your sleep so that it is neither excessive nor indulgent. When you wish to practice seated meditation (*dhyāna*), prepare a thick cushion in a quiet and secluded place.
Fasten your sash loosely to ensure your deportment is dignified and orderly. Then, sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), first placing your right foot upon your left thigh.
First, place the left foot upon the right thigh; alternatively, one may sit in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), provided that the left foot simply presses down upon the right foot.
Next, place the right hand upon the left hand, with the palms facing upward, and join the two thumbs so that their pads touch.
Slowly raise the body and stretch, then shake it from side to side, and finally straighten the torso.
Sit upright. Do not lean to the left or right, nor bend forward or arch backward. Let the vertebrae of the waist, spine, head, and neck support one another like a pagoda.
Furthermore, do not hold the body too erect, as this will cause the breath to become labored and uneasy.
Ensure that the ears are aligned with the shoulders and the nose with the navel. Press the tongue against the upper palate, keep the lips and teeth touching, and the eyes must be slightly open.

This prevents falling into drowsiness. If one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), its power is most supreme. In antiquity, there were eminent monks who practiced concentration and sat with their eyes always open.
Chan Master Fayun Yuantong also rebuked those who sat in meditation with their eyes closed, calling it "a ghost cave in the black mountains.
There is a profound meaning here that the enlightened understand. Once the physical posture is settled and the breath is regulated, then...
Relax the abdomen and belly. Do not deliberate upon any good or evil at all. When a thought arises, be immediately aware of it; once you are aware, it vanishes.
After a long time, forgetting external conditions, one naturally becomes a single whole. This is the essential technique for sitting meditation (*zazen*).

I venture to say that while *zazen* is a dharma-gate of peace and bliss, the reason many people fall ill [while practicing it] is that they do not skillfully apply their minds. If one can skillfully attain...

With this intention, the four great elements naturally become light and serene; the spirit becomes sharp and alert, right mindfulness becomes distinct, and the flavor of the Dharma nourishes the mind with tranquil and pure joy.
For those who have already attained realization, it may be said they are like a dragon finding water or a tiger rushing down a mountain.
For those who have not yet attained realization, it is as if adding fuel to a fire when the wind blows—the effort required is not much, provided one simply possesses the resolve.
The mind will certainly not deceive you. Nevertheless, when the Way is lofty, demonic obstacles abound; they manifest in myriad ways, both favorable and adverse.
However, if one can maintain right mindfulness, nothing that appears before them can obstruct or hinder.

As clearly explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Tiantai Zhi Guan*, and Guifeng’s *Xiuzheng Yi*, one must know these demonic affairs so as to be prepared for the unexpected. When wishing to emerge from meditative absorption, do so gradually.

Move the body and rise with composure; do not act with sudden violence. After emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), at all times constantly employ skillful means to protect and maintain the power of concentration, as one would protect an infant.
In this way, the power of concentration will easily be accomplished. Indeed, the gateway of *dhyāna-samādhi* is the most urgent of all tasks.
If one does not practice *dhyāna* and tranquil reflection (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), then upon reaching this point, one will inevitably be utterly bewildered. Therefore:

To seek pearls, one should remain still amidst the waves; if the water is stirred, it will be difficult to obtain them. When the waters of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are clear and still, the jewel of the mind manifests of its own accord.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Unobstructed and pure wisdom all arises based on meditative concentration. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Dwelling in a secluded place, cultivate and collect the mind, abiding peacefully and immovable like Mount Sumeru. From this, we know that to transcend the ordinary and surpass the sages, one must necessarily...
Regarding the conditions for feigned stillness: to achieve liberation while seated or to pass away while standing requires reliance on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If one fears failure even when striving for realization within a single lifetime, how much more so when time is protracted—how can one hope to withstand the force of karma? Therefore, the ancients said: "If you lack the power of concentration, you will meekly submit to the gate of death;

closing your eyes in vain, you return as if wandering in samsāra. I pray that all fellow practitioners of meditation will reflect upon these words three times, so that they may benefit themselves and others alike.
Attaining Perfect Enlightenment:

This self-admonition text illuminates the divine mind; its core principle is the sagely silence. Having now opened the three seals of speech, one should adhere to the four realities. These matters concern the sacred teachings.

Only when one’s principles accord with the refined texts can one truly assist the vehicle of the Teachings and glorify the Way of the Patriarchs; thus, the merit of benefiting others and oneself will not be bestowed in vain.

However, as for privately deliberating on the affairs of court, privately critiquing the officials of prefectures and counties, discussing the abundance or famine of the realm, debating the beauty or depravity of local customs, or even engaging in the minor details of commerce and industry, the idle chatter of the marketplace, or matters concerning the remote frontiers—[these are not the concern of the monk].

Regarding military affairs, bandits in the Central Plains, literature and arts, or food, clothing, and wealth—those who rely on their own strengths while concealing the good qualities of others, magnifying faults and pointing out minor flaws, thereby violating the accumulation of merit and failing to benefit the aspiration for the Way:
such idle talk harms true virtue, squanders offerings of faith, and brings shame before the dragons and devas. The sin begins with a mere trickle, yet its calamity ends in ruin.

To be extinguished at the crown of the head. Why? Because the fire of suffering for sentient beings burns from all four sides; how can one remain complacent and sit idly discussing what is meaningless?
One hundred and twenty questions: Do you revere the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? Do you seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? Have you resolved to awaken to Bodhicitta?
Have you entered the stage of Buddhahood? Are the sentiments of antiquity and the present exhausted? Do you dwell securely in non-retrogression?
Are you like a cliff standing ten thousand fathoms high? Is your observance of the precepts pure and clear?
Are your body and mind tranquil and still? Do you always delight in sitting meditation? Is there profound silence and clarity? Is one thought equal to ten thousand years?
Is there no movement toward objects? Is Prajñā manifest before you? Are the paths of speech cut off?
Has the sphere of mental activity ceased? Upon seeing form, do you see the mind? Upon hearing sound, do you see the nature?
Does Bodhidharma sit facing the wall? Does Longya hide his body? Are there a thousand hands and a thousand eyes?
Do the ancient Buddhas and the pillar commune with one another? Is the Ultimate Way not difficult? Does it resemble the earth upholding a mountain?

Is it like meeting Bodhidharma while lost? Are those within the hermitage unaware of what occurs outside the hermitage? Does the southern mountain give rise to clouds while the northern mountain pours down rain?
Is it the lion’s vigorous display? Is it the compassionate instruction? Is it the protection of the Dharma at the cost of one’s life?
Does the ancient teaching illuminate the mind? Is the spirit clarified through the three contemplations? Do you sport in samādhi? Do you manifest through the Universal Gate?
Have you profoundly exhausted the six characteristics? Do you penetrate and illuminate the ten mysteries?
Are you fused with the perfect cause of the six stages? Are you identical to the ocean of the fruit of the ten bodies? Have you realized that faith and the staff are not different?
After entering the stage, is one’s conduct as Samantabhadra complete? Are one’s deportments carefully regulated? Is one’s speech upright and deliberate? Do mind and speech correspond?
Does one refrain from praising oneself and disparaging others? Can one yield to others by withdrawing for oneself? Can one recognize the merits of others?
Does one refrain from speaking of others’ faults and transgressions? Does one refrain from posing malicious or difficult questions?
Do you refrain from frivolous laughter? Do you always delight in silence? Do you not deceive yourself in private?
Are you as steadfast among the multitude as a mountain? Do you always practice humility? Are you harmonious and free from contention?
Do you act with moderation in all affairs? Do you take pleasure in hearing virtuous words? And do you not resent straightforward criticism?
Are you able to endure suffering with equanimity? Are you able to endure insults and abuse? Are you able to subdue a joyful mind?
Do you refrain from socializing with worldly affairs? Are you free from laziness in your religious practice? Do you refrain from encroaching upon or damaging the communal property of the Sangha?
Do you refrain from misappropriating monastic assets? Do you refrain from hoarding gold, silver, or wealth? Do you refrain from storing books, paintings, or articles of luxury?
Does he not beg or borrow from others? Does he know whether he wears clothing without having spun the silk? Does he know whether he eats food without having plowed the fields?
Does he know whether he enjoys peace without having fought in battle? Is he content with what he receives and uses? Is he able to moderate his food and drink? Is he untiring in practicing giving?
Is he free from greed when receiving gifts? Does he possess no more than his robes and alms bowl?
Do you not preach the Dharma for the sake of profit? Do you not seek the love and respect of others? Are you not greedy for disciples? Do you not long for fame and reputation?
Do you not associate with kings and ministers? Do you not rely on power and influence? Do you not interfere in public affairs?
Are you cautious and fearful of the royal law? Do you not practice divination or physiognomy to determine good and ill fortune?
Do you not form intimate attachments [to women]? Do you not envy the worthy or the capable? Do you not resent the excellence of others? Do you not despise the poor or the lowly?
Do you guard the sense-faculties of others? Do you not cause affliction or harm to sentient beings?
Do you constantly practice the release of living creatures? Do you constantly keep in mind the protection of life? Do you honor the elderly and show compassion to the young?
Do you provide for the sick? Do you take pity on those in prison? Are you able to bestow kindness upon the hungry and cold?
Do you compassionately gather those who have been at war? Do you treat the Chinese and the barbarians as equals? Do you repay the grace of the sovereign and his ministers?

Do you answer the debt of gratitude to your parents for their procreation? Do you requite the instruction of your teachers and friends? Do you keep in mind the kindness of your patrons for their provisions?

Do you cherish your relatives and acquaintances (the kindness of their assistance)? Do you look after your attendants (the kindness of their diligent service)? Do you reflect upon the dragons and devas (the kindness of their protection)?

Do you recognize the merit of military officers (the kindness of their defense and protection)? Do you take pity on the various heavens (regarding their decline and affliction)? Do you feel compassion for the human realm (regarding its eight sufferings)? Do you grieve for the asuras (regarding their battles and strife)?
Do you lament for the realm of hungry ghosts (regarding their hidden sorrow)? Do you mourn for the animal realm (regarding their ignorance and darkness)?
Is there no sorrow in the hells? Are enemies and kin regarded with equality? Are all revered as Buddhas? Are all loved as parents?
Is there a vow to deliver all without exception? Is there inspection at the three times of day?
Is the work of a lifetime accomplished? Has mastery over the self been attained? Has Great Nirvana been realized?

Admonish the śrāmaṇeras before their tonsure: prepare five-strip robes (which properly correspond to the five-strip *kaṣāya*), lower garments, shirts, bowls, and sandals. First receive the five precepts;
next, receive the ten precepts. Under no circumstances must they wear seven-strip or nine-strip robes, nor use head-bowls for sitting or reclining.

When sharing a monastic bed with the great monks (bhikṣus), one should pay respects to them as prescribed by etiquette; one should identify oneself, saying, "I am a śrāmaṇera," and may freely trouble the great monks to return the salutation.
Having received the śrāmaṇera precepts, one must constantly maintain mindfulness and practice them. If one violates the śrāmaṇera precepts, one will not obtain the six classes of bhikṣu precepts.
One should always be diligent in worship and mindfulness, aspiring to seek the full ordination (mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara) and engage in recitation and study.
The *Śrāmaṇera-śīla-sūtra*:

Form for Recording the Application. A novice of such-and-such monastery, surnamed [Name], aged [Number] years, originally from [Village/Town] in [District] of [Prefecture], or a resident of the city center.
Arrived at this monastery on the [Day] of the [Month] in the [Year].
Having left the household life (if one has parents, state that they have sent [the candidate] to leave the household life), I pay homage to the presiding monk, [Name], as my teacher.

I have now purchased at [Location] a blank ordination certificate (if purchased from a guest, state "purchased from guest [Name]") under the name of [Name]. I wish to request that you fill it out so that I may become a monk;
there are no obstacles whatsoever. Please submit this formal petition, etc. Dated [Year, Month, Day], signed by [Name/Position].
A Memorial by [Name]:
On the Re-engraving and Supplementing of the *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Eight;
and the Re-engraving and Supplementing of the *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Nine.
The Text for the Ordination of a Śrāmaṇera:

When the practitioner first requests the *duò* (ordination certificate), he presents it in a lined box to his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), as well as to the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) and the heads of the community.

He performs three prostrations of gratitude to each. On an auspicious day, he undergoes tonsure. The *karmadāna* shall request one person to serve as the ordination preceptor (*karmācārya*) and lead the request for the *śrāmaṇera-śīla*. The *ācārya* is then invited.
One person serves as the *upādhyāya* (preceptor), and one person serves as the *ācārya* (instructor). The night before, they shave the head, leaving only about one square inch at the crown.
On the appointed day, they are arranged in the Sangha hall or the Dharma hall; a high seat for the Preceptor of the Precepts (*śīlācārya*) is established, with felt mats spread before it.

Upon the incense altar are placed a hand-incense burner, a pure water pitcher, the text of the precepts, and two boundary lines. Furthermore, a seat is set up opposite the Preceptor for the candidate.

The seat for the Brahma Ācārya shall be provided with one *kṣaṅ* (gong). If this is in the Dharma Hall, then separately arrange two small tables for offerings of sacred images, incense, and flowers, along with two double-layered chests:
one to hold the *kāṣāya* (robe) and one to hold the lower garment (*śāṭaka*) and upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
These are placed in front of the Holy Monk or the sacred image. On the floor below the hall, prepare mats for prostration. One person shall be appointed to manage the assembly (if using...).

The ritual for welcoming and leading proceeds from the Hall for Junior Practitioners to the Hall of the Local Deity and then to the Great Hall; thereafter, one enters the Sangha Hall to have the head shaved (the practitioners bow three times at each location).
Once the practitioners have finished shaving their heads, they wait before the Sangha Hall until the assembly has gathered.

After the Preceptor and the two *Ācāryas* have performed three full prostrations before the sacred image, the Preceptor chants the *brahman* verses while the *Ācāryas* take their seats, and the ritual proceedings begin.
The Inviting Preceptor (before the Preceptor of the Precepts, spreads his sitting mat fully, performs three prostrations, kneels with the right knee on the ground, and joins his palms).
The Preceptor of the Precepts asks; the Inviting Preceptor answers.

"Is the Saṃgha assembled? (It is assembled. "Is it in concord? (It is in concord. "What shall the Saṃgha, being now in concord, do? (Shall we shave the head and confer the precepts upon the attendant of this monastery, so-and-so? "So be it."
The Preceptor who Leads the Invitation (having gathered up his sitting mat and risen, leads the practitioner into the hall).

The Practitioner (performs three prostrations before the Holy Sangha—bowing upon hearing the sound of the chime and rising when the chime sounds again—and then performs three prostrations before the Preceptor of the Precepts, kneeling with palms joined).
The Inviting Ācārya (also spreads the sitting mat, kneels with the right knee on the ground, and joins the palms).
The Brahmā-Ācārya (performs the *Upali-brahman*; if unable to do so, performs the "How is it? brahman): "How shall one reach the ultimate further shore in this sutra?

We pray that the Buddha will reveal the subtle and secret [teachings] (incanting over the incense) and explain them extensively for the sake of sentient beings—for those who have shaved their heads and received the precepts."
The Preceptor says:

"Upon hearing the Brahma-voice, he holds the incense burner and proceeds to the most secret place to recite mantras over the incense, which together with the manifest text of the precepts, perfumes [the assembly] as follows: the fragrance of morality, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, and the fragrance of liberation."

The fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation: clouds of radiant light pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Making offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, the infinite Dharmas of the ten directions, and the infinite Sanghas of the ten directions—those who see, hear, or are universally perfumed by this shall realize nirvana. So it is for all sentient beings as well.

The Preceptor (repeating the Sanskrit at the end) speaks thus for those receiving the precepts after having their heads shaved. This marks the commencement of the head-shaving ceremony this very morning.
By the merit of receiving the precepts, may the Emperor live for ten thousand years; may his ministers govern for a thousand autumns; may the world enjoy peace and the Wheel of Dharma turn eternally.
May the dragons, devas, and local deities increase in majestic radiance; may they protect the Dharma and its practitioners, so that no calamities or difficulties arise.

May the donors from the ten directions be adorned with blessings and long life; may all those gathered at this site of practice have peace and joy in body and mind; and may the spiritual endeavors of teachers and parents flourish.
Exceedingly sublime! May the shramanera who has shaved his head practice without hindrance; may all those in the three evil realms and eight difficulties be liberated from the wheel of suffering;

and may all beings within the nine abodes and four modes of birth ascend together to the shore of enlightenment. We look up to and rely upon the venerable assembly to recite the Dharma-body of purity (and so forth, until) Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

Requesting the Preceptor (holding the incense burner, say: "The words for requesting the Master should be recited by you yourself. If you are unable, follow my voice. At the point [某甲處], state the name). "Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, [Name], now request the Virtuous One to act as my preceptor for shaving the head and receiving the precepts.

Because of the Virtuous One, I shall obtain the shaving of the head and the receiving of the precepts. Out of compassion, [please grant this]. (Recite three times; at the third repetition, say "Out of compassion" three times.)

The practitioner (performs three minor prostrations for each of the first, second, and third [sections], followed by three major prostrations; then kneels with the right knee on the ground and joins the palms).

"Good son" (each time he is addressed as "good son," the practitioner should respond with an assent). The source of the mind is limpid and tranquil; the ocean of Dharma is profound and deep. Those who are deluded therein will sink and wallow for eternal kalpas; those who awaken to it are liberated in that very place.
If you wish to devote yourself exclusively to the wondrous Way, there is nothing that surpasses the liberation and expansiveness of leaving the household life.
It is like the purity of empty space, resembling the bright moon. When the conditions for practice are complete, the fruit of the Way is not far off.

Beginning with the merit of moment-to-moment mindfulness, one ultimately realizes the stage of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One renounced the precious throne of the Golden Wheel;
at the hour of midnight, he leaped over the city walls; he cast off his precious dragon-robe and cut his hair on the green mountains, allowing the magpies' nest to remain.
Atop his head, he hangs a spider’s web between his brows; by cultivating cessation, he clarifies the eternal truth, and by severing worldly toil, he achieves perfect enlightenment.
The Buddhas of the three periods have never said that one can attain the Way while remaining a householder. Among the patriarchs of the six generations, who ever practiced defilement to save others?

Therefore, from Buddha to Buddha the hand is extended, and from patriarch to patriarch the lineage is transmitted: only by remaining unstained by worldly conditions does one become a vessel for the Dharma.
Consequently, the celestial Māra folded his hands in submission and the heterodox practitioners turned their hearts toward the Way. Above, he repaid the fourfold debt of gratitude;

below, he rescued sentient beings from their suffering. Thus it is said: "While wandering through the three realms, one cannot abandon the bonds of affection; by casting aside such affection, one enters the state of non-action."
"To truly repay their kindness, after one has left the household life, one’s conduct transcends ordinary sentiment: one does not bow to kings, nor does one bow to one's parents.

You should now leave this seat, set aside thoughts of the king’s grace in providing the land and water, and the parents’ virtue in giving you birth and upbringing, and with single-minded devotion, perform a formal farewell prostration; thereafter, you shall not bow."
The Preceptor who Leads the Invitation (having gathered up his sitting mat and risen; leading the practitioner out of the hall while both exchange greetings):

The practitioner (bows in farewell to the King and parents beneath the hall; having discarded their secular clothing and donned the lower robe and shirt, the Preceptor who Leads the Invitation leads them before the sacred image to perform three prostrations, then performs one prostration at the foot of the Preceptor’s seat, and approaches to kneel with palms joined).
The Preceptor (recites the verse, holds the flask of water to pour over the head, and shaves the hair; the attending monks recite along with him).
"Excellent, O Great Man! Able to realize the impermanence of the world, You have abandoned the secular life to seek the Nirvāṇa— Rare indeed, and inconceivable!
(Recited three times. The Śrāmaṇera withdraws and performs three prostrations.)
The Preceptor (the officiant) invites [the candidate] (the officiant prostrates once before the seat of the Root Teacher, then approaches, kneels with palms joined).
The Root Teacher holds the razor and says: "This final knot is called the *cūḍā*. Only a Buddha alone is able to sever it.
I shall now remove the hair from your crown for you; do you consent? He replies, "So be it. The Root Teacher says:
Look up to the great assembly and recite the verse for shaving the hair in unison:
Destroying the form to preserve the will and integrity, Severing attachment to bid farewell to kin, Leaving home to propagate the Holy Way, I vow to deliver all sentient beings.
(Recite three times. Withdraw and perform one prostration. Return to the master’s presence, kneeling with palms joined.)
The Master, holding the *kāṣāya*, recited this verse:
"How great is this robe of liberation! The field of merit, free from marks; Clad in it, I uphold the Tathāgata’s precepts To widely deliver all sentient beings."

Once the śrāmaṇera has finished donning the kāṣāya (he performs three prostrations to his preceptor, three prostrations to the sacred image, and three prostrations to the preceptor of the precepts; then he kneels with palms joined).
The Preceptor who invites [the candidate] (also spreads his sitting mat, kneels with the right knee on the ground, and joins his palms):

"Virtuous son, the Dharma is like a great ocean; one enters it gradually and becomes increasingly deep. Since you have left the household life, you must first receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts before you may attend upon the Great Sangha.
Next, you shall receive the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera, whereupon you may share in the benefits and offerings of the Sangha."

The matter lies in single-minded sincerity; one should not be negligent or casual. I now invoke the Triple Gem on your behalf to bear witness to this Buddhist rite (extending through the Ten Precepts).

I reverently entreat the boundless ocean-treasury of the Buddha-jewels and the golden texts: may those in the ten stages, the three levels of worthiness, the five fruits, and the four directions of progress alike descend in response to my invocation and together act as witnesses. (Recite this three times.)
"Noble son, those who wish to seek refuge and receive the precepts must first repent and cleanse their transgressions and flaws. It is like a person who washes their clothes before applying dye.
Now, with utmost sincerity, follow me in repentance."
All the various evil karmas I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion,
Produced by body, speech, and mind— I now repent for them all. Good son,
since you have thus purified the karma of body, speech, and mind, you should next take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
I take refuge in the Buddha. I take refuge in the Dharma. I take refuge in the Saṅgha. I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings.

I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One free from desire. I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among assemblies. The taking of refuge in the Buddha is complete. The taking of refuge in the Dharma is complete.
The taking of refuge in the Saṅgha is complete.
The Tathāgata, the Most Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One, is my teacher on the Path. I now take refuge in him;

from this day forward, I acknowledge the Buddha as my teacher and shall no longer take refuge in demons, heretics, or outsiders. Out of compassion (recite three times; for the third repetition, recite "out of compassion" three times).

The Śrāmaṇera (performing one small prostration for each of the first, second, and third [precepts], followed by one great prostration of three bows, kneeling with palms joined): "O son of good family,
since you have abandoned the heterodox and returned to the orthodox, and your precepts are now complete, if you wish to recognize their characteristics and maintain them,
you should receive the five precepts."
For as long as life lasts, one shall observe the precepts of abstaining from killing and abstaining from stealing.
Abstaining from sexual misconduct,
abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from intoxicants.
"These are the characteristics of the five precepts. Are you able to uphold them? (He answers: "I am able to uphold them.
"Regarding the above five branches of pure precepts, not one may be transgressed. Are you able to uphold them? (He answers: "I am able to uphold them. (Three questions and three answers.
"In this manner, you shall uphold these matters."
The Śrāmaṇera (performs three prostrations according to the Great Rite; kneels with the right knee on the ground and joins his palms).
"Good son, the five precepts are the primary cause for entering the Dharma and the foremost means of escaping the three miserable realms. Next, you shall receive the ten śrāmaṇera precepts;

thus your physical form will be fully equipped with the ritual deportment of the Dharma. This is called the 'Diligent Encourager' (śikṣamāṇa). You shall dwell in reliance upon a teacher and receive benefits equal to those of the Saṃgha."
This is what a śrāmaṇera who accords with the Dharma should receive upon the crown of his head:
for as long as life lasts,
he shall refrain from taking life, and shall not wear flowered hair-knots, necklaces, or apply fragrant oils to his body.
One does not steal; one does not go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or musical performances;
one is free from sexual misconduct; one does not sit or lie on high, wide, or large beds;
one does not speak falsehoods; and one does not eat at improper times.
Not drinking alcohol, and not handling gold, silver, money, or treasures—these ten items above are the precepts of a śrāmaṇera. Are you able to uphold them? (He replies: "I am able to uphold them."

Regarding the ten branches of pure precepts mentioned above, not one may be transgressed. Are you able to uphold them? (He answers: "I am able to uphold them. (The question and answer are repeated three times.
Thus shall this matter be upheld.
The śrāmaṇera (performs three prostrations with the Great Rite; kneeling on the right knee with palms joined):
"O son of good family, after you have now received the precepts, you must receive them upon the crown of your head and uphold them. You must not violate the precepts you have undertaken.
Make offerings to the Triple Gem and diligently cultivate fields of merit. Toward your upādhyāya and ācārya, act exactly as prescribed by the Dharma."
As for the teachings: one should always maintain a mind of reverence toward superiors, equals, and inferiors. Practice the Way with diligent application to repay the kindness of one's parents.

As for clothing, take plain cloth rather than dyed or patterned fabrics; as for food, take what sustains life rather than indulging in flavors. Let flowers, perfumes, ointments, and powders not come near the body.
Regarding pleasant sounds and seductive sights, do not look or listen to them at all. Speak slowly and maintain rectitude; do not proclaim the faults of others. Should there be...

To resolve disputes is to harmonize two opposing views. There is distinction between men and women; there is no injury to grasses or trees. One does not befriend those who are not virtuous, nor does one revere those who are not sages.
Dharma-robes and alms-bowls are always kept at hand. One does not eat at improper times, nor speak what is not in accordance with the Dharma.

Diligently applying oneself to contemplate the meaning, one reviews the old to know the new. When seated, one practices meditative contemplation; when rising, one recites the scriptures. Thus, one closes the gates to the three evil realms and opens the way to Nirvana.
Entering the gates of the Dharma, one increases right action within the discipline of a bhikṣu; the bodhicitta does not regress, and the wisdom of prajñā remains perpetually luminous.
Universally delivering all sentient beings with the aspiration to achieve perfect enlightenment—one whose mind functions in this way is a true disciple of the Buddha.
Regarding the *brahmācārya* (the term *brahma* refers to a divine being or immortal): an immortal is one who possesses the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

As for the practitioner of incantations (*mantra*), for the sake of those who possess shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*), and to restrain those who lack them, the Tathāgata established the prohibitions and precepts (*śīla*). He proclaimed them fortnightly.
Having explained the benefits of the precepts, I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas.

The Preceptor (holding the incense burner while reciting the *Brahma-voice* [mantra] until its conclusion, performs the dedication as follows): "The foregoing tonsure and reception of the precepts are first dedicated to the Abbot, that he may forever serve as a bridge across the sea of suffering;
to the eminent officials and administrators, that they may eternally act as the pillars and beams of the Dharma-gate;

to the pure assembly of the entire hall, that they may together board the vessel of Prajñā; and for the novice monk who has had his head shaved, that he may swiftly reach the shore of Bodhi. To the Four Debts of Gratitude..."
As a collective recompense, may all beings throughout the three realms of existence be equally sustained; may all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm together perfect the wisdom of all modes.

For these aforementioned causes and conditions, I take refuge in and contemplate all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as all Honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and the Great Prajñāpāramitā.

The Abbot, acting as the *ācārya*, strikes the chime and says: Dwelling in the world like empty space, Like a lotus flower unsullied by water, With a mind pure and transcending that, I prostrate in homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
By taking refuge in the Buddha, one’s bodhicitta for attaining the path of enlightenment shall never regress.
By taking refuge in the Dharma, one attains the great gate of *dhāraṇī*.
By taking refuge in the Saṅgha, one quiets disputes and enters together into the ocean of harmony.
The merit from the aforementioned tonsure and reception of the precepts constitutes an infinite, most excellent, and virtuous cause that radiates throughout the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*.
I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones. [At this point, the officiating master (*ācārya*) hears the call, gathers his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), rises, and directs the śrāmaṇera to prostrate.]

The śrāmaṇera (performs three prostrations to the Preceptor of the Great Rite; next, three prostrations to the Holy Sangha; having inquired after their well-being, he exits and stands outside the hall).
The Preceptor and two Ācāryas perform three full prostrations before the Holy Sangha and exit to stand outside the hall.

Three strikes of the small bell are sounded in front of the Sanghārāma, and the assembly descends from the hall. Each member, maintaining their dignified deportment, performs a celebratory greeting in the Dharma Hall.
The Abbot (having shaved the head in the Dharma Hall, immediately performs a prostration of greeting within the [Kui] Hall).

The Preceptor and the two Ācāryas (perform one *zhanyun*: "We have been appointed to administer the precepts and dare not decline; our conduct has been negligent and we have long detained the Venerable One. We are overcome with the utmost trepidation. They perform another *zhanyun* to exchange greetings, saying:

"We humbly pray that the Master’s health and daily life are blessed with myriad blessings. They then perform three prostrations with touching the ground). The Abbot (says: "The novice's shaving of the head has troubled you in your noble practice. I shall permit him to go to his quarters to present [the offerings].")

[The recipient] bows in thanks). The administrative official offers congratulations (performing one *zenshin*, saying: "It is a great fortune for the Dharma-gate that you have donned the black robes with supernormal powers. My humble feelings are filled with boundless joy. [Another *zenshin* to express the warmth of the season]. Then, he performs three prostrations).

The Abbot (says): "The novice has undergone tonsure; we have troubled you with this matter, Master Jue. Please permit him to go to your quarters to express his gratitude. The assembly performs the rites of congratulation (the wording for the master is the same as for the administrative officers).

The Abbot (says): "This novice has received the precepts; we have troubled you with this matter, Master [Name], to serve as witness. Please permit him to go to your quarters to express his gratitude. The attendants and junior disciples perform the rites of congratulation (performing three full prostrations, saying:

"The novice has attained ordination; the entire assembly shares in this joy. Looking up to your venerable kindness, our delight is all the more profound. [They perform another three prostrations]. They then exchange greetings regarding the weather and perform three more prostrations). The administrative officers and the assembly return to their respective quarters and each prepares...
The incense and lamps were arranged in rows for the attendants. At that time, as soon as the assembly had withdrawn, the *śrāmaṇera* performed three prostrations, saying:

"I have received the full tonsure; by good fortune, I am now draped in the field-cloth (*kāṣāya*). Thus I have escaped the prison of the mundane world and forever cast off the net of craving. My humble feelings are filled with boundless gratitude. (Three prostrations. He then exchanged greetings and again performed three prostrations. The Abbot circled the quarters and then paid respects to the administrators (*karmadāna*), the heads of departments (*śreṣṭhin*), the precept masters (*śikṣācārya*), the *ācāryas*, and all fellow practitioners (*dharmabandhu*).

**Words of Thanks for the Great Precepts:** "On the occasion of the Ten-Thousand-Year Anniversary of the Heavenly Peace (*Tianning*) Festival, this frost-chamber was specially opened. Having completed the threefold *karmavācanā*, I have already ascended to the rank of the Precepts. This is because..."

A certain person has long since received the Buddha’s prediction, vowing to deliver the deluded masses; with nothing more than a heart bound by grass, they seek to respond upward to the gift of the life-preserving float, while reflecting downward upon their boundless sense of gratitude.

Regarding the instruction of novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*): when a novice first arrives to enter the monastery, the preceptor must thoroughly investigate his origins. Only if he possesses the right causal conditions may he be admitted.
If his intention is merely to seek food and clothing, to evade corvée labor, to flee from some matter, or if his parents do not permit it, he shall not be accepted.
In all cases, they must not be retained. ○ Form for Submitting a Petition to the Monastery:

A novice boy of such-and-such a surname and such-and-such a name, aged so many years, originally from such-and-such a prefecture, such-and-such a county, such-and-such a district, and such-and-such a village (or a resident of the city). He has no tattoos on his body, no criminal record, and is free from all other disqualifications.
Now, because the matter of birth and death is of great importance, he has long admired the Empty Gate (the Buddhist path). Having received permission from his father...
The mother has graciously consented to allow [him/her] to enter this monastery to become a novice (if there are no parents, state: "I now wish to enter this monastery to become a novice").
I humbly entreat the Abbot, out of compassion, to grant acceptance. This formal petition is respectfully submitted. Dated [Month, Day, Year], signed by [Name of Petitioner].
[If there are parents, their names shall be written on the petition. The incumbent abbot signs the petition and hands it to the administrative officer (zhishi).
Once the newly arrived novice (tongxing) has finished paying respects at the administrative office (kusī), he shall take his luggage to the Novice Hall.
After paying respects to the Hall Master (tángzhǔ), the Hall Master will assign him a place to stay and point out his sleeping quarters.

At the evening assembly, when the assembly of practitioners has taken their positions in the hall, the Hall Master shall have the newly arrived novice perform three or six prostrations to the Preceptor (cāntóu) and those below him; the Preceptor shall not return the prostration.
Circumambulate the hall once and stand at the lower position. The current regulations are detailed below. Now, the Way does not operate in isolation; it is brought forth by people.
If one wishes to establish a pure monastic community (*ārāma*), one must not neglect even the smallest of practices.

This is especially true for those who have already entered the monastic order upon the ground covered with gold within this field where Buddhas are selected. You should feel profound joy and gratitude. Therefore, the instructions provided here briefly outline three chapters.
If one properly relies on the practice, one becomes a true son of the Buddha, foremost in establishing one's person.
A lay follower (*upāsaka*) who attends upon the great monks (*bhikṣu*) should observe the five precepts. First, do not kill living beings (one must not kill any creature that possesses life).
2. Do not steal (taking what is not given constitutes theft). 3. Do not engage in sexual misconduct (remain far removed from lust as one would avoid a pit of fire). 4.

Do not speak falsely (for those who have left the household life, sincerity and faith are the foundation). 5. Do not drink alcohol or eat meat (one may sacrifice body and life, but must never violate this precept).

Except for rice gruel during the fast, one must not consume miscellaneous foods (this includes fruits, vegetables, drinks, cakes, and cooked rice; none of these should be eaten). Unless on a regular assignment, one must not go outside the gate. Not...
For matters of great importance, one must not request leave. Furthermore, those who practice *zazen* and seek the Way must restrain body and mind;
they must not allow them to become distracted. Those who recite sutras and seek deliverance must study their scriptural duties; they must not be indolent.

Moreover, one should constantly bear in mind that through cultivation one repays the grace of the sovereign and ministers for their support, the grace of donors for their provisions, the grace of parents for their upbringing, and the grace of the teacher...
One should long cherish the kindness of their teachers. Furthermore, one should constantly contemplate that parents who have passed away may fearfully enter the evil realms;
thus, one ought to rescue and deliver them through spiritual practice. As for parents who are still living, one should exhort them to take refuge in the Triple Gem and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

Moreover, when wearing clothes or eating food, one should always be mindful of their source. If one does not engage in practice, by what means can one repay such kindness? Furthermore, the practitioner—above...
The *zhiduò* (straight-cut robe) is the standard formal attire; all other secular garments are not the robes of one who has left the household life.
Shoes must be white and may not be purple or black. One must wear a waistband and should not use a head-wrap or arm-strap. Furthermore, clothing must always be clean and well-arranged;

the hem of the *zhiduò* must not expose the cuffs of the trousers underneath. In both winter and summer, the hems should be hemmed and bound. Additionally, it is permitted to wear leggings for walking.
When attending tea or soup services, one must wear shoes and socks. While walking, one’s hands must be held in a composed manner; while sitting, the body must be upright.

One must not lean against anything, nor swing one’s arms, nor walk arm-in-arm with others. Furthermore, when encountering fellow monks in various places, one should compose the body, yield the path, and inquire after them so they may pass.
When meeting officials or donors traveling together, one should first inquire after the members of the monastic community, and then...

One should merely perform a slight bow (*pratyutthāna*) toward officials and donors. Having left the household life to uphold the precepts and wearing the *kāṣāya* and *zhiduo* robes, one must never kneel or prostrate before laypeople.
Even upon seeing one’s parents, one may only perform a slight bow.

Furthermore, with impure hands, one must not grasp sutra scrolls or handle items intended for ritual purity (such as incense burners, flower vases, or vessels used by the Sangha for food and drink). Also, during the two meal times of gruel and rice...
Each person shall recite the Heart Sūtra three times. This is to repay the benefactors of the ten directions who provide for the monks’ labor and the loss of life [of animals] as they walk;

even for insects and small creatures, one must maintain a focused mind while receiving food and must not engage in conversation. Every evening, during the assembly, one shall prostrate before the Buddha in the Buddha Hall;
all must chant and prostrate with single-minded devotion, ensuring that the mind does not dwell on other matters while the mouth joins in the chanting and sounds, as is customary.
When the work period has ended, those practicing meditation should sit in seclusion, and those reciting scriptures should go to their desks to study.

You must not gather together to joke or laugh, nor speak words that are contrary to the Dharma. If you engage in mutual abuse, fighting, or various forms of contention, these are strictly unbecoming of those who have left the household life;
you must strictly observe these prohibitions. After the evening assembly, if there is no business, you must not pass through the hall or walk side-by-side.

In the abbot’s quarters, the storehouse, the lower hall, the practitioners' quarters, the work areas, and even in secluded places, those who engage in idle chatter must be mutually monitored by the wise.
Anyone serving as a practitioner must maintain a solitary and pure character and conduct their affairs with clarity.
One must not involve oneself in matters of suspicion that would defile the assembly of the pure.
Section Two: Attending the Assembly. Having already left the household life to join the pure assembly, one should constantly maintain a mind of gentleness, flexibility, and virtuous compliance;

one must not harbor arrogance or pride. Those senior in age are to be regarded as elder brothers, and those junior as younger brothers. Speak slowly and with rectitude, and do not proclaim the shortcomings of others.
Should there be those who dispute, let them reconcile with one another; simply direct toward each other a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and do not use harsh words to wound others.
If you bully your peers or spread rumors to incite strife, such monastic life is entirely without benefit.
You must not misappropriate the property of others, nor may you move the robes or bedding belonging to another. Furthermore, you must not stand upon a bed.
When putting on robes, one must not turn one’s back toward the Noble Sangha while ascending the platform. When lifting the door curtain, one should always keep the trailing edge behind.

One must not make clattering or knocking sounds. Within the hall, one must not expose the head or wear one's upper garment open. This applies from after the striking of the signal for silence until before the opening of the signal for the end of meditation.
Except for matters concerning the permanent residents, one must not converse within the hall or near the quarters of the novices.
Within the hall, one must not write upon, deface, or damage the walls. One must not hang scrolls, paintings, or maps, nor post miscellaneous writings or notices.
A scripture desk may not be placed at the head of the bed. Pillows or screens may not be set at the head of the bed. Old clothing or shoes [must not be left there].
Place your socks beneath the bed. Keep your robes, bedding, pillows, and covers always neat and orderly. Within the hall, one must never speak loudly or engage in chatter that disturbs the assembly.
One must always tread lightly with feet tucked back. Unless it is one’s own bedding, one must not sit or lie down there to engage in idle conversation.

The head of the assembly (sanchou) and the hall master (tangzhu) must constantly and earnestly oversee this; they should also request their neighbors to reprimand and restrain those who fail to comply.
Cease. One must not stir the fire or tap the fire tongs to make a sound within the brazier. One must not sit for too long in the brazier, as it obstructs others.
When the board is struck for tea or soup, one must attend together with the assembly. The sutra hall and quarters must be tidied and kept clean.
One must not speak. Within the bathhouse, one must not remain naked nor engage in loud speech or laughter.
One must not stand upon the bed while putting on clothes, nor stand upon the bed while combing one's hair. The Hall Master shall constantly maintain silence and ensure tranquility.

When the practitioners hear the signal for the end of silence (*kaijō*), they shall rise immediately and must not indulge in sleep. If offerings of money or goods are bestowed, [they shall be accepted according to the rules].
One must not conceal anything; one should report it and receive one share from the communal distribution.

Third, regarding manual labor: upon hearing the signal for general work (*pǔqǐng*), one must ensure that everyone arrives early and in unison. At the work station, one must not engage in conversation;
for fear that saliva might fall into the food of the Sangha, the resulting offense would be no small matter. At the site of general work, one must not raise one's voice.
One must not speak, much less engage in clamor, shouting, or laughter; one should always remain silent to inspire wholesome thoughts in the laity.

When wishing to perform a service, one should first roll up one’s sleeves and wash one’s hands until they are clean. One must not converse in front of the Sangha hall, nor lean against it or stand slouching.

One must not drop one's hands or release things carelessly in a discourteous manner. One must not make noise while performing household chores. When entering the monks' quarters, [one should proceed with decorum].

One must not walk with haste or large strides; one should proceed with composure. When serving the food, one must observe how much each member of the monastic community requires and adjust accordingly at the time.
One must not carry the salt or vinegar buckets by hanging them from the hands. If one happens to sneeze or cough while serving, one should turn one's back.
If one is carrying a bucket, one should hold the spare hand against the chest; one must not [hold it otherwise].

With arms hanging down, those who serve meals in the Hall, the Abbot’s quarters, the storehouse, and the various monastic lodgings must always exercise the utmost care and frugality in protecting and cherishing the property of the Sangha, regarding these communal affairs as they would their own eyes.
They must support them with all their heart, ensuring that the Abbot, the administrators, and the assembly of monks do not have cause for concern.
When it is their turn to perform communal labor, they should each return to their assigned meal-serving locations at the designated time.

Regarding the sequence of duties in the kitchen: each practitioner should exhaust their own skills to manage the affairs of the Sangha. One must always ensure that food, drink, and kitchen matters—such as those concerning the stoves—are prepared in advance and coordinated;
one must not engage in disputes or contention at the last moment. Each should serve the community with a mind of the Way and not shrink from diligent toil.
Although there may be slight hardship now, great benefit will be obtained later. The practitioners of the various halls shall take charge of sweeping and cleaning.
Offer pure and fragrant flowers with meticulous attention to orderliness. Should a wind arise, lamps must not be lit within the various halls.

At the conclusion of each day’s offerings, one should perform prostrations and make this vow: "May the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, the local deities, dragons, devas, and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm together realize the wisdom of the seeds.
The bell-ringer must not miss the appointed time, and the grounds must always be kept swept and clean.
At all times during the *zhāi* (fasting/observance), burn incense and prostrate yourself, vowing that upon hearing the sound of the bell, all may attain liberation.

The gatekeepers and attendants shall inspect the monks as they enter and leave their quarters; those who wander the streets without cause or who frequently request leave to come and go must be strictly monitored at all times.
Be cautious with fire and candles, especially at the hearth; always know when to be diligent and when to relax. Do not conflict with those who serve in their assigned order.
The head of the kitchen, the storehouse attendant, and the tea master must constantly supervise the fire and candles, as well as inspect the tea and hot water.
The garden overseer (yuántóu xíngzhě) shall always be diligent and work with a unified mind to provide for the assembly; he must not be indolent or refuse his duties.

Furthermore, all tasks performed by the various attendants (xíngzhě) shall be delegated by the garden overseer; they must not allow affairs to go astray. The responsibilities entrusted to the various estate attendants are no light matter:
first, they must be upright and incorruptible, never encroaching upon the communal property (chángzhù); second, they must manage affairs to completion.
First, one should serve the authorities. Third, one should skillfully harmonize the laborers and the master of the estate, maintaining peace and preventing strife.
Fourth, one should know the proper time for plowing and sowing, ensuring that all tasks are performed appropriately.

Fifth, one should care for the draft animals with a compassionate heart so they do not become emaciated, and ensure that those who drive the oxen do not strike them indiscriminately. Sixth, one should provide protection.

The seventh [precept] is that the precepts restrain the practitioner from committing improper or transgressive acts; they guard the monastery’s guests so that they do not steal the permanent assets of the Sangha, such as money and grain.
The eighth is to be diligent and constantly visit the various fields to supervise the boundaries and all types of crops.
The ninth is that those who do not provide for the Three Jewels with devotion are merely laboring without purpose. The tenth is that the practitioners at the head of the assembly must always...
The head attendant shall ensure that the livestock are well-fed and that no *hu* or *dou* measures of fodder are lacking.
At the place where they stay overnight, he must guard the fodder and watch over their conduct. They must not drink alcohol, eat meat, or engage in any improper or unlawful acts.

The *can-tou* (head of the assembly) and the *tang-zhu* (hall master) must always act with public-mindedness; they must lead the multitude without harboring private interests. If the members commit any transgression, they must be duly reported.

On major matters, they shall oversee the affairs of the *zhuchi* (abbot) and his attendants; on minor matters, they shall report to the *dianzuo* (head cook), who shall impose fines to be distributed among the assembly.
If the practitioners are assigned by the head of the group (*candou*), they must not disobey or allow even the slightest delay.

The aforementioned rules and regulations are all the minute details of monastic conduct. If one can implement them thoroughly and in detail, they will serve as the very foundation for attaining liberation (*dīkṣā*).
When the time comes that you receive the tonsure, the models of the eminent monks will all be fully realized before you.
By using these methods to instruct beginners, you will naturally cause the Dharma to endure for a long time. If you knowingly violate them, or having violated them...
I repent. Not only have I failed the Fourfold Debt of Gratitude and received the offerings of the faithful in vain, but I am unacceptable to the dragons, devas, and local deities.

As for the karmic fruits of the three miserable realms, where could I possibly escape them? Since you belong to the ranks of those who have left the household life, you must naturally distinguish between cause and effect.
If you do not obscure the true cause during your daily practice, you will certainly possess the potential to attain Buddhahood.
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Nine;
Re-engraved and Annotated *Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Ten:
Exhorting Donors.

A lay bodhisattva should first serve the Buddha with the utmost diligence and solemnity. They must forever renounce pungent foods and alcohol, firmly uphold the precepts of the fast, and vow never to transgress against the defilements of sensual desire.
They should associate with spiritual friends to clarify their own insight and practice according to the Dharma as they enter into realization.
For those who are beginners and are unable to immediately eliminate pungent foods and alcohol, they should at least eat vegetarian food during the morning hours. First.

Within a month, one will already be able to reduce it by half. Through long-term practice and mastery, one can naturally and permanently sever the long fast, as well as those for whom the obstacles of desire are thick.
Such persons should first observe the five precepts, and thereafter advance to the pure, great bodhisattva precepts.

If one is unable to draw near to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one should simply read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras to assist in the development of right view. If one has not yet realized the *mudrā*...
Regarding those who disparage the Prajñāpāramitā: they should simply practice in accordance with the Buddha’s words, never wasting even a moment of time.
A bodhisattva studying the Prajñāpāramitā should diligently make this vow: "Namo Buddha. Namo Dharma. Namo Saṃgha. May my body and mind be peaceful and happy;
may I advance along the Path without demonic interference. Within every thought-moment amidst the light of Prajñā, may I always awaken through Prajñā."
For all sentient beings: I universally pray that all sentient beings may suddenly awaken to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā and together achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Ritual for Feeding the Sangha:

The method for feeding the Sangha takes reverence as its fundamental principle. One should simply extend the invitation according to the monastic order and must not arbitrarily give rise to feelings of partiality or discrimination.

For ordinary people with the physical eye, who can distinguish between the holy and the wise? To mistakenly give rise to a mind of contempt will surely invite meager merit. Should one happen to encounter [a holy person] in person...
The Brahma-realm has been prepared for the vegetarian feast; this person will surely receive a natural retribution in future lives.
Nevertheless, the principle of the pure field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) requires single-mindedness; it is not appropriate to invite many guests and thereby confuse the primary cause.

If one brings along relatives and friends to share in the joy of this superior occasion, they may only partake of food and drink equally with the assembly, each following the group; they must not be permitted to dwell [within the sacred precinct].
Those of high station enjoy double the abundance of refined offerings, while monks, being at the lower end of the stream, receive what is meager according to circumstances.

On the day of the vegetarian feast, one should likewise be careful to guard the three karmas; one must not drink alcohol or eat meat. If one can act in this manner, the merit and virtue will be immeasurable.
A Verse on Baizhang’s Rules and Regulations:
According to the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang, since the Chan school originated at Shaoshi and continued down to Caoxi, practitioners had mostly resided in Vinaya monasteries.
Although they maintained separate quarters, their methods of preaching the Dharma and maintaining the community did not accord with proper standards. Therefore, [Baizhang] constantly...
Feeling deeply concerned, he said: "The Way of our ancestors was intended to be propagated widely so that it might endure forever in the future;
how could it possibly follow along with the various *āgama* teachings (the old term for *āgama*, the new term is *āgama*, which refers to the Hīnayāna teachings)?
Someone asked: 'Why do you not rely upon the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, or the Mahāyāna precepts? The Master replied:"
What I venerate is neither confined to the Mahāyāna nor the Hīnayāna, nor is it distinct from them.

One should synthesize the broad and the concise to find the middle way, establishing rules and regulations while ensuring they are appropriate to the occasion. Thereupon, he conceived this idea and established a separate meditation retreat.

In the past, while residing at Yul Temple, a separate cloister was established to open the gates of Chan. It was only after the Great Wisdom Chan Master’s time that the dignity of the ancestral Way became known.
Those who possess the eye of the Way and merit worthy of emulation are titled "Elders" (Changlao), just as those of high attainment and seniority are designated in the Western Regions.

"Long" refers to those such as Subhūti whom he summoned. As the master of transformation, he resided in the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters), which was like the room of Vimalakīrti and not a private sleeping chamber.
Only those whose virtue and morality flourish together can truly succeed their ancestors. Subhūti’s refined title is Vimalakīrti;

as for his family tradition, he did not establish a Buddha hall but constructed only a Dharma hall. This signifies that the Buddhas and Patriarchs personally transmitted [the teaching] to him, and that he is honored as the preeminent one of the present age.
Entering the gate, there is no Buddha hall; ascending the seat, there is only the empty hall. This is the transmission of the mind-seal;
know that this is the Dharma King’s way.

Regarding the assembly of students gathered here, there is neither more nor less, nor any distinction of high or low. All enter the Sangha Hall and are seated according to the order of their years of seniority (*kṣetra-vāra*).
Arrangement: Set out long connected beds, clothing racks, and stands for hanging monastic requisites.
Regardless of whether the disciples are few or many, or of high or low status, they enter the Sangha Hall; the requisites are placed on the racks, and broad beds are arranged around the perimeter.

When lying down, one must always rest the head askew upon the edge of the bed. Sleeping on the right side, the auspicious posture, is done merely to rest briefly after long periods of seated meditation;
it maintains all four modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Reclining with the head slightly propped against the edge of the bed, one sleeps peacefully on the right side. For a short time, one regulates the four great elements;
then, having spread out a seat, one returns to tranquil meditation.

Except for entering the room to seek instruction, this may be practiced according to the diligence or laxity of the practitioner—whether at the beginning or the end of the day—and is not restricted by fixed rules.

Entering the room to inquire into the profound principle, and drawing back one’s robes to request instruction—let them be diligent or indolent as they may, there is no fixed protocol for such matters.
The entire assembly of the monastery gathers at dawn and dusk; when the Elder ascends the hall and takes his seat, the administrators and disciples stand in formation like geese.

Standing to the side and listening intently, when the guest and host engage in questions and responses to clarify and exalt the essential tenets, it demonstrates abiding in accordance with the Dharma.

At evening assemblies and morning audiences, whenever the master and disciples gather, one must stand in a "wild goose" formation upon entering the hall and listen with ears pricked for the profound mysteries.
The morning and evening meals should be prepared as appropriate, with equal portions at both times; this frugality symbolizes the simultaneous practice of the Dharma and food.
The practice of *fǔqǐng* (universal labor) ensures that those above and below contribute equally their strength.

Ten administrative duties are established, termed "lodges" (*liáoshè*), each managed by one leader who oversees many workers, ensuring that everyone attends to their respective stations. (The one in charge of rice serves as the Head of Rice; the one in charge of vegetables serves as the Head of Vegetables; all others likewise.)
(Act accordingly).

One should practice the dual cultivation of Dharma-food and material food; whether the food is fine or coarse, it must be passed over at the proper time. In assigning tasks to various sections, the general labor (fusō) should be valued for its even distribution.

Should there be those who assume false names or steal the outward appearance [of a monk] to mingle among the pure assembly, causing various disturbances, the Hall Attendant (Tangsi) and the Rector (Weina) shall investigate and expose them.
They shall be removed from their assigned seats, their registration cancelled, and expelled from the monastery, so as to ensure the peace and stability of the pure assembly.
If one does not believe in the True Buddha but comes as a false bhikṣu, he shall be expelled from the community immediately; do not look back.
Should he commit any offense, the assembly must gather to strike him with a staff, burn his ritual implements, and drive him out through the side gate.
Those who exit through a side gate are shown disgrace.
For one who has committed a grave offense and burned his robes and bowl, one should assemble the multitude; with a mountain cane used merely to show shame, he shall be expelled through a side gate.
A detailed examination of these regulations reveals four kinds of benefit. First, it prevents those who defile the pure assembly from undermining the faithful devotion of others;

since their three karmas are unwholesome and they cannot dwell together with the community, according to the Vinaya they should be disciplined through the Brahma-maṇḍala rite and expelled from the monastery.

Once the pure assembly is settled in peace, respectful faith will arise. Second, it ensures that the outward form of a monk is not destroyed, thereby complying with the Buddha’s precepts; thus, appropriate punishments may be meted out as the situation requires.

1. Retaining the Dharma robes: later, one will surely regret this. 2. Not disturbing the public offices: this is for the sake of reducing litigation and lawsuits. 3. Not leaking [secrets] to the outside: this is for the sake of protecting the fundamental tenets and principles. 4.
When those from afar come to dwell together, who can distinguish the ordinary from the sage? Furthermore, even when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, there was still the faction of the Six Groups;
how much more so now in this age of semblance—how could they be entirely absent? Previously, I saw a certain class of people who, upon seeing a single monk...

Whenever a fault occurs, people immediately join in derision and mockery; yet they fail to realize that by thus slighting the assembly and treating the Dharma with contempt, the harm is exceedingly great.

Now, if the Chan school is free from such obstacles, it would be appropriate to follow the regulations of Baizhang’s monastic community (*senglin*) and allocate duties according to the needs of the situation.
Although establishing rules to prevent misconduct is not itself the mark of a truly worthy person, it is better to have the rules and no violations than to have violations.
Yet there was no formal instruction. To deliberate upon Master Baizhang’s benefit in protecting the Dharma, it was truly great.
