What benefit would there be in banishing and expelling [the monks]? By practicing meditation in peace without disparaging the Sangha, the public offices will have no lawsuits, and the reputation of the patriarchal seat will spread as a glorious sound.
The distinct practice of the Chan school originated with Baizhang. I shall briefly set forth its essential points for the universal instruction of future generations;

it is the hope of scholars that they will not forget their foundation. These thirty articles, which have been universally observed by all quarters since antiquity and which address urgent matters of communal affairs and the essentials for remedying defects, are presented here for those to come.
It is vital that you receive them with detailed attention, maintain them with firm resolve, and perpetuate them forever.
This serves as a model of conduct, ensuring that unsightly deeds and defiled reputations do not spread beyond our ears.

It is not only a source of flourishing glory for the monastic community in this degenerate age, but also one aspect of the protection of the Dharma. The specific matters, names, and numbers are itemized as follows:
Baizhang preserved the fundamental principles; the various quarters weighed the ancient and the modern. Throughout the thirty matters from beginning to end, each one protected the monastic community.

In the Hall of the Abbot, all monks who have registered for residency must be assigned their places according to the sequence of their precept ordination age (*śīla-varṣa*) based on the Six Recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). Or...
If the chief administrators (*jishi*) and those who have turned others toward the path through their guidance are to be moved, they may only be shifted up three or five ranks.
If their seating order has already been high for some time, they must not be moved further. Alternatively, the stewards (*jianshou*) and minor heads (*xiaotou-shou*) need not be moved or altered.

Or, if there are monks from various regions or those who assist the monastery and possess great virtue and reputation, once they have completed their initial registration (*guadaba*), they should subsequently inform the abbot (*zhuchi*) of their desire for a higher rank.
The low and the high shift according to the occasion;

when assigning monks to their positions, the order of seniority by precepts (kaṣāya) is followed. While the administrative duties may be adjusted slightly, the various minor heads of departments should remain as they were before.
Those who assist and support the monastic community are those whose fame is great and whose virtue is lofty.
Upon arrival, first register for lodging; then report to the Abbot and perform one round of the hall during the morning session.
You must enter the hall according to the order of your registration. When the evening session and the hall circuit are concluded, each person shall return to their own quarters.
After performing a formal greeting (*wenshen*), they may then come to unfold their bedding.

If you encounter chanting during the evening *zan*, you must temporarily return to your quarters. After exchanging greetings and finishing with the hot tonic (*tang*), return and spread out your bedding anew.
For the first three days after arriving, you should wait in the hall for the tea and tonic services; you may not yet return to your quarters.
After the morning gruel, when you lie down to rest, you must rise early so as not to disturb the quiet assembly by seeking out others in the hall to ask questions or borrow items.
Within the first three days of arrival, attend the tea and soup service; after the gruel, it is appropriate to rise first.

During the midday meal, tea is specially served for those who have newly arrived at the mountain gate while they are still in the hall; this rite is of the utmost importance. In all matters of serving and receiving the cups and vessels, one must be scrupulously reverent and careful.
One must bow respectfully to both superiors and subordinates, never acting with negligence or disrespect that would cause a loss of ritual propriety.
The Mountain Gate is as if specially established; the intent of the ritual is as weighty as the mountain itself. Attend according to the proper seasons;
let not body or mind be negligent.

A single request for leave to travel the mountains may last no more than half a month. Should one exceed this limit, they must submit a report to the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu) and return to abide by the Hall regulations once again.
If one violates these protocols, they shall be subject to the disciplinary measures of the monastery.

For those who request leave to travel to the mountains, they must return within the period of half a month; if this time has elapsed, they must re-register for residency and resume the hall duties as before.
After newly arriving and being assigned a lodging, if you wish to depart on a journey, you must wait until the fifteen-day period of the hall rituals is complete;
furthermore, you must notify the Hall Office before you may leave, so as to ensure that your bedding register is cleared.
The Hall Protocol: Every half-month, one must report to the Hall Superintendent upon rising from the hall. It is most important to clear one's bedding register;
thus, when departing now, one does not hesitate.
Upon encountering the opening of a Dharma assembly for the Imperial Birthday, or if one wishes to rise and depart for a period of wandering travel, one must first ascend to the main hall once.
One must first attend the scripture recitation before departing; do not presume upon your own ease.
A guest beneath the field-of-merit robe has been exempt from taxes and corvée since ancient times. It is not because of prayers for blessings that one encounters such a sagely dynasty;
when the forest monasteries meet the auspicious festival of the Emperor’s birthday, they take turns in advance to attend the scripture recitation.
Only after the task is completed may one depart; in repaying kindness, do not treat it lightly.
During the two daily meals of rice and congee, one must sit according to the order of the monastic register (*guàtá*). One must not bypass those of higher rank.

Furthermore, one must wait for the long wooden board to sound before setting down the alms bowl. While eating, one must not make noise by scraping the bowl with spoons or chopsticks, thereby disturbing the stillness.
If ghosts and spirits perceive thoughts of hunger and thirst, their retribution will be immeasurable; one must therefore be exceedingly humble and discreet.

When circulating through the hall, follow the order of seniority as established by one's formal registration. The same applies to the distribution of congee and rice. Even the francolin partridge, the eagle, the macaque, and the elephant can recognize the rules of propriety;
thus, when placing the alms bowl, do so according to the proper timing and protocol, arranging it so that it rests upon the shoulder.
After the long wooden board at the third watch [of the night] and before the midday meal, when eating porridge or rice, one should eat slowly and quietly so as not to let the bowl make a sound;
otherwise, ghosts and spirits will suffer distress, and the harm to oneself will not be slight.
Once you have been assigned to a residence, your bedding and robes must always be kept neat and orderly. You must not arbitrarily use a single mat that does not belong to you.

When moving a stool or spreading out bedding, one must act with extreme care and gentleness. Furthermore, one must not stand upon the bed to drag or fold bedding and garments, nor should one mount the bed from behind.
Regarding one’s own bedding and robes, one must always keep them orderly. When others have laid out their covers, do not move them without permission.
When wishing to ascend the long couch, one should always face the Sacred Monk; when spreading the mat, the mind should be attentive.
When opening the cover, the hands should be light. If one hears the signal for the end of silence in the latter part of the night:
When folding bedding for sleep, do not stand upon the bed; such conduct is a grave violation of ritual propriety.
Once lying down, one must not push the *kāṣāya* robe onto the headboard or the shrine of the Holy Monk (*śāstṛ-piṭaka*).
It should instead be folded with a clean cloth as a liner and placed before the pillow. Next, place the upper garment (*uṣṇīṣa*) and other robes there.
The Buddha ordained that one must remain separated from one's robes while sleeping; arrange them before the pillow.
Whether on the headboard or the desk, avoid the suspicion of treading upon a melon field. Do not sleep with your skirt or shirt unfastened; within the hall, avoid wearing only a single garment.
The sages of old ordered the loosening of the belt; this is provisionally permitted for beginners.
Before the morning gruel and after the evening *can* (the end of the session), one must not open the chests or cabinets.

Furthermore, within the hall, one must not huddle together to converse, nor sit leaning against the wooden headboards. If one goes outside the three gates to stroll or warms oneself by the brazier, one must not speak or laugh loudly, nor poke at the fire.
When encountering the lowering of the curtains or screens, one must wait for the bell to ring. One must...
Ensure everything is perfectly orderly. When the evening session ends, lower the curtains; when the bell tolls, each person shall draw their blinds. Open the chests and cabinets early;
you should know how to avoid causing public suspicion. Be diligent in seated meditation beneath the hall; do not wander idly about the monastery grounds.
First, one should strictly observe these prohibitions: keep your entire body leaning against the edge of the wooden board. While walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), one must remain silent;
how much more so when sitting by the hearth! Do not poke the fire or engage in idle chatter.

Knowing that your conduct is coarse, you must rise before the first watch of the night or the striking of the board-bell. When entering or leaving, you must absolutely lower your voice and lift the curtain quietly.

One may wear slippers while moving about. At the place for washing the face, one must not make loud noises by sneezing, spitting, or striking the buckets and ladles, thereby disturbing the pure assembly.

Sneezing, spitting, and dragging one's sandals are things that the pure assembly will surely find detestable during the quiet night; therefore, lift the buckets and ladles with light and careful hands.
Gently draw back the door curtains and hang up the signboard;
officials must arrive together to receive them. Ensure that everything is orderly and dignified. This is the heart of providing external protection for the student-monk.

When noble officials visit a Buddhist monastery, their coming and going should always be conducted with solemn propriety within the Zen grove. Their conduct and movements ought to be perfectly regulated.
To give rise to the mind of external protection:
at all places where communal labor (*fǔqǐng*) is required, one must wear the five-strip robe (*wùtiáo yī*) and the entire community must go together.
With the exception of the head of the quarters (*liáozhǔ*), once at the place of communal labor, one must not gather in groups to converse.
When the entire community is called for communal labor (*fushō*), the *shōryō* (cell master) shall wear the five-strip robe (*gōjō*). During this work, one must remain silent;
clamor and noise are not permitted.
Regarding those appointed as *shōryō* for the various quarters: they must serve their term in rotation according to the order of seniority, holding office for a period of one month.
It is essential that ranks, both high and low, be equal and orderly, with each person serving the other so as not to fall into confusion and avoid groundless criticism.
If one is appointed as the head of the quarters, it must be according to the order of seniority; this is not merely to avoid slander, but is what is truly valued in achieving uniformity and harmony.
In the hall of a single Buddha statue, one may only burn incense and pay reverent homage. One must not lean against the railings or gather together to speak and laugh.
Furthermore, when wearing informal robes, one must not enter the hall; this is to avoid inadvertently touching the sacred images with disrespect.
In the halls and pagodas where one practices ascetic refinement, dragon spirits provide secret protection;
to lean against the balustrades and engage in idle chatter and laughter will undoubtedly diminish one’s merit. According to the *Anantamukha-sādhaka* Sūtra, regarding the robes used for work:
if they pass by a venerable hall, one’s reverence and worship will surely be impaired.
In all dormitories, only the dormitory master and one senior monk (upādhyāya) from within the dormitory are permitted to sleep inside.
This does not apply when the Hall Office requests someone to sleep there.
In the quarters for attendants, only the Head Seat (shouzuo) is permitted; beyond this, the Hall Attendant (tingtangsi) and the assembly are allowed.
For idle persons, it is entirely unsuitable to enter these areas.
If one loses clothing or other items within the hall or the quarters, one must provide a detailed account of the items' color, quantity, time, and location.

Report what has been heard to the Head Administrator. Verify whether it is true or false, and whether it is substantial according to reason. If the matter is grave, report it to the Hall Administration to assemble the community for a search of the hall and the quarters.
Punish the offender publicly; if the accuser is found to be lying, they shall be expelled from the assembly.
If one loses something among the assembly, the items must be clearly distinguished. If the object is of great value, it must be thoroughly searched for;
if the matter is minor, it may be evaluated accordingly.
When the drum sounds at the time for bathing, one must arrive early; to be late would be an obstacle. First, the practitioner shall wash.
At the second signal of the gong, the assembly of monks enters the bathhouse. At the third signal of the gong, the masters and officials of the mountain gate bathe;

at the signal for the cessation of activity, the practitioners bathe. Ensure that these groups do not become intermingled. Inside the bathhouse, one must use a bathing towel to cover the body, each person avoiding the gaze of others.
When the monks of both halls bathe, the attendants shall arrive at the third watch. Upon hearing the signal drum, the lay assistants (karmadāna) shall proceed in order without confusion.
If the bathing takes too long, it hinders the pure assembly; if one arrives late, it obstructs the lay assistants.
One’s lower robe and upper garment must cover the body, and speech or laughter must not be excessive.
First, in all the quarters, one must not read or recite scriptures aloud, nor engage in miscellaneous secular writings.

One’s own station for Chan practice and instructional texts must always be kept covered and orderly. Whether sewing, shaving the head, cutting paper, compounding medicines, drying shoes, or handling robes and bathing implements, these activities must all be conducted in secluded areas behind the buildings.
Furthermore, they must be cleared away at appropriate times to avoid leaving things in a state of disorder.
When occupying the quarters of others, one’s desk and furnishings should be kept simple and elegant; one should always maintain a quiet dignity.

Be cautious in speech as if remaining silent, and dwell among the multitude as if living in the mountains. When threading needles or compounding medicines, when cutting paper or shaving the head—treat these tasks with the same gravity.
Laboring tasks disturb the quiet assembly; they are entirely unsuitable within the quarters.
Drying shoes, placing bathing implements, or even touching robes—these should all be done in a secluded spot behind the quarters. When putting things away, one must be careful and thorough.

Furthermore, if within the noble assembly there are those who steal, indulge in wine or women, engage in strife, defile the community with noise and disorder, or violate the rules of discipline, [they must be dealt with].
In all such matters, assemble the community and expel the offender from the monastery. Should they not comply, report it to the authorities.
Stealing property, engaging in mutual strife, indulging in wine and women—these corrupt the ranks of the Sangha. Expel them swiftly from the pure assembly;
to tolerate their presence is to destroy the community.
First, if the head monk or others feel unwell, they may simply rest in their quarters for three days if the condition is slight;
however, if the illness is serious, they must inform the *vina* (karmadāna) and move to the Longevity Hall (*yanshou liao*).

If one falls ill for three days, one must return to the Yan-shou Hall (Longevity Hall). Those who hold administrative posts within the monastic community (*sōrin*) should not feel despondent upon reaching this point; rather, they should perform their duties alongside the general assembly.

Within the hall, if the pure assembly (*qingzhong*) is insufficient, the head of the community shall manage the affairs of the mountain gate, while simply following the assembly in their daily labors and meals.
Aside from attending the morning and evening meals, you should each examine yourself, maintain your respective duties, accumulate merit, and promote the Way to bring glory to the monastic community.
You must not interfere in the affairs of the monastery beyond your station, nor arbitrarily alter regulations or stir up trouble to fan the flames of dispute.
Do not disturb the pure assembly and fail to maintain tranquility; those who violate this shall be dealt with according to the monastery’s regulations.
A guest beneath the three rafters / May find peace by realizing his own nature. / Fortunately there are monastics to attend to affairs;
/ Why must you force yourself to emerge?
/ When sitting within the hall, one must not lean against the front of the platform. One must adjust one’s robes, sit toward the back, and remain steady. Depart.
The edge of the seat shall be five inches wide; it must not be uneven, so as to inspire a sense of reverence and careful observation.

One must never sit upon the edge of the seat. Garments should hang straight down; one should leave sufficient space on the ground for the placement of the bowl, ensuring that the front and back are not uneven.
First, when escorting a deceased monk, one must not speak, laugh, or engage in music; rather, one should maintain a sense of sorrowful remembrance.

Fearing that his path of practice was not yet clarified and that he may have lived in vain and died in obscurity, each person should reflect upon themselves. Furthermore, at the time of auctioning the deceased’s belongings, the purpose is originally to create karmic affinity with the pure assembly to collectively break through stinginess and greed.
One must by no means conduct a frivolous auction or sell items at high prices to strip away the remaining value; this is not for the sake of the ten directions [of the Sangha].

Regarding the collection of funds for the distribution of robes (*cīvara-vikraya*): after deducting the expenses for administrative duties, the remainder shall be distributed equally among the pure assembly (*śuddhasaṃgha*) for the purpose of reading scriptures.

Those who arrive temporarily to witness or participate in the distribution of robes shall receive one-third of the total. The same principle applies to funds from donors intended for the reading of scriptures.
In sending off the deceased, one should appropriately pursue the path of grief; Guard against the fact that your Way has not yet been perfected.
Any remaining wealth should be distributed outside the funeral procession for the purpose of sponsoring sutra recitations, To break the karma of stinginess and greed.

If a monk dies and one must chant the *kāṣāya* (robe) inventory to seek worldly profit, This is not the way of one who has left the home life; It is merely seeing the goods of a deceased monk as commodities to be appraised.
One-third is received as one part; reading the scriptures is like arriving late. The distribution of benefits is discussed in the same manner.
Regarding the head seat (śrāmaṇera), for all morning and evening sessions in the hall, as well as the early morning assembly and the two times for meals and gruel, one must arrive first at the hall.
If there are matters among the holy assembly that are irregular or inappropriate, when the great assembly has gathered before the gruel, one must announce them and offer exhortations.
Exert yourselves! It is essential to maintain order.
Let the Head Seat serve as the standard. At dawn and at evening, all shall sit together in the hall. Arriving first for the morning assembly and for the rice gruel and meal is the norm.
Should you wish to report matters within the hall, do so when the assembly has gathered at the hour of the Tiger (7–9 a.m.).
If a single word accords with the truth, what need is there for prolixity?

Once you understand the duties and offices of your station, you must act with supreme impartiality when facing affairs. Each person shall uphold the laws and regulations and strive to support the monastic community.

As for internal and external matters that have not yet been fully understood, they must be deliberated upon through consultation between superiors and subordinates, and discussed during morning and evening assemblies.
Whenever the community is mobilized for urgent tasks, all must assemble together; the priority is to lead the group.

Generally, if a worker commits a transgression while on duty, they shall simply be summoned into the library or hall during the evening assembly to be reprimanded and exhorted. Furthermore, when official guests are present for the midday or morning meals, no one may be dispatched on errands at those two times, lest it disturb the minds of the assembly.
One should thoroughly understand one’s duties; maintain integrity and purity with full responsibility.

With a sincere heart, expand the benefit for the great assembly and exert one's strength to support the monastic community. When difficulties or doubts arise in affairs, deliberate together without discordant hearts;
let your harmony be like water and milk. By grasping the earth, you can transform it into gold; in the storehouse and hall, punish those who are guilty.
It must be during the evening *zhan* (late-night assembly) that the rice porridge and the visiting officials arrive; upon hearing this, one will surely knit their brows.

The head administrators (*zhushou*) divide the duties among various offices. Each office holds charge of the great and small affairs of the mountain gate, each having its own long-established regulations and articles.
One should attend to the duties of one's own office to accomplish the work; one must not create disturbances outside of one's jurisdiction, for the goal is to maintain peace and stability.
Be tranquil; do not allow disorder to reach the point of violating the monastic order.
When the monasteries divide their leadership, each must have its own designated authority. Guarding one’s own station involves no affairs;
encroaching upon authority is what violates the monastic order.

Once every five days there is a morning service; on the third and eighth days of each month, there is an evening service. These are performed for the sake of the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence, following the standard of six times per month.
When the chanting coincides with the third and eighth days, or the fifth day of ascending the hall, one should follow the noble examples established by the sages of old.
In future generations, let there be no mutual discord.
Every abbot, upon the first day of each month, must inspect the quarters to ensure the well-being of the pure assembly.

He should inquire whether there are any deficiencies regarding daily necessities within the quarters and provide for them immediately. Whenever the two daily meals of rice and congee are served, the abbot shall attend.

The Hall. When the two sets of drums sound and the bell in front of the hall rings, one enters the hall; if the sounds cease before entry, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) must immediately raise the matter for inspection.
Whether it be a communal work request involving the assembly, or the escorting of a deceased monk and the auctioning of his belongings, one must personally attend in all such instances.
If these rules are violated, they shall be investigated and reported. Furthermore, there must be no visiting guests and no illness; one must attend the hall.
It is not permitted to separately prepare congee or food. The administrative officers of the mountain gate (the monastery) shall all follow this same standard.
The Ancient Custom of Inspecting the Quarters: To ensure the safety and well-being of all bhikṣus, One should inquire whether anything is needed and provide assistance without delay.
At the two assemblies, when the drum sounds before the kitchen, Do not arrive too late;
when the bell rings before the hall, That is precisely the time to enter the hall for the distribution of robes and the communal work (pūjā).
When sending off a deceased monk with rice gruel and food, the abbot should personally attend first; for matters in the monastic community are not trivial.

The abbot and the administrative officers must ensure that the serving of gruel and food does not deviate from the regular routine; unless one is ill or has official guests, everyone should attend the hall.
The preceding regulations are the models established by the former masters. The pure assemblies of the ten directions should each observe and practice them accordingly.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Shanxiang of Yue Province, together with the Bhikṣu Faguī of Wenzhou, who performed the collation.

Newly Added: The Method for Filtering Water (with Verse).
Among the eighteen items in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, the water filter bag is the ninth; it should always accompany one’s person, just as a bird [carries its wings].
Two Wings. The verse says:
When practicing *dhūta*, observing the summer retreat, or traveling abroad, the water-strainer must never be parted from;
it is just like a bird born with two wings, flying together toward the east, west, south, or north.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "The bodies of animals are minute, as small as one-tenth of a mote of dust; yet the largest may reach a million *yojanas*.
Therefore, one should know that filtering water is an act of great compassion and a cause for attaining Buddhahood. The verse says:
"Take one from ten thousand tiny insects; In the teachings, this is used as a metaphor for water-insects.
Diligently filter water and preserve compassion to save them; This is precisely the cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future.
The *Bodhisattva-bahudhātuka-śāstra* states: "Śāriputra, with his pure divine eye, saw insects within the water and in the air, just like [the water itself]."

In the vessels along the riverbanks, there was no place where grain did not exist; consequently, he ceased eating. The Buddha said: "That which is seen by the fleshly eye and that which is caught by the strainer.
The *Ransheng yi* (Rite for Releasing Living Beings) by Tripitaka Master Yijing states: "Those who strain their food and water shall be reborn in the Pure Land in a future life. The verse says:
Grain in a vessel, sand by the water’s edge—the quantity of empty space, water, and subtle dust does not differ.
If one can follow the holy regulations for filtering water, the joy of the precious lotus and golden ground will be boundless.
In the *Vinaya*, it is said that two bhikṣus wished to go to where the Buddha was; one did not drink water containing insects and died of thirst.
He was reborn in heaven; there he beheld the Buddha and attained the Way.
The verse says: A bhikṣu came to see the King of the Dharma; He forgot to bring his water-strainer along.
Better to die than violate the precept against harming insects in water; In a single kṣaṇa, he realized the Way, clarifying the eternal truth.
A certain bhikṣu, after drinking water, went to where the Buddha was. The Buddha asked him the reason for his coming. [The bhikṣu replied: "I have already removed my *uttarāsaṅga* robe;

the Saṃgha has revealed their golden bodies. [The Buddha said: "You foolish man! Why do you gaze upon these bodies composed of the four great elements as being youthful or as places that will eventually become foul?
One who sees the Dharma sees my body. The verse says:
Drinking water harms insects; one's conduct is lax. Pitiable are those companions who travel different paths.
Though they have reached the assembly at Jetavana, They see only the sixteen-foot golden body.

Master Xuan said: "Although the water-strainer and its accessories are small and light, their purpose is extremely great. For those who have left the household life, compassionately aiding others is their duty."
This is the point. Now, even those of superior grade and lofty conduct still drink water containing insects; how much more so for those who are unworthy?
How could this not be spoken of? The Verse says:
Though the water-strainer is a small matter, it is no light task; It is the true and genuine compassion that protects sentient beings.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has clearly issued this injunction: "Why do those who follow the *ūrdhvasrotas* (the upward-streaming) not comply?
In the *Yijing’s Sanzang Jiguai Zhuan*, it says: "In the Western Regions, they use fine white cotton cloth (*dukūla*).

For winter and summer, one should use fine silk, or perhaps press it with rice, or lightly boil it. Furthermore, in the sixth and seventh months, the insects therein are even finer than those in other seasons."

At that time, even through ten layers of raw silk, the insects would pass straight through. Those who delight in protecting living beings should, as a matter of principle, reflect on this and take fine, closely woven cloth to make bags;
only by filtering with these will they be completely removed. The verse says:
A fine cotton cloth is used to make a bag one cubit (*hasta*) in length; this is the ancient tradition of the Western Heavens for filtering water.
In this land, finely woven silk is appropriate according to the rules; thin, coarse, or raw silk is entirely unsuitable.
The *Jiguī zhuan* (Account of Items Sent Back) states: "One may take four feet of well-dyed silk according to the *hù* cubit measure, fold both ends together, and stitch them so they adhere."
The two corners are provided with straps and horizontal poles on both sides; it is spread out to a length of one chi and six cun and fastened to pillars at both ends.
A basin is placed beneath to receive [the water]. When pouring, the bottom of the jar must enter the strainer. Once the water is sufficient, the strainer may be turned over.
Two people each grasp one end and place it inside the vessel for releasing living beings. It is then washed three times with water, and the exterior is further rinsed with water.
Only when one has crossed over the area free of insects may one stop. The verse says:
The pattern of the two sides must be made spacious; Gather and fold the seams to tie them within the pillar.
The water-drawing vessel must pour from its very bottom; When overturning it, the cleansing requires full effort.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "One should make a water-strainer shaped like a ladle, or triangular, or like a large coffin, or like a filtering flask.
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* says: "In places with rivers or ponds, one may install a ringed strainer or use a 'yin-yang' flask to provide temporary relief for practical needs.
Alternatively, making a small earthenware basin with a cloth filter is also economical and essential. In Western monasteries, most are made of copper."
The Verse says:

A *la-yang* or a wooden bowl, or perhaps a jar; Whether it be a triangular ladle, a spoon-shaped vessel, A copper basin, a clay pot, or even a large coffin— Any may be used according to circumstances, wherever one happens to be.
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "When pouring water, the bottom of the vessel must enter the strainer.
If it is not done so, the water will fall to the ground or drop into the basin, and one still cannot avoid the act of killing. A verse says:
The novice monk filtering the water pours it out slowly; The tiny creatures, bewildered and distressed, evoke a heart of compassion.
If even a single drop were left outside the strainer, One would still incur the sin of killing as before. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Now, one who is thorough in observing the precepts, having finished filtering the water, places it in a clean vessel and holds it up toward the sun."
The group looked together. Therefore, those who had [already filtered] water should filter it again as before.
The verse says: "Once filtered, one must observe it closely; If there are insects, filter again and look again.
Only when it is completely pure may one act according to one's will; To use it now is difficult for those who have faith."
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: Once dawn has broken, one should first examine the water in the flask.

One may take a handful of water into a clean copper cup, a conch shell, or a lacquered vessel, and place it upright upon a brick; alternatively, one may prepare a separate vessel specifically for observing the water.
Covering his mouth with his hand, he gazes at it for a long while, or examines it within a basin; even if he finds a worm as small as the tip of a hair, he must maintain mindfulness.
If he sees a worm, he pours the water back into the bottle and rinses the vessel two or three more times with fresh water.
Only when no insects are seen does one cease [using the water]. The verse says:
Copper bowls, conch cups, and lacquerware are all permitted; At midday, observe the water to test for minute insects.
One must wash and cleanse them with skillful means, Only then fulfilling the merit of the Vinaya in saving living beings.

The Tripitaka Master Yijing composed the *Ritual for Saving Life and Releasing Creatures*. He explains the vessels for releasing creatures in great detail. These vessels are made of copper, iron, ceramic, or wood;
the bottom is fitted with a fine mesh and suspended by two ropes. Once lowered into the water, one pulls the ropes to turn the vessel upside down.

After submerging it two or three times to rinse it thoroughly, one then draws it out. Furthermore, during the time of begging for alms, one carries a small copper bottle suspended from the left [arm].

[He] covered his arm with his robe. Vinaya Master Xuán stated: "To harm living beings and obstruct the Path is due to not keeping a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*), or keeping one but not using it, or using it but not straining out insects, or pouring [water) out while harming the lives of insects.
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Sea) says:

To turn the strainer upside down over the mouth of the jar is not yet to understand the vessel for releasing living beings. Even if it reaches the water, how can one doubt that the insects will die? The Verse says:
Place a pair of fine [strainers] beneath the release-vessel; Upon reaching the water, pull the rope and the force will naturally turn it.
To die of thirst within a water-strainer is truly a transgression; to overturn the strainer upon a well is likewise groundless.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Once the water has been filtered, place it in a vessel and return it to its original source to pour it out.
If the original source is distant, and there is a nearby pond where the water does not evaporate for seven days, place the insects therein. The Tripitaka Master Yijing says: "If..."
If the well is deep, one may set aside a separate basin to hold the water, or transport it to a river or pond. Once the water has been poured out, one must rinse and filter the vessel.
In Master Dao’s *Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts*, it states: "Once the water has been filtered, set aside a separate 'fish-release' basin."
One should place it calmly into the water to protect living beings. The verse says:
If the well is distant and the spring deep, and one grows weary of the trouble, To protect life, one should use a release basin;
Calmly pour the water toward a flowing stream, And wait until it has entered the pool before it may be considered complete.

The *Sāṃsiddhika-śāstra* states: "Filter water according to the Dharma and place it in a vessel sufficient for one day's use. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states:
"Regarding any water that has been kept overnight and has not been inspected, whether it contains insects or not, using it will incur an offense."
The verse says:
One must filter water and maintain the vow throughout the day; Fearing that it might become contaminated again, one filters it once more at dawn.
Reflecting that during the nine months of summer there are many ants, One should always observe the ground while walking, lifting one's feet with mindfulness.

The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: At times, there are those who fashion small circular strainers barely large enough to hold one *sheng* or two *he*. Made of coarse, thin silk, they do not examine them for insects at all;
they merely hang them by the side of their bowls so that others may see them. Having no intention to protect life, they incur transgressions every day.
That master and disciple have transmitted this to one another as the vehicle for the Dharma is truly lamentable. The verse says:
The Sage has long been gone and the observance of the Vinaya has declined; The small sieve and coarse silk evoke a sense of sorrow.
Hanging by the side of the bowl, it is seen by others; Suspended above the hall, it serves as a ceremonial rite.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) on the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* by Master Fa’o states: "Nowadays, I observe that in monasteries they constantly use coarse cloth [for ritual implements], which is extremely inconsistent with the proper form. The verse says:
Coarse cloth sewn into a sieve placed atop a cauldron; within a mere instant, tiny insects and fragile lives are consumed.
The boiling water in the cauldrons is not naturally hot; it is the principle of retribution within the gateway of cause and effect.
Tripitaka Master Yijing said: "In the land of China, there are over four hundred cities, and those who have left the household life number in the tens of thousands."
Generally, those who maintain mindfulness regarding the matter of filtering water are few. A verse says:
In more than four hundred cities of the Divine Land, There are many monks renowned for their perfect conduct and virtue;
Those who leap into fire or fall from cliffs are easy to find, But those who filter for insects and observe the water are difficult to encounter.

The Tripitaka Master Yijing said: "Even if one’s learning penetrates the Three Piṭakas, sits in meditation to realize the four dhyānas, constantly contemplates non-arising, and realizes the principle of the emptiness of mind—if one does not protect life and uphold the teachings according to the instructions, one will ultimately not escape the Buddha’s reproach.
Who can take upon themselves the retribution for the first of the ten evil deeds? The verse says:
Wondrously entering the three emptinesses to discourse on Prajñā, The merit perfected through the eight dhyānas to realize the stages of meditation.
If one does not maintain compassionate vows regarding water filtration, One cannot escape being rebuked by the Tathāgata in the same manner.

The *Jiguichuan* (Record of Returning to the Source) says: "If you know that a monastery does not filter its water, it is improper to consume food there; dying of thirst upon the long journey would surely suffice as [retribution]."
A Mirror for Reflection. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a donor invites a bhikṣu to a meal, he should ask whether the water has been filtered.
If it has not been filtered, he himself should filter it. The verse says:
The temple shall not filter the water used in the kitchen; monks have traditionally been forbidden from eating such food.
When there is a vegetarian feast at a lay residence, one should inquire about it; when filtering, one must personally oversee the process.
Among the ten grave precepts in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, the precept against killing ranks first. It is said that a bodhisattva takes compassion as [the foundation].

Fundamentally, sentient beings hold life as precious. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that the ninety-first *pāyattika* is the precept against using water containing insects (the ninety-first), while the sixty-second is the precept against drinking water containing insects.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that [violating] the precept against using water with insects constitutes a *pātayantika*, each instance being treated accordingly.
Vinaya Master Xuanchao stated: "For natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), there is no formal repentance; one must ultimately provide recompense. Thus says the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing.
He said, "As for this transgression, what can be done? I know only that I am at the mercy of the gates of the underworld, leaving my fate to their disposal.

As the Sūtra says: "One who kills living beings shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; even if they should obtain human form, they will be short-lived and plagued by many illnesses. The verse says:
The precept against killing stands foremost among the ten grave prohibitions; the principle that even one insect constitutes a downfall is self-evident.
To drink or consume [water] with a coarse mind and without shame is to have one's hands bound at the gates of the underworld, dragged away by one’s karma.

Master Yijing, the Tripiṭaka Master, said: "Suppose, for instance, a butcher were to lead a sheep into a monastery; it would not take more than a few mouthfuls [of water] before being released and sent on its long journey."
As they were born, the crowd gathered to watch, snapping their fingers and praising them as virtuous. Who would have known that the water used inside the room daily kills a thousand living beings?
A verse says:
All praise the butcher for his spiritual resolve; He offers sheep to the monastery so they may live long lives.
Unaware of the daily water used within the quarters, his karma of killing was such that his offense was not light.
During the Yuanfeng era, at Liudu Monastery on Mount Tan in Wei Prefecture, Vinaya Master Ji of the Zengjie Assembly never filtered his water.
Master Taixian said: "Though it is called 'increasing the precepts,' it is actually increasing one's offenses. Who would not be alerted and awakened by these words of compassion? The verse says:

I recall the assembly for the increase of precepts at Tanshan, where Master Ji, due to his complete lack of consideration regarding the filtering of insects, was severely rebuked by Master Taixian for gathering the monastic community and thereby increasing their transgressions.
Tripitaka Master Yijing said: "All those who harbor life cherish that life; this applies upward even to the wise and virtuous. As for those who die..."
They fear death even down to the smallest insects. The Buddha, out of great compassion, proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma, showing the utmost earnestness in protecting living beings.
As a disciple of the Buddha, one ought to act accordingly. The verse says:
Whether it be an insect, it must die a miserable death; Even if one were a sage or a saint, life would likewise be preserved.
If one contemplates water for insects with this intent, why worry that the practice of compassion will not be fulfilled?

As the ancients said: "I observe a single drop of water, and within it are eighty-four thousand lives. Ordinary people do not see them with their eyes, but those with the divine eye perceive them naturally."
Clearly. The verse says:
All that stirs contains the numinous Buddha-nature; To scoop and strain again and again is spiritual practice.
Behold this ordinary handful of water— How could it not contain thousands and tens of thousands of lifetimes?
*The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*, Volume Five. When Zen Master Zhìyán had not yet left the household life, he served as a lieutenant general.
Although he was amidst the military ranks, a water-strainer was always suspended from his bow. The verse says:
In times past, when generals stood upon the battlefield, a water-strainer still hung from their bows;
to repay the noble practitioners of the Golden Field, making compassionate relief one's constant practice is the norm.
Master Ao remarked: "According to Indian regulations, whether monks are entering or leaving, or even when going on almsround, they must always carry a water-strainer."
This object has been kept with me for a long time in this region. Alas, alas! Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"It would be better to die of thirst than to drink water containing insects until death. Why is this? Because in a single instance of drinking water, one destroys immeasurable lives;

to drink insect-infested water for a single day is a sin greater than that of a butcher for a lifetime. One must especially be cautioned against this. Furthermore, the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* records the story of Śibi...
King Bimbisāra cut his own flesh to save a hawk; the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* speaks of Prince Sattva casting himself down to feed the tigers.
The verse says:
How lamentable that the water-strainer has remained unused for so long! May we, with deep reverence, exert ourselves in practice.

One would not spare even one's own head when feeding tigers or hawks; how much less should one begrudge a single robe for the sake of sentient beings? This is the parable from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding crossing the ocean on an inflatable skin bag:
it means that if one upholds the precepts with the desire to transcend birth and death, one will obtain the karmic fruit of longevity in the present life. As the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing said:
"If one can act in accordance with the teachings, one will obtain the fruit of long life in this very existence. Thus we know that a śrāmaṇera saved ants.
If even saving a few tens of thousands of lives brings about such longevity, how much more so for one who filters water and can thus protect countless sentient beings?
It is clear that since killing leads to rebirth in the three evil realms, protecting life should lead to the happy destinies of humans and devas. The verse says:
Desiring to proceed to the site of enlightenment, today this water filter is my life-raft.
It is a merit that adorns both the human and celestial realms, and it ensures long life in this world and future births.
Master Daoxuan said: "The minute insects in water are countless, equal in measure to motes of dust. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Dust..."

"Ya-chong-ya. These words are true. [This refers to] taking fine silk thread to make a bag for filtering; when ten thousand [insects] are exhausted, the purpose is fulfilled. Tripitaka Master Yijing said:

"Those who act according to these instructions shall be reborn in the Pure Land in a future life. He further stated: "In the Final Dharma Age of Śākyamuni, we together form the causes for compassionate mindfulness;
at the initial realization of Maitreya, we shall both realize the fruit of non-arising. The verse says:
In the turmoil of the dust-like insects, one can never distinguish them; Yet by diligently cultivating cause and effect, one may rescue those submerged in suffering.
At the assembly of the Dragon Flower, they receive the prediction of non-arising; Within the light of the Pure Land, they are people who do not die.
Whenever one filters water, one should vow that all insects will be reborn in the Pure Land and become Buddhas in the future—not merely for a single day.
[He] was spared from death. The verse says:
The Bodhisattva gives rise to compassion with far-reaching resolve; In filtering out living beings, he aspires to be entrusted to a lotus pedestal.
In the future, the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust in the Pure Land— All have been fished out from within the strainer.
In the lower fascicle of the *Ancient Record of Qingliang*, there is an account of a lay devotee whose family name and given name are unknown.
He was about twenty years of age and wore tattered clothing. He claimed to have come from Baofu Mountain.

Those who recognized him passed along the tradition that he frequently wandered through the markets of Bingzhou begging for alms, with which he would craft water-strainers approximately seven or eight inches in size. Having finished making them, he would encourage others wherever he went.
He was employed by people; in total, he produced more than several thousand [images]. The lay devotee’s divine countenance was simple and refined, and his discourse reached the subtlest depths;
all considered him a man of unfathomable character. The verse says:
The lay devotee Qingliang practiced compassion; he begged for silk to sew thousands of *parisrava* (water-strainers), sewing and giving them away as soon as they were requested.
He exhorted others to join him in creating the karmic conditions for life through these filters.
People said that strainers were difficult to install and that many people would not follow [the practice]. In the first year of the Chongning era, at the kitchen of Hongji Monastery—
A large water basin is installed by the well. On top of it, near the rim, a smaller basin is placed with openings pierced at the corners for water to flow out.
A filter cloth is placed beneath it. When the water is poured, there is no splashing or overflow at all, and thus the five groups of practitioners are fully provided for.

The structure behind the bathhouse is modeled after this. Monks performing ablutions at the toilet (dongsi) must likewise filter the water; this is the fundamental path of those who have left the household life. Later, [this practice was established] while residing at Changlu.
There are more than twenty locations for well-water filtration. If the permanent residents do not filter the water, the responsibility for the transgression shall fall upon the person in charge.
I hope that everyone will strive to carry this out.
